For example, when the householder Ugga made offerings to the community of monks, a deity informed him, saying:
"This one is an arhat; this one is practicing for arhatship," and so on, up to: "This one is a srotāpanna; this one is practicing for srotāpatti."

If one is within these fifteen moments of mind, it cannot be demonstrated; one should know that those who are *srotāpannas* are either near or far, and this is called "practice through faith" (*śraddhānusārin*).

As for the "practice through dharma" (*dharmānusārin*), such a person attains the wisdom of emptiness and non-self, and practices in accordance with the Dharma while abiding in the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
That is to say, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth are called the practice of dharmas; these are two types of practitioners.
Upon entering the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), because one sees the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*), it is called the practice of signlessness (*animittacaryā*).

These three kinds of persons are called those practicing for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*); however, because they have not severed the fetters within the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), they cannot be called those practicing for the [other] three fruits.
This matter shall be explained later.
Regarding the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), as stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:

if a person severs the three fetters—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—they are called a *srotāpanna*. Such a person does not fall into the evil realms, will certainly attain right knowledge, and will undergo rebirth for at most seven more existences.
Question:

If the *srotāpanna* has completely exhausted the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) and has extinguished immeasurable suffering—as stated in the *Anupada-sūtra* (The Pool Simile)—why does it say that they have only severed the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*)?
Answer: This matter shall be explained in detail later; namely, that because the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is exhausted, the remaining [afflictions] are likewise exhausted.
As for "not falling into the evil destinies," this shall also be explained in detail later in the section on the accumulation of karma.
"One who will certainly reach bodhi" means that such a person, having entered the stream of the Dharma, will certainly reach nirvana.
It is like a piece of wood in the Ganges River; provided it avoids eight adverse conditions, it will inevitably reach the great ocean.

Regarding "at most seven existences": this refers to one for whom untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) matures within seven lifetimes, just as the embryo (*kalala*) and subsequent stages develop over seven days;
or like consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*), where even a chronic illness is eliminated at the latest after seven days;
or like the ancestral lineage being limited to seven generations.
Furthermore, it is like when a seven-step snake bites a person: by the power of its four limbs, it can reach seven steps, but by the power of its venom, it cannot reach eight;
likewise, the law of deception extends at most to seven lifetimes;
and again, when seven suns appear, the kalpa is consumed by fire.
In this way, through seven lifetimes, one accumulates untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) to burn away all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, according to the Dharma, there are seven existences: there is the *srotāpanna* who enters nirvana in this very life; there is the one for whom there is a second, a third, and so on, up to the seventh existence—this is called a *srotāpanna*.

Regarding those who practice for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin): there are nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through contemplation; if one has abandoned one or two, up to three, four, five, or six, they are called one who practices for the fruit of once-returning.
Some say that it is severed by a single path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*). This is not so;
for in the Buddha’s sūtras it is said that it is severed by immeasurable minds, as stated in the *Pāṣāṇaśilā-avadāna* (The Simile of the Axe Handle).

Furthermore, one who practices as a Sakṛdāgāmin is also called a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner; such a person returns either twice or thrice before attaining parinirvāṇa in their current body. This is what is meant by one who practices as a Sakṛdāgāmin.
The Sakṛdāgāmin is one who returns once more to this world and then enters nirvāṇa.
Because the fetters to be abandoned through contemplation have been attenuated by this person, and because they abide within that state of attenuation, they are called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
Such a person is a Sakṛdāgāmin; they may enter Nirvāṇa in this very life.

As for those practicing toward the state of an Anāgāmin: if they have severed the seventh or eighth category of fetters, such persons are all called "practitioners toward Anāgāmin"; one who has severed the eighth category is called an Ekavīcika (One-Interval).
Regarding those who practice for the state of *anāgāmin* (non-returner), some may enter *nirvāṇa* in this very life.
Because they have completely abandoned the nine grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm, they are called *anāgāmins*.

There are eight distinctions among these *anāgāmins*: namely, those who attain extinction in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), those who attain extinction upon rebirth, those who attain extinction without exertion, those who attain extinction through exertion, those who ascend to extinction at the Akaniṣṭha heaven, those who reach the formless realms, those who undergo a further rebirth, and those who attain extinction in the present life. These distinctions exist according to the superior, middling, or inferior faculties of their roots.
There are also three types of those who attain extinction in the intermediate state (antarābhava): those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties.

There are Anāgāmins who deeply loathe the world; yet, due to slight obstructions, they are unable to attain extinction in the present life. Such persons attain extinction within the intermediate state.
Birth is also of three kinds: those for whom birth ceases, those for whom conditioned formations cease, and those for whom formations do not cease.

Those for whom birth ceases are those who, at the very moment of birth, feel profound revulsion and detachment toward existence and immediately enter nirvana; this is called "cessation through birth" because their faculties are sharp.

There are those who, upon being born, find all untainted paths spontaneously appearing before them; they enter nirvana without applying diligent practice—this is "extinction through non-practice," because their faculties are middling.

There are those who, having been born, feel deep dread of receiving a body and diligently practice the Path until they enter *nirvāṇa*; this is called "extinction upon walking" (*gati-nirodha*), due to dull faculties.
There are also three types of those who attain extinction upon walking: if one passes away from one place and is reborn in another before entering *nirvāṇa*, this is called "sharp faculties";
if one is reborn in two or three places, this is called "middling faculties."
To pass away from all places and be reborn in all places is called having dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*).
From the First Dhyāna up to the Bṛhatphala Heaven is called "fixed" (*niyata*).
Once one has reached Bṛhatphala, if one is reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens, that person will no longer go to the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), because they delight in wisdom (*prajñā*).

If one enters the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), such a person will ultimately not be born among the Śuddhāvāsa deities, because they delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding those who change their rebirths:

if one previously attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) or the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and later, upon changing bodies, attains the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), such a person does not enter the realms of form or the formless realms.
Regarding those who attain extinction in the present life: these are those of the foremost sharp faculties, who enter nirvana within their current existence.

Furthermore, there are two other types of persons: the first is named "liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta), and the second is named "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta); these two differ according to their respective faculties.
If a practitioner of dull faculties on the path of contemplation is called "liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta), one of sharp faculties is called "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
If an anāgāmin possesses the eight liberations, this is called "bodily realization" (kāyasākṣin).
These are all called "practitioners of arhatship" because they are alike in having severed the fetters;
however, one who has completely eradicated all afflictions is named an arhat.

There are nine types of arhats: those of the nature of falling back, those of guarding, those of dying, those of being capable of progress, those of abiding, those of non-decline, those liberated by wisdom, those liberated both ways, and those of non-retrogression.
These Arhats differ because they have attained different faculties, such as faith and the rest.

Those with the most dull faculties are said to possess the characteristic of regression; they fall away from samādhi, and because they regress from samādhi, untainted wisdom cannot manifest before them.
Regarding the "characteristic of guarding": because the faculties are slightly superior, if one guards the samādhi, one does not fall away; if one does not guard it, one falls away.
As for the aforementioned "characteristic of falling away," one falls away even while guarding it.

Regarding those with the "sign of death" (*maraṇanimitta*): their faculties are slightly superior, and they feel a profound weariness toward all forms of existence (*bhava*). Because such persons cannot attain *samādhi*, untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) is difficult to manifest; even if they should attain it, they lose it through joy, and thus they seek death.
Regarding the "stationary state" (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*): if one attains samādhi and neither progresses nor regresses, this is called the stationary state.
The first three types pertain to the samādhi of the stage of decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*), whereas the stationary state pertains to the samādhi of the stage of maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*).
Regarding the "signs of progress": if one attains samādhi that becomes increasingly deep and enhanced, this person dwells in the *vṛddhibhāgīya* (progressive) samādhi.

Regarding the "signs of non-decline": once samādhi has been attained, it cannot be destroyed by various causes and conditions; this person dwells in the *prativedhabhāgīya* (penetrative) samādhi. Because their wisdom is most sharp, they skillfully grasp the signs of entering, abiding in, and arising from samādhi, and thus it is indestructible, due to the attainment of the *nirodhasamāpatti* (attainment of cessation).

There are two types of persons: those who do not attain this concentration are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta), while those who attain this concentration are called "doubly liberated" (ubhaya-to-bhāga-vimukta).
Regarding the characteristic of non-retrogression, all the merits they have attained are entirely free from loss or decline.
As it is said in the Sūtra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If my disciples were to carry me on a palanquin, that which I have previously attained would never decline or be lost.
These nine types are called those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

The eighteen learners (*śaikṣa*) and the nine non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), these twenty-seven persons are called the field of merit for all the world; they are fully present within the Saṅgha, and for this reason, they should be venerated.
Chapter Eleven: The Field of Merit (Puṇyakṣetra) Question:
For what reason are these noble ones called a "field of merit"? Answer:

Because they have eradicated all afflictions such as greed and anger, they are called fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). As it is said: "If weeds and tares are not removed, they will harm the sprouts of the good grain. Therefore, one who gives to those free from desire obtains a great reward and benefit.
Furthermore, because the human mind is empty, it is called a "field of merit.
Why is this? Because by virtue of its characteristic of emptiness, various afflictions such as greed and anger do not arise, and evil karma is not produced.
Furthermore, because all noble ones and sages have attained the state of non-action, they are called fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Moreover, the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) attained by these individuals are entirely pure, for they are forever free from all afflictions, both great and small.
Furthermore, it is called a field of merit because it abandons both sorrow and joy;
it is called a field of merit because it can sever the five fetters of the mind, whereby the mind attains purity;
and it is so called because it accomplishes the eight kinds of fields of merit.
Furthermore, because they well protect the mind through the seven factors of concentration,
and because they can completely extinguish the seven kinds of outflows (*āsrava*), they are free from all leakage and loss. Moreover,

because they are fully endowed with the seven pure dharmas such as the precepts, and because they can accomplish the eight virtues such as few desires and contentment, and because they can cross to the other shore and diligently seek to cross over, they are called fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras:
"Even merely generating the aspiration to practice wholesome dharmas brings great benefit, let alone actual cultivation.
These noble ones (ārya) constantly practice wholesome dharmas; therefore, they are called fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:

"In whichever donor's household there is a precept-observing bhikṣu who, having received offerings, enters the immeasurable meditative concentration, that donor's household obtains immeasurable merit."

Among the assembly, there are those who have entered the immeasurable samādhi, the signless samādhi, and the immovable samādhi; because they can cause the donor to obtain immeasurable retribution, they are called fields of merit.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras:
"One obtains great merit through the conjunction of three factors: first, having faith; second, the object to be given; and third, the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Among the Saṃgha, there are many persons of great merit; within those of great merit, faith arises easily.
Furthermore, giving to the Sangha yields great fruit due to nine causes and conditions.
Moreover, when giving to the Sangha, because the recipients are pure, the gift is necessarily pure.

Furthermore, there are eight types of giving: (1) giving with little purity of mind and few objects to a person of broken precepts; (2) giving with little purity of mind and many objects to a person of broken precepts; (3) giving with little purity of mind and few objects to a person who maintains the precepts; (4) giving with little purity of mind and many objects to a person who maintains the precepts; and (5–8) the same four types apply when the purity of mind is great.
If one gives to the Sangha, one will certainly achieve two or three [of the perfections].
All virtuous persons increase their merit by means of the Sangha, and thereafter dedicate it at will toward Bodhi.
Furthermore, regarding the Sangha to whom one gives, these things shall all result in the fruit of liberation; they can never be exhausted within the cycle of birth and death.
Moreover, whatever is given to the assembly of monks serves to adorn the mind.
Furthermore, while the pure mind of faith toward a single person may sometimes be corrupted, the pure confidence within the Saṃgha can never be destroyed.
Moreover, while the heart of love and respect for a single person may not be extensive, the heart of faith and reverence born toward the Saṃgha becomes vast because its object is immeasurable.
Furthermore, when one gives to those who have entered the ranks of the Sangha, the fruit of retribution is likewise great because the mind [of the recipient] is vast.
For these reasons, the various worthy sages and saints are called "fields of merit" (puṇyakṣetra); therefore, they should be venerated.
Chapter Twelve: On Auspiciousness This chapter on auspiciousness is placed at the beginning of the sutra because it is endowed with the merit of the Three Jewels.
Furthermore, these Three Jewels are the supreme auspiciousness among all worlds, as stated in the *Maṅgalagāthā*:
"The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha—these are called the highest auspiciousness."

Furthermore, there are various sūtras that begin with auspicious words; such that the student’s lifespan increases by ten thousand years and their fame spreads far and wide—this is the intention of the compilers of those sūtras.
For instance, when characters such as "Ā" and so forth are placed at the beginning of a sūtra, this is not an auspicious sign, as shall be explained in detail later.
If one seeks that which is foremost and most auspicious, it is the Triple Gem.
One should take refuge in them, as stated in the *Maṅgalagāthā*:
"Among all gods and men, The Unsurpassed Honored Teacher..."
The Buddha is the Great Awakened One; this is called the supreme auspiciousness.
If a person, in the presence of the Buddha, establishes unwavering faith and upholds the pure precepts, this is called the supreme auspiciousness.
"To stay far away from the foolish, to associate with the wise,
and to honor those worthy of honor— this is the most auspicious. Therefore,
one should pay homage to the Triple Gem, for it is the most auspicious.
The first volume of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Establishment of Truth), as spoken at the beginning of my sutras;
the second volume of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Composed by Harivarman;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: Establishing the Treatise. Now, I wish to discuss the Buddha-dharma to benefit the world.
Because the Buddha, with a mind of great compassion, seeks to extensively benefit all the world, he teaches this Dharma without any limitation.

For instance, if someone were to preach a sūtra on liberation solely for the sake of the Brahmins, the sūtras spoken by the Buddha are intended for the deliverance of beings of the four classes, and even animals are not excluded or restricted.
Question:
One should not compose a treatise to discuss the Buddha’s words. Why is that?
If the Buddha himself were to discourse, it could be called a discourse;
if the Buddha does not discourse, others are unable to discourse. Why is this so?

The intentions of those possessed of all-knowledge are difficult to comprehend; one does not know for what purpose they speak of such matters. If one speaks recklessly without grasping the Buddha’s intention, it will result in self-injury.
As it is said in the sūtra:
"There are two kinds of people who slander the Buddha: first, those who slander out of lack of faith and malice;
second, those who, although possessing faith, cannot accept what the Buddha has taught with true understanding—these too are called slanders of the Buddha."

If even those possessing true wisdom cannot understand the Buddha’s intent and are thus unable to discourse upon what the Buddha has said, how much less can those who have not attained such wisdom attempt to compose treatises to explain the Buddha’s intent?

Why is this so? As stated in the *Vigraha-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke of these matters for the sake of "contact" (*sparśa*); yet, the various heterodox arguments of the bhikṣus and others all failed to grasp the Buddha’s intention.
Furthermore, as the Elder Mahākātyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"It is like cutting down a great tree; one discards the roots and trunk and takes only the branches and leaves.
You are just the same—having abandoned the Tathāgata, why do you question me?"
If even Mahākātyāyana compared himself to branches and leaves during his discourses, how much less could others understand the Buddha’s words?
Furthermore, the Buddha asked Śāriputra:
"What is a learner?"
What is meant by a person who adheres to mere enumeration?
They do not answer when questioned three times.
Furthermore, the Buddha is the root of all dharmas; only the Buddha can understand them, while others cannot.
Furthermore, Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"To encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) constitutes half the benefit in the attainment of the Way;
this also has its道理 (principle/reason). Why is this so?"
Right view arises through two causes and conditions: first, hearing from others; second, one's own correct mindfulness.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"A virtuous friend alone is sufficient for one to fully attain the benefit of the Path."
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"If I preach the Dharma for someone, and that person fails to grasp my intended meaning, they will give rise to disputes.

Now, these various masters of treatises each hold their own attachments; some say that dharmas exist in the past and future, while others say they do not. One should know that such masters of treatises, because they do not understand the Tathāgata’s teachings given according to what is appropriate, give rise to disputes.
Furthermore, when Ānanda explained for the sake of samādhi that all that is felt is called suffering, the Buddha then said to the bhikṣus:
"Observe how Ānanda approximates this meaning."
Furthermore, some proponents of various doctrines claimed that an Arhat ought to receive offerings first.
A bhikṣu, unaware of this, went to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"In my Dharma, those who have gone forth first should receive offerings first.
Yet they are unable to understand even coarse matters such as food and drink, let alone the subtle and wondrous Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata’s intention."
For these reasons, one should not compose a treatise.
The answer is: Not so.
Why is this so? Because there are causes and conditions by which one can know the minds of others.
As it is said in a verse:
One is able to know the direction of the speaker’s intention and also knows what matter the speaker wishes to explain.
There are two kinds of paths: the noble path and the mundane path, which shall be explained in detail later.
By means of this method, one understands the intention of the speaker.
Furthermore, in the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra*, the Buddha also permitted all [contradictory] doctrines.
Moreover, because masters of great treatises such as Kātyāyana grasped the Buddha’s intention, the Buddha praised them all as excellent.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu Udāyin, the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, and others composed treatises on the Buddha-dharma; upon hearing this, the Buddha immediately permitted it.
Moreover, the Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle: those who understand it may compose treatises, while those who do not understand it should desist.
In this manner, the Buddha answered all other questions—such as those concerning the root of all phenomena—with thorough explanations.
Furthermore, one should compose a treatise on this matter. Why is this so?
If treatises are composed based on the sūtras, their meaning will be easy to understand and the Dharma will endure for a long time.
Furthermore, the Buddha permitted the composition of treatises; as it is said in a sūtra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Whatever treatise you compose, you should properly receive and uphold it."
Therefore, one should compose a treatise because, within the sūtras, meanings are extracted to establish arguments that form distinct schools.

Furthermore, the Buddha taught various discursive systems such as those concerning the mundane world for the sake of diverse beings who could be liberated; however, because Saṃti and others were unable to understand them, their minds became confused. These bhikṣus, such as Saṃti, asserted that the cycle of birth and death involves only a single, permanent consciousness.
The Buddha has taught the Dharma in various ways such as these; if there were no treatises (*śāstra*), how could they be understood?
For these reasons, one should compose a treatise.
Chapter Fourteen: On the Gates of the Treatise. There are two gates to the treatise: [the gate of the subject matter and the gate of the exposition].
There are two gates: first, the gate of worldly convention (*loka-vyavahāra*), and second, the gate of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
By means of the gate of worldly convention, it is said that there is a self, as stated in the Sūtra:
"I am always my own protector; by doing good, one obtains good for oneself; by doing evil, one obtains evil for oneself."
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras:
"The mind-consciousness is permanent.
It also says:
If one cultivates the mind throughout the long night, one will attain rebirth in a higher realm upon death.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The agent initiates karma; the agent himself experiences its results."
Furthermore, it is said:
"A certain sentient being is born in such-and-such a place," and so forth.
All such statements are made by way of the world-system (*lokadhātu*).
Regarding the gate of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all things are said to be empty and non-existent, as it is stated in the sūtras:

"Within these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), there is no self (*ātman*) nor anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*). The mind is like a flame in the wind, arising and ceasing from moment to moment. Although various karmas and the retributions of karma exist, neither an agent nor an experiencer can be found."
Just as the Buddha, based on the causal conditions of the continuity of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), speaks of birth and death, there are also two types of doctrinal gateways:
first, the gateway of worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*); second, the gateway of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Regarding the gateway of worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*): it is said that the moon wanes because of worldly convention, yet in reality the moon does not wane.
It is like when Māgandikī’s mother refers to her daughter-in-law as "mother," though in truth she is not a mother.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The tongue can cognize taste; it is by means of tongue-consciousness that taste is known, not by the tongue itself.
This is like saying that when a spear pierces a person, the person experiences suffering; it is consciousness that knows the suffering, not the person who suffers.
Just as a poor and lowly person might be given the name "Wealthy and Noble," the Buddha likewise follows the name of others and calls them "Wealthy and Noble.
Furthermore, the Buddha addresses non-Buddhists as "Brahmins" and also as "Śramaṇas."
Furthermore, just as the Buddha refers to kṣatriyas, brahmins, and others as "noble" in accordance with worldly convention,
and just as a single vessel is given different names according to the country, the Buddha likewise adopts those names accordingly.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"This is my last viewing of Vaiśālī.
Such expressions as these, which follow worldly conventions of speech, are called the conventional gate (*saṃvṛti-mukha*).
Regarding the gate of the noble ones (*ārya*), as it is said in the sutras:
consciousness arises through causes and conditions, and the various faculties such as the eye are like the great ocean.
Furthermore, as another sutra says:
It is merely the combination of the various conditions of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas); there is no agent, nor is there any experiencer.
Furthermore, it is said that all is suffering, as stated in the Sūtra:
"What the world calls pleasure, the Noble Ones call suffering."
The Noble Ones speak of suffering, while the world speaks of pleasure.
Furthermore, the various teachings on emptiness, signlessness, and so forth are called the gates of the noble ones.

There is also the gate of the three periods of time: if something within this context is designated as "form" (*rūpa*), whether that form has existed in the past, will exist in the future, or exists in the present, it is all termed "form."
Consciousness is also like this: if consciousness has known, will know, or is currently knowing, it is all termed "consciousness.
Such designations constitute the method of discourse on the three times.

Furthermore, there is the method of the "If-then" argument (*yukti-mukha*): if there is contact (*sparśa*), it must necessarily have the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as its cause, yet not all six sense bases serve as the cause for contact;
if there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it must necessarily have feeling (*vedanā*) as its cause, yet not all feelings serve as the cause for craving.
Some explain it as a complete cause, such as contact being the condition for feeling.
Others explain it as an incomplete cause, such as feeling being the condition for craving, but not mentioning ignorance.
Alternatively, there is another explanation as stated in the Sūtra:
"When the mind is joyful, the body attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). In the third dhyāna, although there is no joy (*prīti*), there is still bodily pliancy.
Furthermore, it is said that "pliancy is the experience of bliss (*sukha*)," yet in the fourth dhyāna, while there is pliancy, there is no experience of bliss.
This is called a divergent teaching.
Furthermore, there are two types of doctrinal gateways: those that are universally applicable and those that are restricted. As it is said in the sutras:
"If a person sets out on foot to make an offering to a stupa and dies along the way, they will all be reborn in the heavens."
This is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"One who commits a heinous crime (*ānantarya*) cannot be reborn in heaven."
This is called "obstruction.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:
"Those who indulge in various sensual desires commit no evil that they will not do."
This is called "penetration.
Although a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) may experience various desires, they are unable to give rise to karma that leads to rebirth in the evil realms;
this is called "blocking."
Furthermore, it is said in a sutra:
"Visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and forms.
This is called the general rule.
If that were so, visual consciousness should arise in relation to all forms; yet this is not the case.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"Due to the ear and conditioned by sound, auditory consciousness arises," and so forth, implying that visual consciousness does not arise [from those conditions].
This is what is called "obstruction.
Furthermore, both that which is called "penetration" and that which is called "obstruction" possess their own principles and do not subvert the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Moreover, there are two types of doctrinal gateways (*śāstramukha*):
There are two types: the determinate and the indeterminate.
As for the determinate, it is as stated:
"The Buddha is the Omniscient One; that which the Buddha has spoken is the True and Sublime Dharma; and the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples are those who practice correctly."
Furthermore, it is said:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and are the cessation that is nirvana.
Such categories as these are called "definitive."
Regarding "indefiniteness": if one says that all who die are reborn, this is not certain; for one is reborn if craving exists, and ceases to be when craving is exhausted.
Furthermore, it is said in a sutra:
"If one attains concentration of mind, one will all give rise to true knowledge."
This, too, is not fixed; for while the sages who attain meditative concentration can give rise to true wisdom, those of external paths cannot.
Furthermore, as a sutra says:
"Whatever one seeks, one shall obtain."
This is also not fixed; it may be attained or not attained.
If one says that the six sense bases necessarily produce contact, this too is not fixed; there are cases where they can produce it and cases where they do not.
These and others are called the gates of the indeterminate.
Furthermore, there is the gate of the discourse on "being" and "not being. For example, it is said that extraordinary grasses and fragrant flowers do not waft their scent against the wind.

Yet, it is also said that the *kubera* flower can be smelled even against the wind. The former statement—that they do not waft against the wind—is made with reference to human flowers; the latter—that they waft against the wind—is made with reference to celestial flowers.
Furthermore, three types of feeling are taught: painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Moreover, other sūtras state that all feelings whatsoever are called suffering.
There are three kinds of suffering:

the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); it is for this reason that it is said that all sensations whatsoever are suffering.
Furthermore, it is said:

This suffering is of three kinds: new, old, and intermediate. That which is newly experienced is called pleasure; when long endured and wearying, it is called suffering; that which is intermediate is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). Furthermore, it is said:
one is called a "person on the path" (*mārga-pudgala*) for the sake of attaining the path; even those who have not yet attained the path are also called persons on the path.
There are such characteristics by which names are derived based on causes.
Furthermore, there is the method of proximate discourse (*upaniṣad-dvāra*), as when the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If you sever conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), you will attain nirvāṇa."
Although one has not yet actually attained it, it is nonetheless called "attained" because it is proximate.

Furthermore, there is the method of discourse based on common characteristics (*sādharmya*): for instance, when one thing is mentioned, all other things sharing those same characteristics are said to have been mentioned as well.
Furthermore, when the Buddha states that the mind is flighty and restless, he has thereby already spoken of the other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Moreover, there is the perspective of the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra* (The Sutra on Many Elements), as the Buddha said:
"If a person does not know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the two views, they are all said to possess desire; if they can know them, they are all said to have attained detachment."

Even a *srotāpanna* knows the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the two views and yet possesses desire; however, those who possess such knowledge are mostly persons who have already abandoned desire.

Furthermore, there is the method of discourse that speaks of the effect within the cause, such as when it is said that by giving food one bestows five things: life, physical form, strength, happiness, and eloquence.
In reality, it does not correspond to the five things such as "life" (jīvitendriya), but only to their cause.
It is like the expression "eating money":
money cannot be eaten, but because one obtains food by means of money, it is called "eating money."
Furthermore, as the sutras state that women are defilements (*mala*), they are not actually defilements;
rather, because they are the cause for the defilements of craving and attachment, they are called "defilements.
Moreover, it is said that the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are called "desires" (*kāma*).
In reality, it is not desire itself; rather, because it can give rise to desire, it is called "desire.
Furthermore, that which is a cause and condition for pleasure is termed "pleasure," just as it is said that a person who gathers people through the Dharma is "pleasant.

Likewise, that which is a cause and condition for suffering is termed "suffering," just as it is said that dwelling together with fools is "suffering," or as it is said that fire is both "suffering" and "pleasure."
Furthermore, it is said that the cause of life is life itself, as stated in a verse:
"The means of subsistence are all external life; thus, to seize another's property is called taking their life."
Furthermore, it is said that the cause of outflows (āsrava) is itself an outflow, as stated in the *Saptāsravasūtra*.
Among these, two are actual outflows, while the remaining five matters are the causes and conditions for outflows.
Furthermore, there is the case of explaining the cause by means of the effect, as when the Buddha said:
"I must experience my past karma," which refers to experiencing the fruit of that karma.
One should understand all such numerous categories of treatises.
Chapter Fifteen: Praising the Treatise. One should study this treatise.
Why is this so? Because by studying this treatise, one attains the qualities of a person of wisdom.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
In the world there are two kinds of people: one is called a wise person, and the other is called a foolish person.

If one does not skillfully discern the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), sense bases (āyatanas), the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), causes and effects, and other such dharmas, this is called a foolish person;
if one skillfully discerns the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and so forth, this is called a wise person.

In this treatise, the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas) are correctly analyzed and explained; therefore, by means of this treatise, one attains knowledge of persons and phenomena, and for this reason it should be studied.
Furthermore, by practicing this treatise, one is no longer called an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of persons: one is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), and the other is not an ordinary person.

As it is said, although one may have shaved off hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and adopted the majestic deportment of the Buddha, one remains far removed from the Buddha-dharma because one has not accomplished the faculties such as faith.
If one can achieve the faculties such as faith, even while living at home, they are not called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
As it is said in the Sūtra: "There are four kinds of people:

those who possess the deportment of the Saṃgha but do not enter the number of the Saṃgha; those who are in the number of the Saṃgha but do not possess the deportment of the Saṃgha; those who both possess the deportment of the Saṃgha and enter the number of the Saṃgha; and those who neither possess the deportment of the Saṃgha nor enter the number of the Saṃgha."
The first is called the lay ordinary person; the second, the householder noble one; the third, the renunciant noble one; and the fourth, the householder ordinary person.

From this it is known that without the faculties such as faith, one does not enter the ranks of the Saṃgha; therefore, one should practice with diligence for the sake of the various faculties such as faith.

If one wishes to attain faith and the other [virtuous qualities], one should listen to, receive, recite, and practice the Buddha’s teachings as they are taught; therefore, one should study this treatise on the Buddha’s Dharma.
Furthermore, from this treatise one obtains two kinds of benefit: benefit for oneself and benefit for others.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"There are four kinds of persons: those who can benefit themselves but cannot benefit others; those who can benefit others but cannot benefit themselves; those who can benefit both; and those who benefit neither."
If one can personally possess virtues such as ethical discipline (*śīla*) but cannot cause others to abide in ethical discipline and the like, this is called self-benefit (*svārtha*).

Regarding these four types, even if a person can achieve self-benefit, because they cause others to obtain great fruits through giving (*dāna*) and so forth, it is also called benefiting others (*parārtha*).
In this context, the Buddha’s intention was not to say that this benefit [accrues only to others]; rather, if a person is merely able to teach the Dharma to others, this is called benefiting others.
Although such a person does not themselves practice in accordance with the Dharma, because they teach it to others, they themselves also obtain benefit.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Preaching the Dharma for others yields five kinds of benefit.

Here, the Buddha’s intention was not to speak of these; rather, he spoke here only of the foremost benefit, namely, that by practicing according to the teaching, one attains the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).

Therefore, one who preaches the Dharma can benefit others; because they benefit both themselves and others, they are called the most excellent among men, like the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) among all flavors.
Furthermore, such a person now dwells in light and will later enter into light;
whereas most worldly beings pass from darkness into darkness, or from light into darkness.
If one practices even a little of the Buddha-dharma, such a person can likewise pass from darkness into light, and from light into further light.
Why is this? Because practicing giving and other such acts cannot yield as much benefit as listening to the Buddha-dharma.
If one hears even a little of the Buddha’s words, one can attain penetrating wisdom, destroy all decline and affliction, and obtain immeasurable benefit.
As it is said in a sutra:
there are four kinds of people—those who go from darkness to darkness, those who go from darkness to light, those who go from light to light, and those who go from light to darkness.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of persons: those who go with the stream, those who go against the stream, those who abide in the middle, and those who have attained crossing.

If a person listens to the Buddha’s Dharma with a single mind, that person is able to eliminate the five hindrances and cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment. Therefore, such a person cuts off the flow of birth and death; they are called one who goes against the stream, and are also called one who abides, and are also called one who has attained crossing.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of people: those who are constantly submerged; those who emerge for a moment and then submerge again; those who emerge from contemplation; and those who attain liberation.
If one is unable to give rise to virtues such as faith that accords with *nirvāṇa*, this is called being "constantly submerged."
If one gives rise to mundane virtues such as faith, yet they are not firm and are subsequently lost again, this is called "emerging for a moment and then sinking back.
To give rise to virtues such as faith that accord with *nirvāṇa* and to discern between good and evil, this is called "emerging from contemplation."
To fully cultivate and practice the virtues conducive to Nirvana, such as faith and so forth, is called "attaining deliverance.
If a person can understand the true meaning of the Buddha-dharma, they will never sink forever; even if they should temporarily regress, they shall not suffer permanent loss.

Furthermore, this person is called one who cultivates merit; if a person does not cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, they will fall into the evil realms even for committing a small evil deed.
If a person cultivates and accumulates the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, they will not fall into the evil realms even if they commit many evils.

One who cultivates the person uses the wisdom derived from hearing to cultivate the body, feelings, mind, and dharmas. Because they cultivate the body, they are gradually able to give rise to the categories of morality, concentration, and wisdom, and are able to extinguish all karmic actions. Because all karmic actions are extinguished, birth and death are also extinguished.
Furthermore, it is said in a sutra:

"There are four kinds of persons: those whose fetters (saṃyojana) are sharp but not deep; those who are deep but not sharp; those who are both deep and sharp; and those who are neither deep nor sharp."

The first is called "having predominant fetters that come at times"; the second is called "if there are weak or middling fetters that constantly abide in the mind"; the third is called "if there are predominant fetters that constantly abide in the mind"; and the fourth is called "if there are weak or middling fetters that come at times."
If a person hears the authentic treatises on the Buddha’s Dharma, they sever two kinds of fetters that are both deep and sharp.
Furthermore, by understanding the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma, they neither afflict themselves nor afflict others.
When non-Buddhists observe precepts, they afflict their own bodies; if they fall into wrong views, they afflict others, because they claim there is no retribution for sinful or meritorious karma.
If they practice giving, this likewise afflicts themselves and is called afflicting others, such as when many oxen and sheep are slaughtered in celestial shrines.

If one understands the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma, it serves only to bring benefit; one does not afflict oneself nor afflict others, just like those who have attained meditative concentration and practice loving-kindness and compassion.
Therefore, one should study this treatise on the Buddha’s Dharma.
Furthermore, one who studies this treatise is called "one with whom it is appropriate to speak," because they understand the correct meaning.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"When engaging in debate, one should distinguish between those with whom it is appropriate to speak and those with whom it is not."

If a person does not abide in the Dharma of the wise, nor in what is possible and what is impossible, but instead dwells in conceptual discrimination and in [mere] paths, such a person is said to be one with whom one cannot speak;
the opposite of this is said to be one with whom one can speak.
Regarding "those who do not abide in the teachings of the wise": the commentators, having correctly understood the meaning and intent through right wisdom, subsequently grasp and apply them;
these people, however, do not know this, and for that reason they do not grasp them.
For instance, the followers of Nirgrantha and others say of themselves:
"Our teacher is a trustworthy person; we simply follow his words.
As for not abiding in what is possible or impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), it means not abiding in the application of causes.

Regarding the two types of causes—the common cause and the distinct cause—various non-Buddhists may respond with a distinct cause when another states a common cause, or respond with a common cause when another states a distinct cause.
Not abiding within these two kinds of causes means not abiding within conceptual discrimination;
not abiding within metaphors means not abiding within the path of debate.
As it is said: "A proponent of the treatise must not utter harsh words nor abandon the core tenets of the doctrine; rather, they should speak only of what is true and beneficial.
To skillfully exhort and instruct others so that they attain understanding and their own minds are filled with joy—this is called the Dharma of noble speech."
Among these, one may engage in discourse only with a person who correctly understands the Buddha’s Dharma, and not with anyone else.

Furthermore, there are those with whom one should not speak: those to whom a definitive answer should be given but who give an indefinite answer; those to whom a discriminative answer should be given but who give a non-discriminative answer; those to whom a counter-questioning answer should be given but who do not counter-question; and those to whom a question should be set aside but who do not set it aside.
Those who act contrary to these cases are called "fit for discourse."
A question that should be answered categorically has only one cause, such as when it is said, "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is peerless in the world," and so forth.
A question that should be answered by way of analysis involves further causes and conditions, such as the continuity of death and so forth.
Regarding questions that should be answered by counter-interrogation: for example, when someone asks a question, one returns the question to them to elicit an answer.

Regarding questions that should be set aside: if a phenomenon has no substantial reality and exists only as a provisional designation, yet one asks whether this phenomenon is identical or different, permanent or impermanent, and so forth—this is not a matter to be answered; only those who understand the Buddha-dharma can comprehend this.
Therefore, one should study this Buddhist treatise.
Furthermore, there are three types of persons: those fixed in the right [path], those fixed in the wrong [path], and those who are not fixed.

Those fixed in the right will certainly enter *nirvāṇa*; those fixed in the wrong will certainly not enter *nirvāṇa*; the remainder are called "not fixed. If a person can understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma, they will certainly enter the state of being fixed in the right.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of persons: those who are purely sinful, those with much sin, those with little sin, and those who are sinless.
One who is purely sinful is a person who possesses only unwholesome states and lacks even a single wholesome dharma.
One with many offenses has much evil and little goodness.
One with few offenses has much goodness and little evil.
One without offenses possesses only wholesome dharmas and lacks nothing unwholesome.
If a person can understand the correct meaning of the Buddha-dharma, they will certainly enter one of two states: having few offenses or being without offense.
Furthermore, if a person understands the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, their suffering will be finite, because they will inevitably attain nirvana.
Chapter Sixteen: The Four Dharmas. If one practices this treatise, one attains the superior means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*). As stated in the Sūtras:
there are four means of integration—generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*).
Regarding giving, such as clothing, food, and other material things: by using these material gifts to attract sentient beings, one may instead cause them to fall into ruin.
Regarding kind speech, speaking words that accord with their wishes is likewise faulty, for it merely seeks to capture their favor.
Regarding "benefiting through action" (*arthacaryā*): seeking benefit for others, or assisting them in accomplishing their affairs when there is a cause or condition, this too may be destroyed.
Regarding "sharing common interests" (*samānārthatā*): as when traveling on the same boat, one's sorrows and joys are shared; this, too, may be destroyed.
If one gathers sentient beings through the four means of attraction—giving according to the Dharma, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and consistency of purpose—they cannot be destroyed.
To gather them by means of the Dharma refers to practicing this treatise.
Furthermore, by studying this treatise, one attains the supreme reliance, as stated in the Sūtras:
"Rely on the Dharma, not on the person.

Even if someone says, "I heard this from the Buddha," or "I heard it from a learned bhikṣu," or "I heard it from two or three bhikṣus," or "I heard it in the midst of the assembly," or "I heard it from a venerable elder," one does not accept those words merely out of faith in that person.
If these words enter into the Sūtras, do not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma, and accord with the Vinaya, only then should they be accepted.
"Entering the Sūtras" means entering into the Sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha).
The *nītārtha-sūtra* refers to those whose meaning and intent do not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

As for the characteristics of phenomena, they accord with the *vinaya*; "vinaya" means cessation (*nirodha*). For example, if one contemplates conditioned phenomena as permanent, blissful, self, and pure, then greed and other afflictions will not cease; however, if one contemplates conditioned phenomena as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, then greed and other afflictions will cease.
Knowing impermanence and so forth is called the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); this is what is meant by "relying on the Dharma and not on the person.

If one speaks of relying on the Dharma, it encompasses all phenomena; therefore, it is next stated that one should rely on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not on sūtras of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The definitive sutras constitute the third reliance, namely, relying on the meaning rather than the words.
If these words and meanings are contained within the sūtras, do not contradict the characteristics of the dharmas, and accord with the vinaya, then they are to be relied upon.
Regarding "rely on wisdom, not on consciousness": consciousness refers to the cognition of phenomena such as form; as stated in the sūtras, "it is called consciousness because it cognizes.
Wisdom refers to the thorough penetration of the true nature of phenomena; as stated in the sūtras:
To know form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Since "as it truly is" is itself emptiness, one should not rely on the apprehension of consciousness; if one relies on wisdom, that is precisely relying on emptiness.
In order to penetrate this supreme basis, one should study this treatise.

Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras that there are four wheels of gods and humans that can increase wholesome dharmas: first, dwelling in a favorable place; second, relying on virtuous persons; third, personally formulating correct aspirations; and fourth, having planted roots of goodness in past lives.
"Dwelling in a favorable place" means residing in a central land, free from the five obstacles.
"Relying on virtuous persons" means being born at a time when a Buddha has appeared in the world.
"Having cultivated roots of goodness in past lives" means not being deaf, mute, or otherwise impaired.
To spontaneously give rise to right aspiration is called right view.
Right view necessarily arises from hearing the Buddha-dharma; therefore, one should study this orthodox discourse on the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, those who recite and study this treatise will attain great and firm benefit throughout their lives, namely, the thorough penetration of the Truths. As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are four firm dharmas: the firmness of speech, the firmness of concentration, the firmness of vision, and the firmness of liberation."
To speak with firmness means: if one speaks of all conditioned phenomena as impermanent and suffering, all things as selfless, and nirvāṇa as tranquility, this is called speaking with firmness.
This is the fulfillment of the wisdom of hearing; based on this, one attains meditative concentration, which is called the fulfillment of the wisdom of reflection.

Because of this concentration, one contemplates conditioned phenomena as impermanent, suffering, and so forth, thereby attaining right view, which is called the fulfillment of the wisdom of cultivation.
Attaining the fruits through the three types of wisdom is called "firmness in liberation.

Furthermore, if one hears the Buddha’s Dharma and its correct treatises, one obtains great benefit, as described in the sutras regarding the four great beneficial dharmas: associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, maintaining right mindfulness oneself, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
If one associates with virtuous persons, one hears the true Dharma, because the true Dharma resides within virtuous persons.
Having heard the true Dharma, right mindfulness arises, whereby one correctly contemplates all phenomena through such [truths] as impermanence.
From this correct contemplation, one is able to practice in accordance with the Dharma, which refers to untainted vision (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, hearing this treatise provides the basis for four virtues: the virtue of wisdom, the virtue of reality, the virtue of equanimity, and the virtue of cessation.

To give rise to wisdom upon hearing the Dharma is the locus of the virtue of wisdom; by means of this wisdom, one perceives the emptiness of the true reality, which is called the locus of the virtue of reality; because one perceives true emptiness, one attains detachment from afflictions, which is called the locus of the virtue of relinquishment; and because afflictions are exhausted, the mind attains quiescence, which is the locus of the virtue of quiescence.

Furthermore, when a person hears the correct discourse on the Buddha-dharma, they are able to plant the four kinds of roots of goodness that accord with Nirvana—namely, the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas.

When one contemplates the five aggregates through such modes as impermanence, there arises a compliant, inferior, and mild root of goodness that can cause the mind to become "heated"; this is called the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*).
When this stage of Heat increases and develops into a middling root of goodness, it is called the stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*).
When the factors of the summit (mūrdhan-dharma) increase, they become the superior roots of goodness, which are called the factors of patience (kṣānti-dharma).
When the factors of patience increase, they become the most excellent roots of goodness, which are called the supreme worldly factors (laukikāgra-dharma).

Furthermore, there are four kinds of roots of goodness: the regressive portion (*hāna-bhāgīya*), the stationary portion (*sthiti-bhāgīya*), the progressive portion (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*), and the penetrative portion (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).
Roots of goodness such as paying homage and reciting scriptures apart from the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) are called the regressive portion.
The wholesome roots attained through meditative concentration and so forth are called the "part pertaining to abiding" (sthānabhāgīya).
The various wholesome roots arising from hearing, reflection, and so forth are called the "part pertaining to increase" (vṛddhibhāgīya).
Uncontaminated wholesome roots are called the "part pertaining to penetration" (nirvedhabhāgīya).
If one hears the Buddha-dharma, one will forever leave behind the stage of regression and attain the three types of wholesome roots.
Chapter Seventeen: The Four Noble Truths. If a person hears the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, they will be able to skillfully know and discern the Four Noble Truths:
the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
The Truth of Suffering refers to the three realms.
The realm of desire extends from the Avīci Hell up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations.
The realm of form extends from the Brahma World up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of the four formless states.
Furthermore, there are the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*):

form, feeling, perception, and formations. Since non-Buddhists sometimes claim that consciousness dwells by depending upon a soul (*ātman*), the Buddha taught that consciousness depends upon these four stations.
Furthermore, there are four modes of birth:
birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation.
All devas and hell-beings are born by transformation; hungry ghosts are of two types, being born from a womb or by transformation; all others belong to the remaining four modes of birth.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of nutriment:
as for edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), whether coarse or subtle—rice and the like are called coarse, while the fragrance of ghee and oil, various drinks, and so forth are called subtle.
The nutriment of contact consists of cold, heat, wind, and so forth.
The nutriment of mental volition refers to those who sustain their lives through intention and aspiration.
The nutriment of consciousness refers to beings in the intermediate state, in the hells, and among the formless realm.
Although one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation lacks manifest consciousness, because consciousness still persists, it is also termed the nutriment of consciousness.

Furthermore, there are six realms of existence: the realm of hell for those with superior offenses; the realm of animals for those with middling offenses; the realm of hungry ghosts for those with inferior offenses; the heavenly realm for those with superior goodness; the human realm for those with middling goodness; and the asura realm for those with inferior goodness.
Furthermore, there are six elements:
earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
When the four great elements enclose space and consciousness resides within them, this numerical designation is called a "person."
Furthermore, there are the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*): the union of the six faculties, such as the eye, with their respective consciousnesses is termed the bases of contact.
Furthermore, there are the seven stations of consciousness (*sapta-vijñānasthiti*): within these stations, by the power of inversion (*viparyāsa*), consciousness dwells with craving and delight.
Furthermore, there are the eight worldly dharmas: gain and loss, praise and blame, defamation and fame, suffering and pleasure.
Because people in the world inevitably encounter these matters, they are called "worldly dharmas."
There are nine abodes of sentient beings, in which all beings dwell by the power of their inverted views.

Furthermore, there are fivefold classifications of phenomena: the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), and the twenty-two faculties (*dvāviṃśatindriya*).

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): the eye and forms constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Based on these, consciousness arises that is able to apprehend the preceding forms; this is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
At that very moment, the mind gives rise to perceptions of male or female, enemy or friend, and so forth; this is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
If one discriminates and perceives enemies, friends, and neutral persons, giving rise to three kinds of feeling, this is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
Within these three feelings, three kinds of afflictions arise; this is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Because these factors arise as the causes and conditions for receiving a body, they are called the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

Consciousness arises by means of four conditions—namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Karma serves as the causal condition;
consciousness serves as the immediate condition, because consciousness arises in immediate succession from consciousness.
Visible form is the object-condition;
the eye is the dominant condition.
In this context, consciousness arises from two causal conditions—namely, the eye and visible form, up to the mind and mental phenomena—which are called the twelve bases (āyatana).
When consciousness is added to these, they are called the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), namely: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and so forth.
How, then, do these factors such as the aggregates (*skandha*) arise?
Because these occur throughout the twelve periods of the day, they are called the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*) is affliction (*kleśa*), and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are termed karma; based on these two factors, consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and sensation (*vedanā*) arise in succession.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*)—these two factors—are termed afflictions.
That which is called "karma" is [the cause];
that which is the first consciousness to receive a body in a future life is called "birth";
the remainder is called "old age and death."
These twelve links of dependent origination manifest as past, future, and present; yet they arise solely from a multitude of conditions and possess no self.
Furthermore, because of the cycle of birth, death, coming, and going, as well as their cessation, the twenty-two faculties are taught.

When all sentient beings first receive a body, consciousness serves as the basis. This consciousness arises in six modes from the eye and the other sense organs; therefore, they are called the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). These are the so-called eye faculty up to the mind faculty (*manas-indriya*); because they can give rise to the six consciousnesses, they are named the six faculties.
Because they can distinguish the characteristics of male and female, they are called the male and female faculties (*puruṣendriya* and *strīndriya*).
Some call them a portion of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
These six faculties are also called the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
From these six bases, six kinds of consciousness arise; therefore, it is called "life. Why is this so?

Because these six sense bases and six consciousnesses attain continuous arising, they are called "life"; because this continuity is severed, it is called "death. Therefore, this matter is termed "vitality" (jīvita).
Among these, what constitutes the faculty?

It is karma. Because of the cause of karma, the six sense bases and the six consciousnesses arise in continuous succession; thus, the karma within this life is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

This karma arises from the various sensations (*vedanā*); these sensations are precisely what are called the five faculties, such as pleasure and so forth. From these five faculties arise all afflictions, such as craving, as well as the karmas of body and speech. Due to the causes and conditions of this karma, one undergoes birth and death once again; this constitutes defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), which are capable of causing the continuity of the causes and conditions of birth and death.
By what causes and conditions can pure dharmas be produced?
They must arise from faith and the like; through the causal conditions of these four dharmas—faith and the rest—wisdom is accomplished.
Wisdom has three stages, namely: that which is not yet known, that which desires to know, and that which has already known.
When the task of cultivation is accomplished, these faculties are all distinctions of wisdom.
Because the Buddha [discerns] the coming and going of birth and death, as well as the cessation of rebirth and the purification from defilement, he taught the twenty-two faculties.
Such dharmas as these are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering; one who is able to know them is said to be "skilled in knowing the Truth of Suffering.
As for the Truth of Origination, it consists of karma and afflictions.
Regarding karma, it shall be explained in the Chapter on Karma.
Regarding afflictions (*kleśa*), they shall be explained in the section on afflictions.
All karmas and afflictions are the causes and conditions for future existence; therefore, they are called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), it shall be explained in detail in the subsequent section on the Truth of Cessation.
These are the mind of conventional designation, the mind of phenomena, and the mind of emptiness; because these three minds are extinguished, it is called the Truth of Cessation.

As for the Truth of the Path, it refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): correctly establishing mindfulness within the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, as well as the wisdom arising from that mindfulness which contemplates the body as impermanent and so forth, abiding securely within these objects of focus, is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
As this mindfulness and wisdom gradually increase, one is able to discern feelings; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of feelings.
As they further become purified, one is able to discern the mind; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the mind.
To be able to discern all phenomena through right practice is called the foundation of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*):

if unwholesome and unvirtuous states have arisen, one perceives their faults and disadvantages and, for the sake of abandoning them, generates desire, exertion, diligence, and skillful means; this refers to knowing and seeing the conditions for unwholesome and unvirtuous states that have not yet arisen, and generating desire, exertion, and diligence as skillful means to prevent their arising. This refers to knowing and seeing the conditions for wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and generating desire, exertion, and diligence as skillful means to bring them into being. This refers to knowing and seeing the conditions for wholesome states that have already arisen, and generating desire, exertion, and diligence for the sake of their increase—by means of the successive applications of superior, middling, and inferior [effort], and for the sake of non-retrogression.

Regarding the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): the cultivation of the factor of the base of psychic power through the accomplishment of the sublime practice of the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*) is as follows. Because concentration arises from desire, it is called the "concentration of desire. Its accomplishment through the sublime qualities (*dharma*) such as desire, diligence, faith, tranquility, mindfulness, equanimity, and relinquishment is termed the "accomplishment of sublime practice."
Because merit increases, they are called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

This increase of desire is called diligence; this is the second [basis]. Because the practitioner possesses both desire and diligence, they cultivate concentration and wisdom, thereby attaining the mental samādhi known as concentration, and the samādhi of contemplation known as wisdom.
Regarding the five faculties: hearing the Dharma and giving rise to faith is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Having attained faith, one exerts diligent effort (*vīrya*) in order to abandon defiled phenomena and to realize pure phenomena; this is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).

Cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness is called the faculty of mindfulness; because through mindfulness one can achieve samādhi, it is called the faculty of concentration; because wisdom arises from concentration, it is called the faculty of wisdom.
When these five faculties increase and become powerful, they are therefore called the five powers.
Regarding the eightfold noble path: the wisdom arising from hearing that enables one to believe that the five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and so forth, is called right view.
If this wisdom arises from reflection, it is called right thought.
Through right reflection, one abandons all that is unwholesome and cultivates all that is wholesome, thereby exerting diligence.
From this point on, one gradually leaves the household life and receives the precepts, attaining three factors of the Path: right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
From this right precept, one next accomplishes the foundations of mindfulness and the various meditative absorptions.
Through these foundations of mindfulness and concentration, one attains knowledge in accordance with reality.
These are called the eight factors of the path; such is their sequence.
Furthermore, among the eight factors of the Path, ethical discipline (*śīla*) should come first. Why is this?

Because the categories of ethical discipline, concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) follow a sequential order of meaning: right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) are termed the category of concentration; diligence (*vīrya*) is present throughout all practices; and since the category of wisdom is proximate to the Path itself, it is explained last.

This wisdom is of two kinds: the coarse and the subtle. The coarse consists of the wisdom of hearing and the wisdom of reflection, which are termed "right thought. The subtle is the wisdom of cultivation; that is, entering into the stages of the Dharma such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, being able to break through conventional designations and the phenomena of the five aggregates—this is called "right view."
To perceive the cessation of the five aggregates through this right view is called the initial entry into the Path.
From this, one subsequently attains the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
Regarding the factor of mindfulness: when a practitioner loses mindfulness, afflictions arise; therefore, one must bind the mind to wholesome objects.
To maintain mindfulness of the right view previously attained is called "discernment of phenomena" (dharmapravicaya).
Not abandoning this discernment is called "diligence" (vīrya).
When practicing diligence, afflictions diminish and the mind gives rise to joy; therefore, it is called "joy" (prīti).
Because the mind is joyful, the body attains pliancy; this is called pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
When the body is pliant, one experiences bliss; when there is bliss, the mind becomes concentrated. This concentration is difficult to attain and is therefore named "vajra."
Having attained the fruit of non-attachment and severed both sorrow and joy, it is therefore called equanimity (*upekṣā*); this is termed the "superior practice.
Furthermore, because the mind neither sinks nor exalts but remains in equilibrium, it is called equanimity.

Bodhi is defined as the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*); practicing these seven factors enables the attainment of bodhi, and thus they are called the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
These thirty-seven factors lead to the attainment of the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
The fruit of *srotāpanna* refers to the thorough penetration of emptiness; by means of this wisdom of emptiness, one is able to sever the three fetters.
The fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* refers to the cultivation of this same path which attenuates the afflictions, such that there remain only two more births within the desire realm.
The fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala) is the ability to sever all afflictions of the desire realm.
The arhat is one who has severed all afflictions.

If one can cultivate this Buddhist treatise on the Dharma, one will be able to penetrate the Four Noble Truths and attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; therefore, one should cultivate this treatise on the True Dharma.
Chapter 18: On the Collections of Dharmas (Dharmaskandha) One who studies this treatise will be able to penetrate the collections of dharmas, such as those that are knowable (*jñeya*).

Because of this penetration, heterodox arguments cannot subdue them; they will also swiftly extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*), and being able to free themselves from suffering, they can likewise rescue others.
The aggregate of knowable phenomena refers to knowable dharmas and cognizable dharmas;
material dharmas and immaterial dharmas; visible dharmas and invisible dharmas;
resistant dharmas and non-resistant dharmas; tainted dharmas and untainted dharmas; conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas.
Mental phenomena and non-mental phenomena; mental concomitants and non-mental concomitants;
phenomena associated with the mind and phenomena dissociated from the mind; phenomena coexistent with the mind and phenomena not coexistent with the mind;
phenomena that follow the mind and phenomena that do not follow the mind; internal phenomena and external phenomena; coarse phenomena and subtle phenomena.
Superior dharmas and inferior dharmas, proximate dharmas and remote dharmas, dharmas that are appropriated and dharmas that are not appropriated,
dharmas that lead to emergence and dharmas that do not lead to emergence, dharmas shared with ordinary persons and dharmas not shared with ordinary persons,
sequential dharmas and non-sequential dharmas, dharmas that possess sequence and dharmas that lack sequence, and so forth.

There are two categories of phenomena. Furthermore, there are three categories of phenomena: material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), and phenomena dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-dharma*); past phenomena, future phenomena, and present phenomena; wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, and indeterminate phenomena; phenomena of those in training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), phenomena of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa-dharma*), and phenomena of neither training nor beyond training; phenomena to be abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya-dharma*), phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-dharma*), and phenomena not to be abandoned (*aheya-dharma*). Such are the various triads of phenomena.
Furthermore, there are four categories of phenomena: those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm, and those that are unbound.

There are also four paths: the path of practice that is difficult and painful, the path of practice that is difficult but easy, the path of practice that is easy but difficult, and the path of practice that is easy and pleasant.
Furthermore, there are four flavors: the flavor of emergence, the flavor of detachment, the flavor of cessation, and the flavor of right knowledge.
Moreover, there are four realized dharmas: the dharma realized by the body, the dharma realized through mindfulness, the dharma realized through the eye, and the dharma realized through wisdom.

The four types of physical existence, the four modes of entering the womb, the four conditions, the four faiths, the four noble lineages, and the four evil conducts—such are the various groups of four dharmas.
