This mind has been defiled by greed and other afflictions throughout the long night.
If the mind were something else [than these afflictions], it could not be said to be constantly defiled.
Furthermore, the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* states:
If the mind constantly cultivates faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom, one will be reborn in higher realms after death.
Furthermore, the *Dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"One who attains the first dhyāna, because the mind has become pliant and supple, is able to proceed from the first dhyāna to the second dhyāna."
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Cittavarga*:
"This mind is constantly in motion, like a fish out of water; therefore, you all should destroy the army of Māra.
Thus, we know that the single mind moves from here to there.
Furthermore, in the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*, a bhikṣu said:
"Within the cave of the five gates, the monkey moves and stirs.
Let the monkey remain still; do not assume it is as it was before."
Therefore, know that the single mind moves within the cave of the body at the gates of the five faculties.
That which is present now is itself the original; thus it is said, "Do not say it is like the original.
It is further stated:
This mind is all-pervasive, like the light of the sun.
A wise person can restrain it, just as a hook restrains an elephant.
Therefore, one knows that the single mind runs among all objects of perception.
Furthermore, because there is no self, it must be the mind that initiates karma.

Since the mind is a single entity capable of initiating all karmas and subsequently receiving their retribution—wherein the mind dies and the mind is born, the mind is bound and the mind is liberated, and the mind that originally experienced things is able to recollect them—one knows that the mind is one.
Furthermore, because the mind is a single entity, it is able to accumulate [wholesome qualities]; if it were to perish moment by moment, there would be no power of accumulation.

Moreover, in the Buddha-dharma there is no self; it is because the mind is one that it is designated as the "characteristic of a sentient being," whereas if the mind were manifold, it would not be the characteristic of a sentient being.

Furthermore, seeing with the left [eye] and cognizing with the right [eye] should not involve different seeing and different cognizing; therefore, one knows that the mind is one, seeing by itself and cognizing by itself.
Chapter 70: On the Absence of Multiple Minds. Although you claim that the consciousnesses of form and so forth are distinct, this is not the case.

Why is this so? If the mind were a single entity, yet performs various activities such as grasping forms, sounds, and so forth—just as a single person in a five-windowed room perceives objects in each direction—it would mean that the mind resides within the eye and, depending on conditions such as light, is able to see forms, just as that same person waits for companions in other places.
This refers to the distinctions within what is known by the mind;

for example, just as this very person who was previously a knower later becomes ignorant again, so too does false knowledge become correct knowledge, just as this very person who was previously pure later becomes impure again.
In this way, doubt-knowledge is itself determinate knowledge; it is like a person who was previously doubtful becoming one who possesses certainty.
An unwholesome mind thus becomes wholesome or indeterminate, just as that same person may at times think of what is wholesome, what is unwholesome, or what is indeterminate.
That is to say, the mind itself can produce the various distinctions of postures such as coming and going, just as this very person performs various postures such as the acts of going and coming.
In this way, the pure mind becomes impure, and the impure becomes pure, just as this very person was previously pure and later returns to being impure.

This means that the mind is associated with pleasure at one time and subsequently associated with suffering again, just as this very same person was originally a person of happiness and later becomes a person of suffering.
Therefore, it is said that while the mind is one, its functions constitute manifold activities.

Your statement that a single consciousness does not perceive the six objects and therefore is not a single mind is incorrect. I maintain that because the sense organs are distinct, the consciousnesses are distinct.
If consciousness abides in the eye, it can only perceive visible forms and not other objects; the same applies to the others as well.

Your statement that the grasper and the graspable are distinct is incorrect; mental phenomena are capable of cognizing their own nature, just as a lamp illuminates itself as well as other objects, or as a mathematician can calculate for himself as well as for others; likewise, the single mind is able to cognize its own nature and also cognize other things.
Your analogy of the monkey is not correct; for just as a single monkey lets go of one branch and then grasps another, so too is the mind: it lets go of one object and then grasps another.
All that has been said regarding the ability to initiate karma oneself and to experience its retribution oneself has already been answered in general.

Why is this so? If the mind were different [at each moment], there would be such faults as performing one action and experiencing another, or dying as one and being reborn as another; therefore, we know it is a single mind.
Chapter 71: The Chapter on the Non-Unity of Mind Answer:
You claim that the mind is a single entity which is long defiled by greed and other afflictions.

This is not so; it is within the continuum of the mind that one perceives it as having a single characteristic. It is like saying that the evening wind is the same as the morning wind, that the river today is the same as the river of old, or that the lamp this morning is the same as the lamp of yesterday.
Just as teeth are called "reborn," yet the original teeth do not actually reappear— rather, they are called "reborn" because something similar arises—
so too, although the mind is different, it is said to be "one mind" because of its continuity.
Regarding your statement about "recollection": a person may recollect their own original mind.
If that original mind has already come forth, what is there left to recollect now?
Furthermore, how could this very mind recollect itself?
There is no single cognition capable of knowing its own essence; therefore, it is not a single mind.
As for your statement regarding cultivation and accumulation: if the mind were always one and the same, what benefit would there be in cultivation?
If, however, there are multiple minds, then they arise in succession according to the sequence of inferior, middling, and superior states; thus, there is cultivation and accumulation.
You claim that the mind possesses a single characteristic; if the mind were one, it would be eternal, and what is eternal is the true self (*ātman*). Why is this so?
Because that which acts now and will act later, being eternally one and unchanging, is called the self.
Furthermore, because one cannot discern the distinct characteristics of the mind, one regards it as a single entity; just as with a continuous stream of poured water, the mind is perceived as one.
It is like a person with an eye disease who sees many hairs as a single mass; if one were able to differentiate these phenomena, one would know them to be distinct.
Furthermore, those of profound wisdom are able to know that the mind is distinct [from the body]. Why is this so?
Because even the Brahma Kings and others are bewildered and confused therein, saying as follows:
This body is impermanent, while the mind-consciousness is permanent.
If even those such as Brahmā are still deluded, how much more so would others fail to cling to permanence?
Therefore, one should carefully contemplate the phenomena produced by various conditions; thus, the perversion of permanence will be extinguished.

As for your statement that seeing with the left eye and cognizing with the right is due to the power of wisdom such that the seer and the cognizer are distinct— just as when one person writes a letter and another person can recognize it,
or as when a noble being can know what another person has done.
Furthermore, future events have not yet arisen and do not yet exist; thus, noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) cannot know them.
Moreover, since there is no recollection of past events, one knows that there is likewise no power of wisdom capable of knowing the future, as it does not yet exist.
This matter shall be explained in detail later.
Chapter Seventy-Two: Elucidation of Multiple Minds. Regarding your statement that a single mind performs multiple functions, this is not so.
Why is this? It is precisely because cognition constitutes the mind, yet the cognition of form differs from the cognition of sound; how could the mind be one?
Furthermore, it is like the manual action of grasping a flask: that very same action cannot grasp another object. Likewise, whichever mind apprehends a form, that same mind does not hear a sound.

Furthermore, this visual consciousness relies upon the eye as its support and takes form as its condition; since these two are impermanent, arising and ceasing from moment to moment, how could the visual consciousness not likewise cease from moment to moment?
For example, if there is no tree, its shadow likewise does not exist.

In the same way, because the eye and visible forms perish moment by moment, the consciousness that arises based upon them also perishes moment by moment; and a phenomenon that perishes moment by moment possesses no power of movement.
Furthermore, various answers have already been given in the *Pūrvācintya-varga* (The Chapter on Prior Intent), and thus the mind does not depart.
Although you say that consciousness abides in the eye and can see by depending on light, this is like saying that it is the person who sees, hears, and so forth.
This is not the case. Why?
Because in this treatise we seek the true meaning of dharmas; "person" is a mere conventional designation and should not be used as an analogy.

Furthermore, one should seek the characteristics of a person (*pudgala*); I teach that the aggregates (*skandha*) constitute a person, and I also speak of the collection of indeterminate consciousnesses (*aniyata-vijñāna-kāya*) as distinct from the collection of determinate consciousnesses (*niyata-vijñāna-kāya*). One does not take the collection of indeterminate consciousnesses to be the collection of determinate consciousnesses; it is thus in all such cases.

Your claim that consciousness is differentiated because the sense organs are differentiated is not correct; the sense organs are the causes and conditions for the arising of consciousness. If consciousness were a single unity, what function would the sense organs serve?

You have used the analogy of a lamp and counting, but this analogy is incorrect; for instance, although a lamp is lit for the purpose of illuminating, the essence of the lamp is not non-illuminating, and thus it does not illuminate itself.
By means of a lamp dispelling darkness, visual consciousness arises; once visual consciousness has arisen, it is also able to see the lamp as well as objects such as vases.
Furthermore, a mathematician can know his own form and also know the forms of others; therefore, it is called "knowing through characteristics."
Regarding your statement concerning karma and so forth, this has already been answered within the refutation of the arguments regarding karma; therefore, there is no such fault.
Furthermore, if the mind were eternally unitary, then there would be neither karma nor retribution. Why is this so?
It functions precisely by means of the mind and its basis.
If the mind were a single [immutable] entity, how could there be karmic retribution?
The same applies to bondage, liberation, and so forth.

Furthermore, your claim that one acts and another experiences the result is also incorrect; for the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha-santāna*) is neither identical nor distinct, as it would fall into the two extremes.

Moreover, since worldly designations (*saṃvṛti-nāman*) such as "various karmas" do not express ultimate reality, there is no fault in employing terms like "this" and "that" within the continuity of the aggregates. Thus, we know that there are multiple minds.
Chapter Seventy-Three: On the Brief Abiding of Consciousness. Question:
It has already been clarified that there are many minds.
Now, do these various minds perish moment by moment, or do they abide for a short duration?
Some say that the mind abides for a short duration.
Why is this? Because it cognizes form and other objects.
If things were to perish moment by moment, they would be incapable of cognition; therefore, they do not remain non-existent.
Furthermore, if things perished moment by moment, then phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) could never be known. Why is this so?
If even a flash of lightning, which endures for but a moment, cannot be fully discerned, how much less could that which perishes from moment to moment be discerned?
Yet, in reality, it is discerned; therefore, we know that the various consciousnesses do not perish from moment to moment.
Furthermore, visual consciousness relies upon the eye and takes form as its object; since these two are not distinct, the consciousness is likewise not distinct.
Moreover, because the mind can apprehend all various forms such as blue and so forth simultaneously, we know that it does not perish moment by moment.

If you think that it is through a continuum (*saṃtāna*) that one can achieve definitive discernment, this too is not the case; for if each individual moment of mind cannot achieve discernment, then even though they form a continuum, discernment still cannot be achieved—just as a single blind person cannot see forms, nor can many such persons do so together.

If you further argue that just as a single thread cannot restrain an elephant while many gathered together can, so too a single moment of mind cannot discern an object while a continuum can—this is also not the case. Each individual thread possesses a small amount of strength, and thus their combination is effective;
however, within a single moment of mind there is no such small amount of strength, and therefore a continuum should likewise be incapable of such discernment.
Since there is indeed a realization [of objects], we know that the mind does not perish moment by moment.
Furthermore, if the mind were to perish moment by moment, past and future karmic actions would all be rendered useless.

Because it abides for a short duration, it is able to make these actions effective; therefore, we know that the mind does not perish moment by moment, and although it is impermanent, it must have at least a temporary duration.
Chapter 74: The Non-Abiding of Consciousness. Response:

You claim that because the mind possesses discernment, it does not perish moment by moment; this is not so. It is through the power of the mind that various characteristics are clearly discerned, not because they abide.
If it were not so, one would not be able to achieve certain cognition regarding sounds and actions. Why is this?
Because we observe that these things perish moment by moment, yet in reality, certain cognition does occur; therefore, we know that cognition is not possible through the persistence [of an object].

Furthermore, if cognition is taken as the mind, then the cognition of blue is not identical to the cognition of yellow; therefore, even if one momentarily abides in the cognition of blue, one cannot cognize yellow.

Moreover, the time of cognizing blue is different from the time of cognizing what is not blue; a single dharma should not exist across two times, nor should the dharma and time coexist, nor should time and the dharma coexist.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of grasping: first, that which is determinate; second, that which is indeterminate.

If consciousness did not perish from moment to moment, then all objects of grasping would necessarily be determinate. I maintain that when consciousness arises in a long succession, such grasping is determinate; if it arises in a short succession, it is indeterminate.
Furthermore, since the consciousness grasping objects is sometimes slow and sometimes quick, the mind is not fixed.
Your claim that the basis and the object are non-different is already refuted; because matter perishes moment by moment, its basis and object must also be different.

Regarding your statement that it "appropriates completely," you mean that consciousness is called "complete appropriation" because it can pervasively appropriate the various parts of the body; therefore, there is no single consciousness that can pervasively appropriate [the whole]. Why is this so?
Since the mind that has not yet fully grasped an object perishes immediately upon arising, how could there be a mind capable of grasping everything?

Your claim that the performance of karma is useless is incorrect; for example, although a lamp perishes moment by moment, it still possesses the function of illumination. Likewise, although karmic actions and the wind perish moment by moment, they are nonetheless able to move objects. Consciousness is exactly the same.

Furthermore, just as a lamp and such things, though perishing moment by moment, can still be perceived, so too is consciousness: although it perishes moment by moment, it is nonetheless capable of being perceived.
Moreover, all minds, mentals, and consciousnesses perish moment by moment.
Why is this so? Because various colors such as blue and others arise and perish rapidly when assembled before one, we know they do not abide.
Furthermore, a person may give rise to the thought that they can simultaneously grasp all conditions; therefore, consciousness does not abide.
If consciousness were to abide even momentarily, then people would not give rise to this deluded thought. Why is this?

Just as with the continuity of seeds and roots, because there is a momentary abiding, people do not conceive of delusion regarding them, such as by claiming that the sprout, stem, and so forth exist simultaneously; therefore, one knows that consciousness perishes from moment to moment.
Furthermore, when a person sees a jar, they immediately give rise to the recollection of "jar"; because recollection arises following perception, [consciousness] perishes moment by moment.

Moreover, if the various consciousnesses did not perish moment by moment, then a single cognition could be both erroneous and correct—for instance, seeing a person as a person, yet upon grasping, taking them to be a non-person; likewise, a state of doubt or grasping would be identical to a state of certain grasping.
This is impossible; therefore, one knows that [the mind] perishes moment by moment.
Furthermore, because it apprehends various causes and conditions such as discrimination, one knows that it perishes moment by moment.

Moreover, since the cognition arises within the continuous stream of sound and action—which themselves possess the characteristic of perishing moment by moment—one knows that the mind perishes moment by moment.
Chapter 75: On the Co-arising of Consciousness Question:
It has already been clarified that the mind perishes moment by moment.
Now, do the various consciousnesses arise simultaneously, or do they arise successively?
A certain master of the Abhidharma says that consciousness arises simultaneously. Why is this so?

Because there are people who can apprehend various objects at once; for example, while a person sees a jar, they also hear the sound of music, smell the fragrance of flowers with their nose, hold a fragrant scent in their mouth, feel the breeze of a fan against their body, and contemplate a refined melody. Therefore, we know that one can apprehend various objects simultaneously.

Furthermore, if a single consciousness were able to universally cognize suffering and pleasure throughout the body, then a single visual consciousness should likewise be able to apprehend all trees; however, this is impossible. How could a single consciousness fully know the roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits?
Therefore, we know that many cognitions arise simultaneously to apprehend all various objects of contact.
Furthermore, among various colors, cognitions arise at once; yet the cognition of blue is not identical to the cognition of yellow. Thus, we know that many cognitions arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, among the various parts of the body, cognition can arise swiftly; when one part is apprehended, one is able to apprehend all parts simultaneously.
Moreover, within the Buddha-dharma, there is no such thing as a "whole" (avayavin), for it is impossible for a single consciousness to apprehend all its parts at once.
Therefore, we know that a single moment can produce multiple consciousnesses, which apprehend all their constituent parts.
Chapter 76: On the Non-simultaneity of Consciousnesses. Answer:
Your claim that various consciousnesses arise simultaneously is not correct.
Why is this so? Consciousness arises dependent upon mindfulness.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
If the eye-faculty is unimpaired and visible forms enter the range of cognition, yet there is no capacity to produce the mental application (*manasikāra*), visual consciousness will not arise.
Therefore, it is known that the various consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, as they depend upon mental application.
Furthermore, all phenomena that arise are subject to the cause of karma; because the mind arises one at a time, the retributions of the hells and other realms are not experienced simultaneously.
If multiple minds were to arise together, then those retributions should be experienced simultaneously;
yet this is in fact impossible. Therefore, we know that the various consciousnesses do not arise at the same time.

Furthermore, consciousness can rapidly apprehend its objects; just as a whirling firebrand appears as a continuous circle because its rotation is so swift that its gaps cannot be seen, so too it is with the various consciousnesses:
because their duration is so brief, they cannot be distinguished.

Furthermore, if all consciousnesses were to arise simultaneously, then all phenomena that arise could likewise be produced together in a single thought-moment at one time; what obstacle would there be?
If that were so, the arising of all phenomena would not require effort, and even without performing meritorious deeds or karma, one should attain liberation.
Such a thing is impossible; therefore, we know that the various consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, the body is driven by the mind; if all minds were to arise simultaneously, the body would disintegrate because minds such as those of the past and future would arise at one and the same time.
Yet, the body does not actually disintegrate; therefore, we know that minds do not arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, when one sees external objects such as seeds, roots, and sprouts, as well as physical forms such as the kalala, arbuda, and peśī stages, these appear in a sequential order through the stages of youth, adulthood, and old age; the mind, too, should be understood in this same way.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:
"When one experiences a pleasant feeling, two other feelings cease—namely, the painful feeling and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling," and so forth.
If these were to arise simultaneously with consciousness, then one would have to experience all three feelings at once.
In reality, this is not so; therefore, we know that the various consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, because a single mind arises within a single body, it is termed "one person. If consciousnesses were to arise together, then one body would contain many persons;
yet in reality this is not the case. Therefore, the consciousnesses of a single body do not arise concurrently.
Furthermore, if consciousnesses were to arise simultaneously, one should know all phenomena at once.
Why is this? Within the eye, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of consciousnesses arise, and so it is for all others up to the mind; if this were so, one would necessarily know all phenomena.
But in reality this is not so; therefore, we know that the various consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.
Question:
For what reason must the various consciousnesses arise in succession?
Answer: Because of the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), consciousnesses arise one by one.
Question:
Why is there exactly one *samanantarapratyaya* (immediately preceding condition)?
The answer is:
such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Just as you maintain that a single deity possesses a single mind, so too do I maintain that there is a single mind and a single sequential condition (*anuloma-pratyaya*).

Just as a sprout belongs to a seed and must arise in sequence—whereby the sprout does not produce a stem and so forth—likewise, according to the principle that a phenomenon belongs to a specific mind, it must arise from that subsequent mind and not produce other phenomena.
Furthermore, the characteristic of consciousness is necessarily such that each arises and ceases in a sequential order, mutually connected, just as the characteristic of fire is heat.
Therefore, all consciousnesses must arise in succession.

Discourse on Perception 77: Chapter on the Aggregate of Perception, the Seventy-seventh Section within the Collection on the Truth of Suffering. Question:
What dharma constitutes perception (*saṃjñā*)?
Answer: [Perception is]...
It is called "perception" (saṃjñā) because it grasps the characteristics of provisional phenomena. Why is this so?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Some people have few perceptions, some have many perceptions, some have immeasurable perceptions, and some have the perception of nothingness.
Yet, in reality, there are no such phenomena as "few," "many," and so forth; therefore, we know that perception is the grasping of the characteristics of provisional dharmas.

This perception is mostly spoken of in the context of the perversions (*viparyāsa*), such as the perversion of perceiving permanence in the impermanent, the perversion of perceiving pleasure in suffering, the perversion of perceiving a self in what is non-self, and the perversion of perceiving purity in the impure; it is also spoken of in the context of faith-based understanding (*adhimukti*) and the meditative absorptions on the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

Furthermore, perception grasps its objects through three types of distinctions, namely: the hostile, the friendly, and the neutral. From these objects, the three kinds of sensation arise in succession; from sensation, the three poisons arise. Therefore, perception possesses faults.

Because perception (*saṃjñā*) involves error, the Buddha taught that it should be abandoned; as it is said: "When the eye sees forms, do not grasp at perceptions. Therefore, we know that grasping the characteristics of conventional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) is what is called perception.
Question: To say that grasping conventional phenomena constitutes perception is incorrect.
Why is this so? Because this perception can sever the afflictions.
As it is said in a sutra:

Because one skillfully cultivates the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*), one is able to sever all attachment to the realm of desire (*kāmarāga*), attachment to the form realm (*rūparāga*), and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), as well as all frivolity, restlessness, self-conceit (*asmimāna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, it is known that it is not merely the grasping of a conventional designation (*prajñaptidharma*) that constitutes this perception; for if it were merely the grasping of a conventional designation, it would not be capable of severing the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Answer: This is indeed true wisdom, though it is designated by the name "perception" (saṃjñā).
For example, it is said that the experiencer attains liberation from all things, and it is also said that one cuts off all afflictions with the mind (manas).

Furthermore, it is said that through karma that is neither black nor white, one can exhaust all karmas; it is also said that faith can cross rivers, single-mindedness can cross the ocean, diligence can eliminate suffering, and wisdom can bring about purity. Yet in reality, one crosses by means of wisdom alone, not by faith and the others. Thus, this wisdom is spoken of using the name "perception" (saṃjñā).

Furthermore, it is stated in the Sūtras that wisdom serves as a sword; as it is said, "The noble disciple uses the blade of wisdom to sever all afflictions. Therefore, we know that it is wisdom that can sever the fetters, not perception.

Furthermore, among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the term "perception" (*saṃjñā*) is not mentioned; therefore, it does not sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Moreover, the sūtras state that it is the one who knows and the one who sees who can attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), not the one who lacks knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, among the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), it is taught that the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya), and the faculty of "having known" (ājñātāvīndriya) are all designated by the term "knowledge.
Moreover, the Buddha taught that wisdom (prajñā) constitutes the category of wisdom and the category of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana).
Furthermore, it is said that there is no wisdom without dhyāna, and no dhyāna without wisdom.
Moreover, the *Anupūrvika-sūtra* states:
"One who maintains pure precepts has no remorse in mind, and so on, until they master the mind and attain knowledge in accordance with reality."
Furthermore, the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and others are all designated by the term "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

Moreover, among the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), the training in wisdom is the most preeminent; it is also said that one is "endowed with wisdom" and "endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation."
Furthermore, among the seven purifications (*saptaviśuddhi*), it speaks of the purification of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśanaviśuddhi*).

Moreover, because the Buddha taught that he possesses correct knowledge of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samyagjñāna*), this is called unsurpassed wisdom (*anuttara-prajñā*); there is no such teaching regarding "conception" (*saṃjñā*).
Furthermore, according to principle, it is wisdom (*prajñā*) that should sever the various afflictions (*kleśa*), not perception (*saṃjñā*).
Why is this so? As stated in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*:
If a meaning enters into the sūtras, does not contradict the characteristics of the dharmas, and accords with the vinaya, that meaning should be accepted.

Furthermore, it is said that within the correct meaning one places words that follow the meaning, and within the correct words one places meanings that follow the words; therefore, although the sūtra states that the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*) and so forth can sever all fetters (*saṃyojana*), in principle this must be wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, it is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the root of the afflictions (*kleśa*); because one is liberated from ignorance through wisdom (*prajñā*), one cuts off all afflictions by means of wisdom.
Question: You say that various perceptions (*saṃjñā*) grasp the characteristics of conventional phenomena; what constitutes these characteristics?
Answer: Some take provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). There are five such provisional phenomena:
first, the past; second, the future; third, names; fourth, characteristics (*nimitta*); and fifth, persons (*pudgala*).
This is not so. Why is that? Because a person is constituted by the five aggregates;
since their characteristics lack a constitutive cause, they are not a mere designation.
Question: What is the meaning of "marks" (lakṣaṇa) now? Answer:
The condition (*pratyaya*) is itself the sign (*nimitta*). How is this known?

As it is said: when the lion, king of beasts, stands on this bank of a river and perceives the sign of the opposite bank, he crosses the current; if it is not suitable, he returns to this bank, never abandoning his purpose until death.
In this sutra, trees and so forth are taken as signs;
furthermore, it speaks of a bhikṣu displaying signs, wherein robes and the like are also taken as signs;
moreover, it speaks of the World-Honored One manifesting such signs.
Furthermore, it is said that a cook takes on the appearance of what his master desires for food because of the king’s eating.
It is also said that the early morning is the sign of the sun’s rising.
Again, three signs are taught: namely, the sign of withdrawal (*saṃgraha*), the sign of arousal (*samudīraṇa*), and the sign of relinquishment (*utsarga*).

In this context, "concentration" (saṃgraha) and so forth constitute its characteristics. To bind the mind to an object by recollecting any given phenomenon is called the characteristic of concentration.
Furthermore, when the gods are about to fall from their celestial realms, five signs first appear; in this case, these five phenomena themselves constitute the characteristics.
Therefore, one should know that [these] are not taken as characteristics by means of provisional dharmas, nor are they subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra apprehended the characteristics of Pūrṇa’s facial features and so forth.
Moreover, it is stated in the sūtras that when the eye sees forms, one does not grasp at their characteristics.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Dharmamudrā*:
"If a bhikṣu perceives for himself the severance of the marks of form, sound, and so forth, I do not say that this person has attained pure knowledge and vision.
From this, we know that conditions (*pratyaya*) are themselves marks (*nimitta*), and are not merely provisional phenomena.
Question: Conditions are not characteristics. Why is this so?
The signless samādhi also has an object of focus.
Furthermore, it is said that after seeing a form, one does not grasp its signs.
If this were to take signs as its object, how could one see the form yet not grasp its signs?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of signs (*nimitta*): faulty signs and faultless signs. Because one wards off faulty signs, it is said that "when seeing forms, one does not grasp at signs.

Even the signlessness (*animitta*) as an object-condition has faults; this will be explained in detail later in the section on the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), where it is called "signlessness" because it extinguishes the three types of mind.
For a beginner, it is not the case that all mental images (*nimitta*) are entirely faults; if one takes up the image of grasping or develops the image of relinquishing, there is no fault.
Furthermore, since *nirvāṇa* is called a "non-existent dharma," it should not be raised as an objection.

As it is said: if one grasps at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they cannot cause defilement; however, if one grasps at the characteristics of conventional designations (*prajñaptisaṃjñālakṣaṇa*), then afflictions arise. Why is this?
Because by grasping at the differentiated characteristics of enemies, friends, and so forth, sorrow, joy, and the like arise; from these, faults such as greed and anger can be produced.
Therefore, it is known that the grasping of the characteristics of provisional phenomena is what is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
**Chapter 78: The Characteristics of Feeling** Within the *Treatise on Feeling* in the Section on the Truth of Suffering, Chapter Seventy-Eight: The Characteristics of Feeling. Question:
What is feeling (*vedanā*)?
Answer: Suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Question:
What is called suffering?
What is called pleasure?
And what is termed neither-suffering-nor-pleasure?

Answer: If there is an increase in body and mind, it is called pleasure; if there is a decrease in body and mind, it is called suffering; that which is contrary to both is called neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Question:
These three feelings lack a definitive characteristic. Why is this so?
For instance, regarding a single thing, it may increase the body and mind, or cause their diminution, or be contrary to both.
The answer is:
it is the conditions that are indeterminate, not the sensation itself.
Why is this so? It is like a single fire that at times produces pleasure, at times produces pain, and at times can produce neither-pain-nor-pleasure;

while the arising of sensation from conditions is thus determined, this very same single thing, depending on the time, becomes the cause of pleasure, the cause of pain, or the cause of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Question:
At what time does this condition serve as the cause for suffering, pleasure, and so forth? Answer:

In accordance with that which can obstruct suffering, at that time a perception of pleasure arises; it is like a person distressed by cold, for whom the sensation of heat produces a perception of pleasure.
Question:
When this sensation of heat increases excessively, it can again become suffering; it is no longer pleasure. Therefore, we know that pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) also does not exist. Answer:

Pleasant feeling exists by way of worldly names and conventions, but not as an ultimate reality; it is merely that when a person encounters a hot touch according to their preference, it serves to increase their well-being.
Furthermore, it is by counteracting prior suffering that the perception of pleasure arises at that time.
If one were free from prior suffering, this hot touch could not produce pleasure; therefore, it does not exist substantially.
Question: You say that pleasure exists merely by way of names and signs; this is not so. Why is that?
In the Sūtras, the Buddha himself spoke of three types of sensation.
If pleasure truly did not exist, why would he speak of three?
Furthermore, he said that if form were invariably suffering, sentient beings would not give rise to attachment toward it.
Furthermore, it is said: what is the gratification (āsvāda) in form? It is that which, by means of form, gives rise to joy and pleasure.
It is also said: a pleasant feeling is pleasant when arising, pleasant while persisting, and painful when passing away;
a painful feeling is painful when arising, painful while persisting, and pleasant when passing away.
Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not know suffering nor does one know pleasure.

Furthermore, pleasant feeling is the retribution for merit, while painful feeling is the retribution for transgression; if there were truly no pleasant feeling, then merit and transgression would have only the fruit of suffering, yet this is not actually the case.

Furthermore, there is also the sensation of pleasure within the desire realm; if there were truly no sensation of pleasure, there should be no sensation at all in the form and formless realms, yet this is not the case.
Moreover, it is taught that the latent tendency of craving resides within the sensation of pleasure; if there were no sensation of pleasure, where would craving reside as a latent tendency?
It cannot be said that the latent tendency of craving exists within painful feeling; therefore, we know that pleasant feeling truly exists.
The answer is:
if pleasant feeling truly exists, its characteristics should be explained—what constitutes pleasure?
In reality, it cannot be so described; one should know that it is merely designated as the "characteristic of pleasure" within the various distinctions of suffering.

All worlds, from the great hells below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above, are characterized by suffering. Being tormented by abundant suffering, one gives rise to this characteristic of pleasure within the midst of minor suffering.
Just as when a person is afflicted by the suffering of heat, they perceive cool contact as pleasure,
so too there is no contradiction in the various sūtras making such statements.
Question:
It may also be said that all things in the world are pleasant, yet within subtle pleasure one perceives the characteristic of suffering;
otherwise, one could not say that one conceives the notion of pleasure within subtle suffering.
The answer is:
Because the characteristic of painful sensation is coarse, subtle pleasure cannot be considered suffering.
Furthermore, although pleasure may be subtle, it does not possess the characteristic of affliction.
Why is this? Because no one is seen to raise their hand and cry out upon receiving even a slight pleasure.
Furthermore, because it receives what is increasingly subtle, it is called the mark of quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*), just as the higher stages become progressively more quiescent.
Therefore, to say that the aspect of suffering arises within subtle pleasure is merely a statement;
however, it is logical that ordinary, foolish people falsely conceive the aspect of pleasure within subtle suffering.
Chapter Seventy-nine: The Chapter on the Suffering of Conditioned Phenomena (Saṃskāraduḥkhatā). All sensations are suffering. Why is this?
Clothing, food, and other such things are all causes of suffering, not causes of happiness.
How do we know this?
We observe that when the excesses of food and clothing increase, suffering likewise increases; therefore, they are called causes of suffering.
Furthermore, sufferings such as hand pain can be pointed out through their characteristics, but the characteristic of pleasure is not so.
Furthermore, clothing, food, and other such things are all for the purpose of treating illness; it is like a person who, not being thirsty, finds no pleasure in drinking.
Moreover, when a person is tormented by suffering, they perceive the semblance of pleasure within another form of suffering, just as one who fears death regards punishment as a pleasure.
Furthermore, all causes and conditions of suffering—such as whips, staves, swords, and spears—are determinate, whereas the causes of pleasure are not so.
Moreover, since all that is required ultimately results in suffering, one should know that it is perceived only later, after its prior existence, just as a sandal gradually wears away.

Furthermore, regarding such things as female beauty, one first gives rise to the perception of pleasure, only to later feel revulsion; thus we know that this perception of pleasure arises from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), and that by abandoning such improper attention, one sees its faults.
Furthermore, female beauty and the like are all causes of suffering, such as the ailment of consumption; therefore, they are not pleasure.
Moreover, at the time of renouncing desire, one abandons these conditions; if they were truly pleasure, why would one abandon them?
Furthermore, as soon as a person experiences a state of pleasure, that very same thing subsequently gives rise to suffering; therefore, one knows it is not true pleasure.

Moreover, the body is a field of suffering, not a field of pleasure. Just as in a wild field where fine grain is difficult to cultivate while weeds easily grow, so too in the field of the body, manifold sufferings readily accumulate while empty pleasures are difficult to produce.

Furthermore, when a person first gives rise to the perversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure, and subsequently develops craving and attachment, if that pleasure were even slightly real, it would not be called a perversion. Just as the notions of permanence, self, and purity are entirely unreal and non-existent, so too is pleasure; both are equally inverted.

Furthermore, people may give rise to a sense of pleasure amidst suffering and hardship, such as when shifting a heavy burden from one shoulder to the other; thus, we know that there is no true pleasure.

Moreover, in the Sūtras, the Buddha taught that one should contemplate pleasure as suffering, contemplate suffering as an arrow piercing the heart, and contemplate neither-suffering-nor-pleasure as impermanent, mindful of its arising and its ceasing.
If there were truly pleasure in meditative concentration, one should not contemplate it as suffering.
You should know that ordinary beings perceive pleasure within suffering; therefore, the Buddha said:
"Wherever ordinary beings perceive the basis for pleasure, you should contemplate it as suffering."
Furthermore, these three types of sensation are all subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); if they were truly pleasant, how could they be subsumed under the Truth of Suffering?
Moreover, suffering is the reality, while the characteristic of pleasure is illusory.
How is this known?
It is because one observes that it is through a mind of suffering that one can sever the various fetters, not through a mind of pleasure; therefore, we know that all things are suffering.
Furthermore, all phenomena are causes of suffering, just like enemies or thieves.
There are two kinds of enemies and bandits: some inflict suffering immediately, while others are mild and kind at first but later cause harm.
All things are likewise: some initially produce goodness, while others later turn into harm; therefore, one knows that all are suffering.
Furthermore, sentient beings never tire of their desires; like drinking salt water, they are never satisfied, and thus it is suffering.

Moreover, the absence of seeking for desires is what is called happiness, whereas seeking is called suffering. Since one does not see anyone in the world who is free from seeking, we know that there is no happiness.
Furthermore, because physical suffering and mental suffering constantly pursue all sentient beings, we know that the body is suffering.
Moreover, the body is like a prison, always bound by fetters and shackles. How do we know this?
The extinction of this body is what is called liberation; because it is bound by fetters and shackles, there is suffering.

Furthermore, all things, gradually and in succession, are all contemptible and loathsome—such as the body in the hells and so forth, the seasons of winter and summer, the faculties of infants and so forth, and the perceptions of cold and heat. Since one comes to detest them all upon subsequent reflection, one should know that they are all suffering.

Furthermore, the body has many enemies and thieves—namely, the casket of venomous snakes, the five bandits with drawn swords, the thief who feigns intimacy, the thief who destroys the empty village, and the near shore of the great river; as all manner of sufferings constantly pursue it, one knows that it is entirely suffering.

Furthermore, one knows that the bodies of sentient beings are pursued by various sufferings; namely, because the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of frustrated desires constantly accompany them, the body is thus a collection of manifold sufferings.

Furthermore, because there is a body, there arise the notion of "mine," craving, attachment, and the accumulation of all such afflictions; thus, one knows that the body is the causal condition for manifold sufferings.
Moreover, among the sentient beings of the five destinies, there is no happiness whatsoever in their performance of the four modes of deportment.
Why is this so? As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Form is suffering; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering."

When form arises, one should know that it is precisely the arising of old age, sickness, death, and all such decays and afflictions; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Furthermore, the body is constantly preoccupied with activity, performing various deeds through body, speech, and mind; the performance of these various deeds is all termed suffering.
Furthermore, the noble ones find joy in the exhaustion of the body; if this were truly happiness, why would they experience such rapturous joy upon losing that happiness?
Therefore, we know that it is all suffering.
Chapter Eighty: On the Suffering of Change (Vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā) Question:
Although you have elucidated suffering through many causes and conditions, people still crave pleasure; they consider it happiness whenever they obtain what they desire.
Answer: This has already been answered previously: because ordinary persons are deluded, they perceive pleasure within suffering.
Furthermore, being harmed by ignorance and confusion, how can they be trusted?
Even when one obtains what is desired, one should still contemplate it as suffering. Why is this?
Because all these things are impermanent;
at the time of their destruction, they give rise to suffering.
As the Buddha said in a sutra:
"Devas and humans love form, delight in form, and crave form; when this form decays, great sorrow and suffering arise. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
Because it is subject to decay and ruin, one should know that it is also suffering.

Furthermore, when a person experiences illusory pleasure, they give rise to craving and attachment; through the conditions of such craving and attachment, faults such as the need for protection arise. Therefore, one should contemplate that pleasure is even more [suffering] than pain.

Furthermore, pleasure serves as the gateway to suffering; because of craving for pleasure, one gives rise to unwholesome karma from the three poisons, falls into the hells and other realms, and undergoes various afflictions—all of which should be known to have pleasure as their root.

Furthermore, all unions are characterized by separation; when one is parted from what is beloved, one undergoes intense suffering, whereas this does not occur through parting from what is not beloved. Thus, it is known that pleasure exceeds suffering.

Furthermore, the arising of all objects of pleasure serves only to deceive sentient beings and cause them to fall into various sufferings; they are like wild birds lured by baited fish hooks, all for the sake of capture. Objects of pleasure are likewise so; therefore, one should contemplate them as suffering.

Furthermore, because one obtains only a slight taste within pleasant sensations, one incurs immeasurable faults; just as fish and beasts derive very little flavor yet suffer many calamities, one should therefore contemplate them as suffering.
Furthermore, pleasant feeling is the locus where afflictions arise. Why is this so?
Because one craves the body, one desires what is required for it; and due to these conditions of desire, afflictions such as hatred arise in succession.
Furthermore, pleasant feeling is the root of birth and death. Why is this so?
Because pleasure gives rise to craving;
as it is said in the Sūtra, "craving is the root of suffering."
Furthermore, all sentient beings engage in whatever they do for the sake of pleasure; therefore, it is called the root of suffering.
Moreover, the attachment to pleasant sensations is more difficult to relinquish than shackles.
Furthermore, within the cycle of birth and death, one is bound by the craving for such pleasure.
Why is this so? Because of their craving for pleasure, they do not escape birth and death.

Furthermore, this pleasant sensation always gives rise to suffering: there is the suffering of desire when seeking it, the suffering of recollection when losing it, and even when one obtains it, there is no satiety—like the ocean swallowing rivers—and this too is suffering.
Furthermore, pleasant sensation is the cause of non-exhaustion. Why is this so?

When sentient beings seek the causes of pleasure, they regard even perilous hardships as pleasure; thus, their minds do not grow weary or exhausted. For this reason, the wise person should contemplate suffering.
Furthermore, pleasant sensation is called the cause for the arising of various karmas.

Why is this so? Because through craving for pleasure one can initiate wholesome karma, and for the sake of present pleasure one initiates unwholesome karma; it is also the cause for the acquisition of all bodies.
Why is this so? By grasping at pleasure, craving arises; because of craving, one receives a body.
Furthermore, the sensation of pleasure is contrary to Nirvana.
Why is this so? Because sentient beings are greedily attached to the pleasures of birth and death, they do not delight in Nirvana.
Furthermore, those who have not yet abandoned desire cherish these pleasant sensations; since craving gives rise to suffering, one knows that pleasant sensation is the root of all suffering.

Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra that there are two kinds of seeking that are difficult to sever: first, the seeking of acquisition (*lābha-paryeṣaṇā*); second, the seeking of life (*jīvita-paryeṣaṇā*).
Seeking various desires according to one's wishes is called the seeking of acquisition.
To seek to obtain a lifespan in order to experience these various desires is called the pursuit of life.

Both of these pursuits have pleasant feeling as their basis; therefore, the wise find them difficult to abandon, yet they must be abandoned by being able to contemplate the characteristics of pleasant feeling as they truly are.

Furthermore, the savoring of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) can also defile the minds of those who have not yet attained the great wisdom that is free from desire; because it is so difficult to sever, it is even more severe than painful feeling.
Moreover, the savoring of pleasant feeling is the cause of craving and other afflictions; if there were no pleasant feeling, there would be nothing to crave.
Furthermore, the true wisdom that discerns the flavor of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is able to sever [craving]. Why is this so?
Because all worldly wisdoms must grasp the flavor of a higher stage in order to be able to relinquish a lower stage; thus, one knows that pleasant feeling is far more excessive than suffering.

Furthermore, the minds of sentient beings are bound to their places of birth; even animals cherish their bodies out of greed and attachment. One should know that this is entirely due to the savoring of pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*).
Therefore, one should contemplate pleasant sensation as suffering (*duḥkha*).
Chapter Eighty-One: Discourse on the Three Feelings Question:
It has already been understood that all things are suffering; by what distinction, then, are there three types of feeling?
Answer: It is simply a single sensation of suffering that, due to differences in time, is of three kinds:
that which is capable of afflicting and harming is called "suffering" (duḥkha).

Once they have been afflicted and harmed, they further seek other forms of suffering to counteract the previous suffering; because of this seeking through aspiration, great suffering temporarily ceases, and at that time it is called "pleasure.
When sorrow and joy are not clearly distinguished, and there is neither aspiration nor seeking, at that time it is called "neither-suffering-nor-pleasure."
Question: Is that which is neither painful nor pleasant not called feeling (*vedanā*)? Why is this so?
Because suffering and pleasure can be perceived, whereas neither-suffering-nor-pleasure cannot be perceived.
The answer is:
this person is touched by three types of contact—namely, painful contact, pleasant contact, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact; since the cause exists, one should know that the fruit exists.

Just as when a person is extremely hot, they experience pleasure upon encountering a cold touch, pain upon encountering a hot touch, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure upon encountering a touch that is neither cold nor hot; thus one knows that this neither-pain-nor-pleasure exists.
You may think that feeling cannot arise from a contact that is neither painful nor pleasant; this is not so.
Why? Because when a person perceives a contact that is neither cold nor hot, the very awareness of that object is itself called feeling; how then can you say it does not exist?

Furthermore, there are three distinctions among objects: the enemy, the friend, and the neutral person. One gives rise to joy toward a friend, sorrow toward an enemy, and equanimity toward the neutral person. Thus, we know that these three feelings exist because of the discrimination of perception (*saṃjñā*); it is due to the distinction of the objects that these three perceptions arise.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of conditions: those that are beneficial, those that are detrimental, and those that are both; those that are pleasant, those that are unpleasant, and those that are both; likewise, there are objects of greed, objects of hatred, and objects of delusion; there are states of joy, states of displeasure, and states that are both; and there are fruits of merit, fruits of demerit, and fruits of the imperturbable. Since these various conditions give rise to the three types of feeling accordingly, we know that this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling exists.

Furthermore, that which is agreeable to the mind is called pleasant feeling; that which is contrary to the mind is called painful feeling; and that which is neither contrary nor agreeable is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Furthermore, regarding the eight worldly dharmas—gain and loss, defamation and fame, praise and blame, suffering and pleasure—the ordinary person finds the four dharmas beginning with loss contrary to their mind, while regarding the four dharmas beginning with gain as agreeable. There must necessarily exist noble ones who have transcended desire and can relinquish both; this relinquishment is called the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Therefore, it is not non-existent.
Question:
If the three types of sensation exist by virtue of causes and conditions such as contact, then all mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) would be called sensation. Why is this so?
All mental activities present within the body are [experienced as] suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
The answer is:
so it is; all mental activities are termed "feeling" (vedanā).
Why is this so? The Sūtras speak of eighteen mental activities (*manopavicāra*);

herein, there is but a single mind with eighteen distinctions, namely: six activities of joy, six activities of sorrow, and six activities of equanimity. Because they are differentiated by perception (*saṃjñā*), there are portions of suffering, portions of pleasure, and portions of equanimity. Thus, one knows that all mental activities are none other than feeling (*vedanā*).
Furthermore, it is stated in the Sūtras that all feelings are suffering; therefore, we know that the mental formations existing within the body are all termed suffering.
It is also said that if form arises, it is the arising of suffering.
Why is form called suffering?
Because it is the cause of suffering, one knows that conditions and the sense faculties can only produce suffering.

Therefore, all mental formations are termed "feeling" (*vedanā*); because they are the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) should be contemplated as suffering.
Because of the suffering inherent in change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), one should contemplate pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*) as suffering;
the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*) is itself suffering.
These three types of suffering all arise from the combination of various conditions and perish moment by moment; therefore, the noble ones contemplate them as suffering.
Therefore, all mental activities are termed "feeling" (vedanā).
Question:
Are the untainted (anāsrava) feelings also suffering?
Answer: It is also suffering. Why is this so?

The noble ones also gradually abandon all untainted sensations (*anāsrava-vedanā*), from the first dhyāna up until the realization of the cessation of all perceptions (*sarva-nirodha-samāpatti*); in all these stages, there is suffering.
Furthermore, what is the difference between the pleasure of tainted dhyāna (*sāsrava-dhyāna-sukha*) and the pleasure of untainted dhyāna?
All contaminated (*sāsrava*) dhyānas are suffering because they have "self" as their cause;
all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dhyānas are likewise suffering for this reason.

Furthermore, when a noble one (*ārya*) abides in an uncontaminated mind, they feel profound revulsion toward everything; thus, when an uncontaminated mind arises, they experience deep weariness and aversion toward it, just as if a hair had entered the eye.
Ordinary beings do not understand this; they all take suffering to be pleasure.

Because the wisdom of the sages is profound and subtle, their revulsion for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) exceeds that of others who feel weary of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); therefore, untainted suffering (*anāsravaduḥkha*) is compared to tainted suffering (*sāsravaduḥkha*).
Furthermore, when the various noble ones attain the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), it is directed solely toward *nirvāṇa*. Why is this?

Because at that time, these persons clearly perceive all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as suffering; if they were to experience the pleasure of the untainted state, they would instead feel joy and delight, and would not give rise to a mind further directed toward *nirvāṇa* (*niyāna*).
Question: If all mental activities are called "feeling" (vedanā), how can there be other distinct dharmas such as the various types of mind? Answer:
This is simply a single sensation (*vedanā*); it is differentiated because the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) operate differently within its objective conditions (*ālambana*).

Although all mental factors (*citta-dharma*) likewise operate with different conditions, it is specifically at the time when consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes an object that this formation is designated as "mind" (*citta*).
As previously explained, these [phenomena] are called "feeling" (*vedanā*) because when all dharmas reside within the body, there are various distinctions such as benefit and so forth;
furthermore, it is often called "feeling" at the time when the mind is able to give rise to afflictions.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"The latent tendency of attachment resides in pleasant feeling; the latent tendency of aversion resides in painful feeling; and the latent tendency of ignorance resides in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Therefore, among the objects of conceptualization through perception, mental states such as joy and so forth are termed "feeling" (vedanā).
Why is this so? Because at that time, it is capable of giving rise to all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question:

If there are three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) within each of the [three] feelings, why is it definitively stated that the underlying tendency of craving (*rāgānuśaya*) exists only within pleasant feeling?
The answer is:
the underlying tendency of craving cannot exist within painful feeling.
Delusion is an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) in all circumstances because of the power of delusion.
Due to the power of delusion, one conceives the notion of pleasure within suffering; because one does not know or see things as they truly are, suffering gives rise to aversion.
Because the sensations of neither-pain-nor-pleasure are subtle, greed and aversion are not perceived therein.
Why is this? Because such a person does not give rise to perceptions of suffering or pleasure within this state.
Since they do not know or see the reality of things, only the latent tendency of delusion arises.
Furthermore, regarding the conditions for equanimity (*upekṣā*), if greed and hatred do not arise, ordinary persons claim that they have mastered those conditions.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"You have not mastered these conditions; it is simply because you have not awakened that greed and hatred do not arise."
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Whatever equanimity ordinary persons experience toward forms all relies upon form. If they surpass this object, they will either increase the notion of 'self' or diminish it, thereby giving rise once again to greed and hatred; thus, one knows that they have not yet surpassed the object."

Furthermore, the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant has the characteristic of quiescence, like the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). Because of this quiescence, the activity of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is subtle; consequently, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) conceive the notion of liberation therein. For this reason, the Buddha taught that within this state there exists the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*).

Furthermore, because the conditions have not yet been discerned, suffering and pleasure are not clearly perceived; if one knows these conditions, then suffering and pleasure are clearly perceived, and at that time, greed and hatred arise.
Question:
If the perception of these conditions gives rise to the characteristics of suffering and pleasure, then there should only be the sensations of suffering and pleasure.
The answer is:

At times, within these conditions, such a person does not give rise to a mind of pleasure nor a mind of suffering; therefore, it is not that there are only pleasure and suffering. As previously stated, all are suffering, yet there are three distinctions.
Question: You say that one perceives this object and subsequently gives rise to the notion of pleasure.
How does one perceive it?
It cannot be known through the awakening of ignorance.
The answer is:
because this person first grasps at signs within these conditions, there arise either the latent tendency of ignorance or the latent tendencies of greed and hatred within these conditions.
Question: Ignorance arises only with respect to suffering and pleasure,
as it is said in the Sūtra:
Regarding these various feelings, such a person does not know, as they truly are, their origin, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape.
Because of this ignorance, it is said that the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) underlies those feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant.
Therefore, the latent tendency of ignorance arises only with respect to pleasure and pain, not with respect to that which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
The answer is:

This sutra itself states that because one does not know, as they truly are, the origin, cessation, and gratification of the various feelings, the latent tendency of ignorance functions within that which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Question: Although this has been stated, the meaning is not so.

Why is it that because one does not know the arising and cessation of suffering and pleasure, the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) operates within the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
Why is this so? Because one is ignorant regarding other matters and is driven by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) toward other matters.

Therefore, this sutra should be stated as follows: because this person is ignorant of the origin and so forth regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) drives them within that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; or else, the latent tendency of ignorance does not drive them within that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The answer is:

Within the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, this person gives rise to three kinds of mental states. Because they conceive the notion of cessation and the notion of being neither painful nor pleasant, a mind that is neither painful nor pleasant arises. If they grasp at signs with false wisdom, a mind of pleasure arises; if they grasp at the flavor of bliss in higher realms, a mind of suffering arises.
Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of various feelings in many words. Why is this?
Because all feelings are driven by ignorance (*avidyā*), yet these neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are distinguished into three types according to their respective occasions.

Furthermore, if one has not yet fully realized suffering, its origin, and so forth, at that time one gives rise to the perception of pleasure within a painful sensation, and also gives rise to the perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; therefore it is said that because one does not know the origin and other aspects of the sensations, the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) drives them, though the latent tendency of ignorance predominantly drives the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Chapter 82: Inquiry into Feeling (Vedanā-vicaya). Question:
It is stated in the Sūtra that when this person experiences a pleasant feeling, he knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing this pleasant feeling."
"What kind of feeling is known as it truly is?
Past and future feelings cannot be apprehended as feelings, and a present feeling cannot be known by itself.
He replied:
The intention of this sutra is to speak of the feelings experienced by persons; therefore, there is no fault.
Furthermore, since feelings such as pleasure arise within the body and can be apprehended by the mind, there is likewise no error.
Furthermore, the names "pleasure" and so forth are applied to the instruments of pleasure; this is because in the world, one may also speak of the effect by means of the cause.

Moreover, such a person first experiences the feeling of pleasure and subsequently grasps its characteristics; therefore, it is said that they "know truly as it is when experiencing the feeling of pleasure."
Question: Is it called "feeling" (vedanā) because there is a feeler, or is it called "feeling" because it is that which is felt?

If it is called "feeling" because there is a feeler, then feeling would be distinct from pleasure and so forth; yet the sūtras speak of pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
If that which is capable of being felt is called "feeling," who is it that feels it?
It is called "feeling" by virtue of the act of feeling itself.
The answer is:
Pleasure is spoken of in relation to its conditions, just as fire is said to be either painful or pleasant; therefore, because one perceives the conditions, it is called "experiencing pleasure.
Furthermore, because sentient beings experience this sensation, that which is experienced is termed "feeling" (*vedanā*).
Question: Sentient beings are not called "feeling" (vedanā), yet the sūtras state that feeling is feeling. Answer:

The meaning of the name is as follows: where there is a characteristic (*nimitta*), there is activity (*abhisamskāra*). Within conventional designations (*prajñapti*), there are characteristics; when suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure exists in the body, the mind is able to perceive it. Therefore, feeling (*vedanā*) is called "feeling."
Question:

The sūtras state that when a practitioner contemplates feelings as being conducive to feeling (*vedanānupassī*), how do the characteristics of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure arise at that time?
At that time, does this person not give rise to the perception of suffering in all cases?
The answer is:
This person has not yet realized that "all is suffering"; they merely recollect the three types of feeling.
Question:
If one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness using the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), why is bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) mentioned? Answer:
Regarding all sensations, one should maintain mindfulness in this way: "This is physical pleasure; this is mental pleasure.

Furthermore, when practicing the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), a mark of pleasure arises within the body; because one maintains mindfulness upon this, it is called "physical pleasure."
Question:
If all sensations are mental phenomena (*cittadharma*), why is "bodily sensation" (*kāyikavedanā*) spoken of? Answer:
This was taught for the sake of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
The non-Buddhists claim that all sensations (vedanā) depend upon a self (ātman); therefore, the Buddha taught that all sensations depend upon the body and mind.
Question:
What is bodily sensation?
The answer is:
sensation produced by means of the five sense faculties is called bodily sensation; sensation produced by means of the sixth faculty is called mental sensation.
Question: How is this feeling (vedanā) called "defiled" (saṃkliṣṭa),
and how is it called "pure" (viśuddha)?

Answer: All afflictions (*kleśa*) are called "defilements" (*mala*). That which is experienced under the influence of these afflictions is called "defiled"; that which is not experienced under the influence of these afflictions is called "pure."
Question: In what sense is painful feeling called "pure"? Answer:
The painful sensation of one who has severed the afflictions is called "pure.
Furthermore, the painful sensation that is contrary to the afflictions is called "pure. Question:

The defilements and purities have already been explained; for what reason, then, are they further explained as being based on greed and based on renunciation, given that greed is affliction and renunciation is purity?
The answer is:
previously, defilement was explained in general terms; now, it is specifically explained that greed is the cause of defilement.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
there is joy with impurity, joy that is pure, and joy that is pure within purity.
Joy with impurity is the joy arising from the five objects of desire.
"Pure joy" refers to the joy of the first dhyāna.
"Purest joy within the pure" refers to the joy of the second dhyāna.
If one experiences [joy] solely for the sake of nirvāṇa, this is called "relying on emergence"; therefore, it is explained further.
Question:
Among the five faculties, why are the feelings of suffering and pleasure each divided into two, while the feeling of equanimity is not? Answer:

Sorrow and joy arise necessarily from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*); suffering and pleasure do not necessarily depend on conceptual discrimination. Because the conceptual discrimination of the neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is subtle, it does not constitute these two.
Question: Within the third dhyāna, why is that which is experienced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) called "pleasure" (*sukha*), and why is it not called "joy" (*prīti*)?
Answer:

This bliss is called "bliss" because it is profound and pervasive throughout both body and mind; whereas joy (*prīti*) can only pervade the mind and cannot pervade the body. Therefore, within the third dhyāna, the Buddha distinguished joy from bliss and stated that one experiences bliss with the body (*kāyena sukhaṃ vedayati*).
Question:
Among these three types of sensation, which one is capable of producing deep-seated afflictions? Answer:
A certain master of the Abhidharma says that pleasant sensation can arise. Why is this?
Because it was previously stated that due to causes and conditions such as decay and ruin, one undergoes great suffering.
Furthermore, the masters of the treatises say that painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*) can give rise [to afflictions]. Why is this?
Because sentient beings, being oppressed by suffering, give rise to deep afflictions (*kleśa*) in their quest for pleasure.

Furthermore, various forms of pleasure can be surpassed by even a slight amount of suffering; for example, when a person is fully immersed in the enjoyment of the five sensual desires, the mere intrusion of a mosquito or gadfly gives rise to a perception of suffering, whereas the pleasure of the five sensual objects such as form does not do so.
Furthermore, as it is said that the joy of having a hundred sons is not equal to the suffering of losing one son,
so too within the cycle of birth and death, the characteristics of painful feelings (*duḥkhavedanā*) are numerous, whereas pleasant feelings (*sukhavedanā*) are not. Why is this so?
There are many sentient beings in the three evil realms, while those born as gods or humans are few.

Furthermore, suffering is obtained naturally without the need for exertion, whereas seeking happiness through effort may or may not be attained; it is just like weeds that grow spontaneously in a field, while fine grain does not.
Furthermore, heavy karmic offenses arise because of painful sensations.
Why is this? Within painful sensations there lies the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), and the sūtras state that aversion constitutes a grave offense.
Furthermore, the masters of the treatises say that neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] can give rise [to craving]. Why is this?
Because within it there is the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*), and delusion is the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, this feeling is subtle, because the afflictions within it are difficult to perceive.
Moreover, this feeling is the fundamental nature of sentient beings, while suffering and pleasure are adventitious.
Furthermore, this feeling pervades all three realms, whereas the other two do not.

Furthermore, this sensation is the cause of long life; because of craving for this sensation, one lives for eighty thousand great kalpas, enduring for a long time the aggregates that manifest as suffering.
Moreover, this sensation is contrary to Nirvana.
Why is this so? Because within these [feelings], one gives rise to the mark of quiescence and the mark of nirvāṇa; consequently, one is no longer able to attain true nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, these feelings can be transcended by means of the Noble Path, as it is said that liberation is attained through the nature of detachment (*virāga*). Likewise, painful and pleasant feelings can also be transcended by means of the worldly path.
Furthermore, these feelings cease when the continuity [of existence] is severed at the ultimate limit of saṃsāra; therefore, they are capable of generating profound and thick afflictions.
Chapter Eighty-three: The Five Feeling Faculties (Pañca-vedanendriya-varga). Question:
Where does the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) reside, and where do the faculties up to equanimity (upekṣendriya) reside?
The answer is:
Suffering and pleasure reside in the body, following whichever body is obtained, up to the fourth dhyāna;
the remaining three [feelings] reside in the mind, following whichever mind is obtained, up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).

Question: As it is said in the Sūtras, the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) ceases in the first dhyāna; the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) ceases in the third dhyāna; the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) ceases in the fourth dhyāna; and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) ceases in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Therefore, what you say is not correct.
He replied:
"If you believe this sutra, then the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) should exist in the first dhyāna."
In your own system, however, it is actually the case that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) does not exist in the first dhyāna; therefore, you should not place faith in this sūtra.
[The opponent] asks:
In the realms of form and formlessness, one deeply cultivates wholesome dharmas, so there ought to be no sorrow or suffering.
Answer:
