Furthermore, it is like a dark room filled with venomous snakes: before the lamp has illuminated it, one feels attachment and pleasure; once they are seen, one abandons them. Sentient beings are likewise:
when fallen into existence through ignorance, they delight in the world; but when wisdom arises, their minds feel weary and seek renunciation.
In this way, craving is the root of the body.
Why is this so? Because it is through craving that one seeks.
There are two kinds of seeking: the seeking of sensual desires and the seeking of existence.
Seeking various sensual desires in the present is called the seeking of sensual desires; further seeking a future body is called the seeking of existence.
Thus, one should know that craving is the root of the body.

Furthermore, if one is attached to the five aggregates, the view of a self arises; this is called the grasping at the expression "self," and because of this grasping, the other three types of grasping arise. With grasping as a condition, there is becoming; with becoming as a condition, birth occurs. One should know, therefore, that the afflictions are the fundamental source of the body.

Furthermore, this body is entirely suffering; yet, regarding this suffering body, one gives rise to the perversion of perceiving it as pleasure. From this perversion of pleasure, inverted craving arises; by means of this inverted craving, one is able to receive a future body. Thus, we know that craving is the causal condition for the existence of the body.
Furthermore, this body subsists by means of the condition of food; because it clings to edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it does not transcend the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

As stated in the *Karmavarga*, because of craving for fragrance and taste, one is born in places such as latrines; because of clinging to touch (*spraṣṭavya*), one is born from a womb; and because of clinging to sensations of warmth or coolness, one is born from an egg or from moisture—all of these do not transcend the Desire Realm.
Because three kinds of feeling arise from three kinds of contact, it is said that contact is the condition for feeling; the same applies to the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*).

Forming the aspiration for a future body, thinking "I shall become this," with the view of self and consciousness as its basis, leads to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which brings about a future existence. Thus, all four nutriments arise from craving.
All sentient beings subsist by means of food; therefore, one knows that they are born through the causal condition of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Furthermore, regarding the four modes of birth—oviparous, viviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born: it is because of lustful craving that one is born oviparously or viviparously; it is because of greed for odors, flavors, and so forth that one undergoes moisture-birth; and it is by following what one craves that one gives rise to earnest karma and thus undergoes transformation-birth. Therefore, one knows that the distinctions among the four modes of birth all arise from greedy craving.

Furthermore, there are four ways of receiving a body: some can be killed by oneself but not by others, and so forth; these four all exist due to the distinctions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Thus, we know that the body exists through the causal conditions of craving.

Furthermore, among the four bases of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), consciousness abides in accordance with form, relying on form and taking form as its object, with joy acting as the moisture; the same applies to feeling, perception, and formations. Yet, consciousness itself is not called a "basis of consciousness," because at the time of consciousness there is no affliction (*kleśa*). Thus, we know that the body exists due to the causes and conditions of afflictions.
Furthermore, all twelve links of dependent origination arise from ignorance.

Why is this so? Because the mind that follows conventional designations is called ignorance; based on this ignorance, one gives rise to meritorious formations, non-meritorious formations, and imperturbable formations.

To desire the peace and happiness of sentient beings is called meritorious action; to cause suffering to sentient beings is called non-meritorious action; and to collect the mind in equanimity, compassion, and so forth is called immovable action.

Following these various karmas, consciousness abides within the subsequent body; depending on consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling arise. These four are the retributive fruits of the karma and afflictions of previous lives. Furthermore, based on this craving, craving, grasping, and becoming arise; these karmas and afflictions are able to produce future birth, old age, death, and so forth.
Thus, the continuity of these twelve links of existence all has ignorance as their root; therefore, one knows that the body exists due to the causal conditions of the afflictions.
Furthermore, birth and death have no beginning.
How is this known? It is stated in the Sūtras:

"The sense faculties, such as the eye, arise from the causal conditions of karma; karma arises from craving; craving arises from ignorance; ignorance arises from false recollection; and false recollection, in turn, arises from delusion due to the eye perceiving forms."
Thus, one knows that the cycle of birth and death is beginningless.

If one were to say that it is caused by Īśvara or other such entities, then it would not be beginningless; since this is untenable, one knows that the body exists due to the causal conditions of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, by extinguishing the afflictions (*kleśa*), one attains liberation.

Moreover, the bodies of sentient beings consist of various diverse categories; if these were caused by an *Īśvara* or similar [single cause], they would not be diverse. Since afflictions and karma are manifold, the bodies are likewise not uniform.

Furthermore, among the twenty-two faculties, the six consciousnesses arise based on the six sense-faculties; within these, there are the male and female faculties. Because these various dharmas continue in succession without interruption, it is called "life."
What is the root of this life? It is karma.

This karma is caused by afflictions (*kleśa*), and since afflictions depend upon sensation (*vedanā*), the five sensations serve as their roots. Thus, through this successive progression, birth and death continue in a stream; yet, by relying on the faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*), one is able to sever this continuity.
Thus, these twenty-two faculties circulate through birth and death; therefore, one knows that the body exists solely because of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, those who seek liberation give rise to the categories of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).
What is the purpose of this?
It is entirely for the sake of extinguishing all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because the knower perceives its benefit, they rely upon these various chapters; thus, one knows that the body exists due to the causes and conditions of the afflictions.

Furthermore, the various afflictions are extinguished in succession: by severing the three fetters, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*; by attenuating greed and other defilements, one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*; by exhausting the fetters of the desire realm, one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*. It is likewise within the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*): as each stage is successively exhausted, one finally attains the fruit of *arhat*.

In this way, because the afflictions are extinguished sequentially, the body also gradually perishes; if it were caused by Īśvara or other such deities, it would not perish gradually. Therefore, we know that the body exists due to the causal conditions of the afflictions.

Furthermore, all virtuous people seek to eradicate afflictions such as craving; they must perceive that through the causes and conditions of craving, one will encounter decline and distress in both this life and future lives, and for this reason they seek to eliminate it. If it were otherwise, they would not seek its elimination.

Since those who claim the body has its cause in Īśvara and so forth also seek to eliminate craving and the like, we know that the body exists by virtue of the causes and conditions of craving and the like.

Furthermore, the wise know that liberation is attained through wisdom; they know that bondage arises from a lack of wisdom, and thus they understand that the body exists due to the causal conditions of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Moreover, the Buddha has stated in various sūtras that one attains right liberation through the exhaustion of craving and delight.

Why is this so? It is because the eye and forms, and so forth, are not called "bondage"; rather, craving and delight are bondage. By destroying craving and delight, the mind attains right liberation; with a rightly liberated mind, one can enter *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, we know that it is due to the causes and conditions of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that there is a body.
Furthermore, because one attains liberation through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, we know that the body exists due to the causes and conditions of afflictions. Why is this so?

By contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena, one finds no signs to be grasped; because signs are extinguished, one does not aspire for a future body. Therefore, emptiness is called a gate of liberation.
When there is contradiction, there is bondage.
For these reasons, it has been clarified that the body exists by virtue of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This concludes the section on the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Chapter 141: The Section on the Truth of Cessation; Subsection One: Establishing Conventional Designations. The Treatise states:

The cessation of three kinds of mind is called the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya); namely, the conventional mind (*prajñapti-citta*), the dharma-mind (*dharma-citta*), and the empty mind (*śūnya-citta*).
Question:
How does one extinguish these three minds? Answer:

The mind of conventional designation (*prajñapti-citta*) is extinguished either through the wisdom arising from the condition of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), or through the wisdom arising from the condition of reflection (*cintā*). The mind of phenomena (*dharma-citta*) is extinguished within the stages such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) by means of the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*). The mind of emptiness (*śūnya-citta*) is extinguished upon entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or it is extinguished when entering *nirupadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa* at the moment the continuity [of existence] is severed.
Question: What is meant by "provisional name" (prajñapti)? Answer:

Because of the conceptual distinctions inherent in the aggregates (*skandha*); for example, as one speaks of a "person" based on the five aggregates, or as one speaks of a "jar" and so forth based on form, odor, taste, and touch.
Question: For what reason are these considered mere designations (*prajñapti*)?
Answer: In the sūtras, the Buddha said that just as the combination of axles and other parts is called a "chariot," so too the combination of the aggregates (skandhas) is called a "person.
Furthermore, as the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

All phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self; they arise from a multitude of conditions and lack any fixed nature, existing merely as names, merely as mental recollections, and merely as functional utilities.
Therefore, the five aggregates give rise to various designations, such as "sentient being," "human," "deva," and so forth.
Since this sutra negates the existence of truly real dharmas, it states that there are "only names."
Furthermore, the Buddha taught two truths: the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Ultimate truth refers to phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and nirvana; conventional truth refers to that which exists only as a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such as a jar formed through the causes and conditions of form and so forth, or a person formed through the causes and conditions of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Question:
If these do not exist within the First Truth (paramārthasatya), what is the purpose of speaking of them in terms of conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya)? Answer:
Sentient beings in the world experience conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
How is this known?
It is as when it is said that people believe in and accept a painted fire.
The Buddhas and noble sages, wishing to cause the world to transcend provisional designations (*prajñapti*), therefore speak by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As the Buddha said in a sutra:
"I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me, for the wise have nothing with which to dispute."
In ancient times, because people wished to utilize things, they established names for the myriad phenomena as they arose, such as "vase" and so forth.
If these were merely dharmas in their ultimate sense, they could not be utilized; therefore, the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is taught.

Furthermore, if one speaks of the two truths, then the Buddha-dharma is pure: because of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the wise do not triumph; because of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the ignorant do not dispute.

Furthermore, if one speaks of the two truths, one does not fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism, nor into wrong views or the extremes of suffering and pleasure; thus, karmic actions, their fruits, and retributions can all be established.

Furthermore, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is the foundation of all the Buddha’s teachings; it refers to the retribution of giving and observing precepts, which leads to birth in a favorable realm.
If one uses these dharmas to make the mind supple and pliant, such that it is capable of receiving the path of the Dharma, only then does one explain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Thus, the Buddha-dharma does not initially become profound all at once; rather, it is like the great ocean, which gradually deepens. Therefore, one speaks of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, only when one is able to achieve the wisdom that attains the Way can one be taught the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dharma*).
The Buddha thought to himself:
"The bhikṣu Rāhula is now able to achieve the wisdom of the Path; I shall preach the True Dharma for him.
It is like a ripe abscess: it is easy to break when it has ripened, but difficult to burst while it is still raw."
In this way, one uses the wisdom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to make the mind supple and pliant; thereafter, one should use the supreme wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*) to dismantle it.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"First one must know the differentiation of all phenomena (*dharmas*), and only then should one know Nirvana."

The practitioner first understands that all phenomena exist as provisional designations and exist as ultimate reality; only then can they realize the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Furthermore, the various afflictions are extinguished sequentially, from the coarse to the subtle:

for example, one eliminates the signs of "male" and "female" by means of the signs of "hair," "pores," and so forth; one eliminates the signs of "hair" and so forth by means of the signs of "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth; and finally, one eliminates the signs of "form" and so forth by means of the sign of "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). This is like using a wedge to extract a wedge; thus, it is taught according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, it is by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that the Middle Way is established. Why is this so?

Because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise in continuous succession, they are not annihilated; because they perish moment by moment, they are not eternal. To be free from these extremes of annihilation and eternity is called the Middle Way.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"When one sees the arising of the world, the view of non-existence is extinguished; when one sees the cessation of the world, the view of existence is extinguished.
Because there is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one can see its arising and its cessation; therefore, the conventional truth is taught.

Furthermore, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), all teachings of the Buddha are real; that is to say, the gateways of "self" and "non-self" are both valid. If there is no fault in asserting a self from the perspective of conventional truth, then it is likewise real to speak of non-self from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Furthermore, there are questions that are set aside as answers based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); however, if one proceeds from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dharma*), all such questions can be answered.
Moreover, to perceive sentient beings as truly existent is great delusion and darkness; yet, to say they do not truly exist is likewise to fall into delusion and darkness.

Why is this so? These views of existence and non-existence constitute the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, causing practitioners to emerge from the extreme of existence only to fall back into the extreme of non-existence.
If there were no conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), by what means could one emerge [from saṃsāra]?

Furthermore, if a person who has not yet attained the wisdom of true emptiness says that there are no sentient beings, this is called a false view; because it implies that there are no sentient beings undergoing birth and death, it is therefore termed a false view.
If one attains the wisdom of emptiness and says that there are no sentient beings, then there is no fault.
As it is said in a sutra, an Arhat bhikṣuṇī said to Māra:
"What do you take [as real]?"
Sentient beings are merely an empty collection of the five aggregates; in reality, there are no sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is said:

this body is a continuity of the five aggregates, empty and non-existent, like a transformation or an illusion that deceives ordinary people. It is designated as an enemy or a thief, like an arrow or a wound; it is suffering, empty, and without self, being nothing but the characteristic of arising and ceasing, of decay and ruin.
Question:
Since both are minds that perceive nothingness, why is one called "wrong view" while the other is called "the ultimate truth"? Answer:
If a person has not yet given rise to the wisdom of true emptiness, they will experience fear upon hearing the teaching of non-self because they still harbor a sense of self.
As the Buddha said:
"If ordinary worldlings hear that there is no self and that they shall no longer act, they will be greatly terrified."
Therefore, one should know that as long as the wisdom of emptiness has not been attained, because of the existence of the notion of a self, one fears *nirvāṇa*, which constitutes a false view;
once the wisdom of true emptiness is attained, knowing that [all things] are originally non-existent, there is nothing to fear.
Furthermore, this person has not yet attained true emptiness; if they perceive only non-existence, they fall into wrong views, namely the nihilistic view and false views.

If, however, this person first understands through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that there is a self and believes in karmic retribution, and later contemplates the characteristics of impermanence, arising, and ceasing of all phenomena, gradually realizing the extinction of the self and the mind, thereby extinguishing the mind of greed—then hearing the teaching of non-existence will involve no fault. For this reason, conventional truth is taught.
Furthermore, there were non-Buddhists who slandered the Buddha, saying: "The śramaṇa Gautama destroys the true self. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"I speak of the existence of sentient beings according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)."
In my understanding of Right View, it is taught that there are sentient beings who come and go within birth and death; this is called Right View.

However, because ordinary people rely on false conceptualization, they claim that sentient beings truly exist where in reality no such beings exist; thus, one refutes this false conceptualization, not the sentient beings themselves.

Just as objects such as a jar are spoken of by way of conventional designation— wherein neither the form and other [sensory constituents] themselves are the jar, nor does a jar exist separately apart from the form and other [constituents]—
so too, sentient beings are not the aggregates of form and so forth, yet sentient beings do not exist separately apart from the aggregates of form and so forth.

Just as one transcends conventional designations by means of form and so forth, so too does one transcend form and so forth by means of the characteristic of cessation; this is done through analogy to make the meaning easy to understand.
It is just like a painted lamp, which is also called a "lamp," yet in reality lacks the function of a lamp.
Thus, although one speaks of the existence of a jar, it does not exist in reality;
although one speaks of the five aggregates, they do not exist in the ultimate sense. Chapter 142: On Conventional Designations. Question:
How is it known that things such as jars exist only as conventional designations and are not real?
Answer: Within conventional designations (prajñapti), characteristics are indicated; within ultimate reality (bhūtatathatā), no characteristics are indicated.
For example, one may say "this color is the color of a jar," but one cannot say "it is the color of color," nor can one say "it is the color of feeling (vedanā) and so forth."
Furthermore, a lamp can illuminate by means of its quality of color and can burn by means of its quality of touch;
however, such is not observed among ultimate dharmas (*dravyadharma*).

Why is this? Consciousness does not cognize by means of a distinct instrument, nor does sensation experience by means of a distinct instrument; therefore, we know that "possessing instruments" exists only as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

Furthermore, conventional existence is established by depending on distinct phenomena, just as a jar is established by depending on form and so forth; however, a real dharma is not established by depending on distinct phenomena.
Why is this? It is because, for example, sensation is not established by depending on distinct phenomena.
Furthermore, conventional designations possess manifold capacities; for example, a lamp can both illuminate and burn, whereas real dharmas are not seen to do so.
Why is this? For instance, feeling (*vedanā*) cannot simultaneously feel and cognize.
Furthermore, the name "chariot" resides within its wheels, axle, and so forth, whereas names such as "color" do not reside within the object itself; such is the distinction.

Moreover, the wheels, axle, and other parts are the causes and conditions that constitute a chariot, yet the name "chariot" does not exist within them. Thus, although the dharma of a "chariot" does not exist within the causes and conditions of the chariot, it is through these that the chariot is established. Therefore, we know that the chariot is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

Furthermore, just as one can speak of "form" and so forth using the names "form" and so forth, but one cannot speak of "vases" and so forth using the names "vase" and so forth, we know that vases and the like are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Moreover, within conventional designations, mental activity is indeterminate;

for example, when a person sees a horse, they may say they see the horse's tail, or the horse's body, or its hide, or its hair. Or they may say they hear the sound of a lute, or the sound of its strings. Or they may say they smell a flower, or the fragrance of the flower. Or they may say they taste curd, or the flavor of the curd. Or they may say they touch a person, or a person's body, or a person's arm, or a person's hand, or a person's finger, or a finger joint.

The mental consciousness moves among such things as sentient beings, conceiving that "the body is a sentient being" or "the mind is a sentient being," or that "form and so forth are a jar" or that "there is a jar apart from form."
When the mind is fixed and immovable upon such real dharmas, one cannot say, "I see form and also see sound," and so forth.

Furthermore, among things that can be known, it is impossible to say that they are also called "existent" in the same way as [conventional] designations; because things like jars are merely conventional designations, we know that jars and the like exist only as conventional designations (*prajñapti-sat*).
Why is this so? Because dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) cannot be described among [the categories] such as "knowable" (*jñeya*).

Furthermore, while the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of dharmas such as form can be described, the specific characteristics of things such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) cannot; therefore, one knows that these exist only as provisional designations (*prajñaptisat*).
Some say that the characteristic of conventional designation exists elsewhere and not within the conventional designation itself. As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Karma is the characteristic of the wise and the unwise; if one is able to initiate wholesome karma through body, speech, and mind, one is called 'wise'; if one initiates unwholesome karma through body, speech, and mind, one is called 'unwise'."
Physical and verbal actions depend upon the four great elements, while mental action depends upon the mind; how, then, can these three things be characterized as the marks of the wise or the unwise?
Therefore, one knows that they are merely provisional names and possess no intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, although provisional designations and characteristics may exist elsewhere, they are likewise not unitary; for example, it is said that a person experiences suffering and affliction as if a spear had entered their heart—this "affliction and destruction" is the characteristic of form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, this characteristic of feeling is also explained among human beings, as the Buddha said:
"Both the wise and the foolish experience suffering and pleasure; however, the wise do not give rise to greed or anger toward suffering and pleasure, nor do they grasp at them as being more or less."
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the characteristic of perceiving; it is also spoken of in relation to human beings, as when it is said: "I see light" or "I see the performance of forms.

Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the characteristic of initiating activity; they are also spoken of in relation to human beings, as when it is said: "This person initiates meritorious formations, or initiates demeritorious formations, or immovable formations."
Consciousness is the characteristic of consciousness, which is also spoken of among human beings; as it is said:
"The wise one discerns phenomena just as the tongue tastes flavors.
Therefore, even when spoken of in other contexts, the mention of many characteristics refers to conventional designations.
The characteristics of form and so forth do not exist elsewhere, nor are they manifold.
Furthermore, if a dharma is driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), it exists as a conventional designation (*prajñapti-sat*);
a real dharma (*dravya-sat*) is not driven by the underlying tendencies, because it is the underlying tendencies that drive sentient beings.

Furthermore, no cognition arises within mere designations; rather, cognition first arises with respect to form and other such [sensory objects], and only subsequently does one, through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), speak of "I see a jar" and so forth.
Moreover, the cognition of a jar necessarily depends upon form and the other [sensory objects].
Why is this so? It is because one refers to color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility as "a jar.
Within the ultimate dharmas, cognition requires nothing further.
Furthermore, doubt arises regarding conventional designations (prajñapti), such as: "Is this a tree stump or a person?
However, doubt does not arise regarding [the ultimate constituents] such as form (rūpa) and so forth, such as: "Is this form or sound?
Question: [Why is this so?]
There is also doubt regarding form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates: "Is there form, or is there no form? The answer is: Not so.

If one perceives form, one will never doubt that it is sound; rather, it is due to other causes and conditions that one doubts whether form exists or not. For example, having heard it said that form is empty, yet still seeing form, one then gives rise to doubt, asking: "Does it exist, or does it not?"
If one perceives the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), this doubt is severed. Question:
Within the truth of cessation there is also doubt: "Is there cessation, or is there no cessation?"
Answer: Doubt arises regarding that which is grasped, not regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
If one hears it said that cessation exists and also that there is no cessation, doubt arises therein as to whether it exists or does not exist.
At that time, this person does not perceive the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Why is this?
One who perceives the Truth of Cessation no longer has any doubt; therefore, we know that the locus of doubt is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti-sat*).
Furthermore, the arising of multiple cognitions with respect to a single object is a conventional existence (*prajñaptisat*), such as a jar and the like;
it is not so in the case of real dharmas (*dravyasat*). Why is this?
Within the aggregate of form (*rūpa*), the ear-consciousness and other such cognitions do not arise.

Furthermore, that which is subsumed under multiple bases (*āyatana*) exists only as a conventional designation (*prajñapti-sat*), like a jar or similar objects; therefore, some say that conventional designations are subsumed under four bases.
Real dharmas (*dravya-dharma*), however, cannot be subsumed under multiple bases.

Furthermore, if something can perform an action despite lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it exists as a conventional designation (*prajñapti-sat*). This is like saying "a person acts," yet the substance of the person and the substance of the action cannot be found in reality.
Furthermore, all such discriminations as "enemy" or "relative" are merely conventional designations; they do not exist as real dharmas.
Why is this? Because if one directly regards dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, the notions of "enemy," "relative," and so on, do not arise.
Furthermore, all activities such as coming and going, breaking and destroying, burning and rotting, are merely conventional designations; they do not exist as real dharmas. Why is this so?
Because real dharmas are neither burned nor destroyed.
Furthermore, karmic actions such as demerit and merit exist only as provisional designations. Why is this so?
Sins such as killing and merits such as abstaining from killing are neither substantially existent nor conventionally existent;
they are established through mutual dependence, just like this and that, light and heavy, long and short, large and small, teacher and disciple, father and son, or noble and base.
Substantial dharmas are established without depending on anything else. Why is this?
For example, form does not depend on other things to further establish sound and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not by means of emptiness that it is negated; rather, it exists as a provisional designation (*prajñapti-sat*), just as one negates a forest by relying on trees, negates a tree by relying on its roots and trunk, and negates the roots and trunk by relying on their constituent colors and so forth.
If one uses emptiness to refute the existence of these real dharmas, it is like using emptiness to refute form and other such phenomena.

Furthermore, that which follows the sphere of emptiness exists as a conventional designation (*prajñapti-sat*), while that which follows the sphere of selflessness exists as a real dharma (*dharma-sat*).
Furthermore, there are four theories:
first, identity; second, difference; third, the ineffable; and fourth, non-existence. Since all four of these theories entail faults, we know that jars and the like exist as mere designations.
First, [the identity view] is that color, taste, smell, and touch are themselves the jar.
Second, [the difference view] is that apart from color and the other [sensory qualities], there exists a jar separately.
Third, [the ineffability view] is that it cannot be said that color and the others are the jar, nor can it be said that there is a jar apart from color and the others.
"Non-existent" means that this jar does not exist.
Since all four of these arguments are untenable, we know that the jar is a mere designation (*prajñapti*).
143. Chapter 143: Refuting the [Theory of] One Substance. Question:
What fault is there in these four positions?
The answer is:
as for the fault of the first position, it holds that the characteristics of phenomena such as form are each distinct; if [one were to say] they constitute a single jar, that would be impossible.
Furthermore, each individual constituent such as form (*rūpa*) is not called "earth";
how then could their combination constitute earth?
Why is this so? If each individual horse is not called a cow, how could their combination become a cow?
Question:
Just as individual sesame seeds cannot form a heap, yet their combination can do so, so too individual elements such as form (*rūpa*) cannot constitute earth, yet their combination can do so.
Answer: It is not so. Why is this?
A heap of hemp exists as a conventional designation (*prajñapti-sat*); this discussion concerns primary dharmas (*dravya-dharma*). How, then, can it serve as an analogy?
Furthermore, color, odor, taste, and tangibility are four distinct dharmas, whereas earth is a single dharma; thus, the four cannot be identical to the one.
If the four were one, then one would also have to be four; this is impossible. Therefore, we know that form and the other [qualities] are not identical to earth.

Furthermore, everyone in the world speaks of "the color of earth," "the fragrance of earth," "the taste of earth," and "the touch of earth," yet no one says "this is earth" while pointing to its color. Color must be indicated by means of a distinct property, such as saying "the house of so-and-so."
Question:
This does not demonstrate [the nature] by means of a different phenomenon, but rather demonstrates it by its own nature, like the hands and feet of a stone statue. Why is this so?
Just as there is no stone person apart from its hands and feet,
so too, although this earth is not separate from form and the other [sensory objects], what fault is there in its manifesting itself by means of its own essence?
Answer: If it is claimed that earth manifests itself through its own color and other qualities, this is logically untenable.
Although you have cited the analogy of a stone statue, that analogy is incorrect.

Why is this so? If one points to a stone man’s hand, the rest of the body is thereby designated as the "stone man. Furthermore, there can be speech regarding that which is in space, just as when one speaks of a "stone man's body," at that time the stone man has no other [parts] beyond it, yet it is still spoken of.
As the Buddha has taught that within this body there are hair, fur, blood, flesh, and so forth, and that apart from these hairs and other constituents, no separate body exists;

although there is no distinct substratum for these hairs and other parts, it can nevertheless be spoken of as such. Therefore, one should know that the claim regarding a "stone person" is likewise a false teaching.
If you claim that earth is constituted by stones, then there would be no such thing as earth.
In your own scriptures, it is said:
"That which possesses color, odor, taste, and tangibility is earth."
This earth is not identical to its body; therefore, we know that color, odor, taste, and touch are not themselves the earth.

Furthermore, among the various *guṇas* (qualities), they cannot be shown to be one another; one cannot say that color possesses odor, but one can say that earth possesses color, taste, odor, and touch. Thus, we know they are not one.
Furthermore, since the mind of form (*rūpa*) and so forth is distinct from the mind of earth (*pṛthivī*), we know that form and the others are not earth.
Moreover, the names for form and the others are different, and the name for earth is also different.
Question:
If it is argued that the mind and its various designations are all distinct because they exist through conjunction,
the answer is:
if the mind and its designations exist merely through conjunction, then that conjunction itself is but a name.
In that case, "earth" exists only as a name; there is no discussion of it as a substantial entity.
Furthermore, earth can be known by all the sense faculties.
How is this known?
A person forms this thought:
"I see earth, I smell earth, I taste earth, I touch earth.

If color, odor, taste, and tangibility were themselves earth, then one should not form the perception of earth solely within color, saying "I see earth"—the same would apply to odor and the others. Yet, in reality, one forms the perception of earth solely within color; therefore, we know that it is not color and the other [sensory objects] that constitute earth.

Based on the causes and conditions of conventional designations, one portion may also be described by means of conventional names; for example, when a person cuts down a tree, one may say "he cuts down a tree" and one may also say "he cuts down a forest."

Furthermore, regarding the five *guṇas*, the *dravya* (substance) is distinct from that which exists within them as their causal conditions; by virtue of these causal conditions, the theory of non-duality is not established.
Moreover, the Sāṃkhyas assert that the five *guṇas* constitute earth.
This is also not the case. Why?

As previously stated, sound arises in a continuous succession of momentary destructions, distinct from form and other [sensory objects], and does not serve as the cause for the formation of the four great elements; therefore, we know that it is not the case that all four great elements possess sound.
Chapter 144: Refuting the Category of Difference Question:
What faults are there in the doctrine of difference? Answer:
Apart from phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), there is no further "earth" (*pṛthivī*).
How is this known?
The mind does not arise with respect to earth apart from form, odor, taste, and tangibility; rather, the mind arises only with respect to phenomena such as form.
Why is this so? Just as form differs from sound and other objects, the cognition of form arises without depending on sound and the like.
If earth existed separately from form and the others, then the cognition of earth should likewise arise without depending on form and the others.
In reality, it is not that they do not depend [on other factors]; therefore, there is no separate entity called "earth. Question:
It is not that they do not depend on other dharmas; rather, the mind and mental states of form necessarily depend on the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) to arise.

Answer: This shall be explained in the "Chapter on Refuting General Characteristics" (*Saṃanyalakṣaṇadūṣaṇavarga*): apart from form (*rūpa*), there is no separate characteristic of form; therefore, it is not so.
Furthermore, since there are no faculties capable of cognizing dharmas such as earth as distinct entities, we know that there are no separate earths and so forth.
Question:
Earth and the other elements can be apprehended by two faculties, namely the body faculty (kāyendriya) and the eye faculty (cakṣurindriya).
How is this known?
When one perceives with the eye that this is a jar, and touches it with the body-faculty (kāyendriya), one likewise knows that this is a jar.
Therefore, your claim that the earth is not apprehended by any faculty is incorrect.
He replied:
If that were so, this jar would be apprehended by four sense-faculties, as it is also smelled with the nose-faculty and tasted with the tongue-faculty.
Question:
The nose-faculty and the tongue-faculty cannot apprehend the jar.
Why is this so? Because in the dark one cannot distinguish whether it is the scent of a jar or the scent of a basin, nor can one taste whether it is a jar or a basin.
He replied:
Although one cannot distinguish between a jar and a basin, one develops cognition regarding the clay, such as smelling the clay or tasting the clay.
Furthermore, if a jar were buried with only its mouth exposed, whether one sees it or touches it, one could not definitively know whether it is a jar, a cauldron, or a broken tile.
Therefore, one should know that the visual faculty and the tactile faculty likewise cannot apprehend a jar.

Furthermore, although the cognition of a jar arises in the dark, one cannot distinguish whether it is a golden jar or a silver jar; thus, one should know that the visual faculty and the tactile faculty likewise cannot apprehend a jar.

Furthermore, the olfactory faculty and the gustatory faculty are able to apprehend phenomena such as flowers, fruits, milk, and curd; the visual faculty and the tactile faculty, however, cannot. For example, although one may see flowers and the like, one cannot distinguish their fragrant or foul odors, nor their pleasant or unpleasant qualities, nor their sweetness or acidity.
Therefore, it is not the case that the eye-faculty and body-faculty perceive *dravya* (substance) while the nose-faculty and tongue-faculty do not.

Just as the nose-faculty and tongue-faculty possess discrimination even though they do not apprehend distinct *dravyas*, so too it is with the eye-faculty and body-faculty; although there are no distinct *dravyas*, they likewise possess discrimination.

Furthermore, among the five sense faculties, there is no cognition that apprehends conventional designations; therefore, one knows that conventional designations are not obtained by the faculties of the eye, body, nose, or tongue.
Within the sixth faculty, however, there is a cognition capable of cognizing conventional designations.
Why is this so? Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to take all phenomena as its objects.
Furthermore, if the eye were able to see both form and non-form, it should likewise be able to see sounds and other such objects.
If that were so, then the sense organs such as the ear would no longer be required;
however, this is untenable. Therefore, the substance (*dravya*) is not apprehended by means of the visual faculty or the tactile faculty.
Question:
Since the eye can see a substance (*dravya*) by means of its color (*rūpa*), it does not follow that all distinct phenomena (*dharma*) other than color are visible.
Answer:
To claim that one perceives the jar by means of its color is not correct. Why is this so?
Who created the color of the jar?
However, it is through their conjunction that [the jar is perceived]; therefore, color does not apprehend the jar.
Furthermore, if one were to apprehend other dharmas as visible by means of a visible dharma, then since dharmas such as the jar are invisible, color too would have to be invisible.
Furthermore, the jar would have to be of two kinds—both visible and invisible—because it is cognized by means of both visible and invisible phenomena.

Moreover, if it were held that the eye and other faculties are cognizable because they are cognized by means of phenomena such as color-form (*rūpa*), then the characteristic of color-form itself should not be something known by the visual faculty.

Why is this so? According to your doctrine, form is visible because it possesses the characteristic of form (*rūpa-nimitta*). Yet, that characteristic of form itself has no further characteristic; if that were the case, the characteristic of form would be invisible. Therefore, your position is untenable.
Furthermore, if form were visible because it is perceived by means of color, then all the sense faculties should perceive substantial entities (*dravya*).
The auditory faculty should also perceive space, because it perceives sound;
likewise, the tactile faculty should perceive wind, because it perceives touch.
But your doctrine is not so; therefore, there is no such cognition of dharmas.
[The opponent] asks:
Other dharmas cannot function as cognition, but only form (rūpa) can function as cognition.
The answer is:
Not so. Within this, there is no causal condition such that form alone is able to act as a cognitive object while other phenomena cannot.
As you say that there are many substantial entities (*dravya*) and that among them color (*rūpa*) is visible— if this were so,

then one would obtain color by means of color; one ought to perceive color through the characteristic of color (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) before it can be apprehended, for color alone cannot serve as its own perceiver.
If one speaks in this manner, one still does not escape the aforementioned fault.
Furthermore, since the cognition of color arises at one time and the cognition of the jar arises at another time, even if color can be apprehended, what benefit does this provide regarding the jar?

Furthermore, just as a blind person, through familiarity with the measure of a jar, can perceive it as being like a jar even after the faculty of sight has been lost through touch, it follows that color alone cannot be the cause of seeing.
Moreover, the body-faculty of a blind person can also perceive wind; therefore, cognition is not produced solely through the apprehension of color.
Furthermore, your own sūtra also states: "When contact comes and touches the body, it is not earth, water, or fire; one should know that the invisible characteristic is wind.
This, too, is not correct.
Why is this so? When a blind person perceives this wind, they do not know whether this tactile sensation is visible or invisible.
Furthermore, when a person sees phenomena such as quantity with the eye, there is no perception of form therein.

There are those who, upon smelling an odor, can also know that which is not the dharma of odor; likewise, upon tasting a flavor, they can also know that which is not the dharma of flavor. Therefore, it must be held that one can only know a substance (*dravya*) after perceiving its color; however, this is not the case.
Question:
If color is not a cause for perception within the act of seeing, then such qualities as number and quantity—
which reside in invisible *dravyas* (substances) and in wind— should also be visible.
The answer is:

In our doctrine, there is no other dharma visible apart from form (*rūpa*). Therefore, we know that when form arises within the continuum of dharmas, the eye is able to see it; once the eye has seen the form, the conceptualization of a "vase" (*ghaṭasaṃjñā*) immediately arises.
If no form arises within a phenomenon, then even though an eye is present therein, the notion of a distinct jar does not arise.
Therefore, it is illogical to maintain that a jar exists separately from form and the other [sensory qualities].
Chapter 145: Refuting the Ineffable Question:
What faults are there in the doctrine of the ineffable?
The answer is:
Among real dharmas, there is nothing that cannot be described in terms of identity or difference. Why is this so?
There are no causes, conditions, or analogies by which one may know that [things] are ineffable; since dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) truly exist, they are not ineffable.

Furthermore, each dharma possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); for example, the characteristic of form is its susceptibility to being afflicted and destroyed, and there is no other characteristic. How, then, can it be called ineffable?

Furthermore, because there is differentiation according to the differentiation of consciousness, phenomena possess differentiation; for example, visual consciousness cognizes form but does not cognize sound and so forth. Therefore, in this context, there is nothing that cannot be described.
Furthermore, visible form (rūpa) is subsumed under the sense-base of the visible (rūpāyatana), not under the sense-bases of sound and so forth.
If you wish to maintain that there is something inexpressible, then "form is form" is expressible, while "form is non-form" is inexpressible;
the same applies to sound and the other [sense-objects].
Furthermore, all phenomena possess sequential numbering; if they were ineffable, then all phenomena would be without number.
Why is this? Because the first and the second would not be distinct from one another.

Therefore, one should know that in reality there is no such thing as an "ineffable dharma"; it is only within the context of conventional designations (*prajñapti*) that, for the sake of [addressing] identity or difference, one speaks of the "ineffable.
Chapter 146: Refuting Non-existence. Question: What faults are there in the position of non-existence?
The answer is:
If there were nothing, then there would be no retribution for demerit and merit, nor any phenomena such as bondage and liberation.
Furthermore, if one clings to the notion that "nothing exists," that very clinging is also non-existent, because there would be neither a speaker nor a listener.

Furthermore, there are theories such as the doctrine of non-existence (*abhāva*) that are all asserted on the basis of faith: whether through faith in what is seen and known, or faith in what is inferred, or following scriptural authority; however, if one asserts that nothing exists at all, it does not fall within these three categories.

If you think that I merely follow the scriptures, this is not so; for the meaning of the scriptures is difficult to comprehend, as they sometimes speak of existence and sometimes speak of non-existence—how, then, can one place trust in them?
If one relies on inference based on faith, it must first be preceded by direct perception before one can infer.

Furthermore, phenomena such as jars are presently perceived to exist because they are capable of producing cognition; since a phenomenon exists in accordance with its capacity to produce cognition, it is not non-existent.
Furthermore, jars, basins, and so forth currently exhibit distinct differences; if all things were non-existent, how could there be such differences?
If you think that distinctions exist due to false conceptualization, why do you not likewise conceptualize jars and the like within empty space?
Furthermore, if you claim that the mind conceiving of things arises due to ignorance (*moha*), then if all things are non-existent, this ignorance would also not exist; by what cause could it arise?
Moreover, according to your view that all phenomena are non-existent, on what basis could such knowledge arise?
All forms of cognition do not arise without an object; they are called "cognition" because they cognize objects, and thus this cognition should not be said to be non-existent.
Furthermore, if there were no cognition at all, then all people would now be able to act according to their own whims.

Furthermore, all virtuous people delight in wholesome dharmas such as generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, and they distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas; therefore, we know that [the external world] is not non-existent.

Moreover, dharmas such as vases can be known through present perception, yet you claim that all present things are non-existent. Since you thus deny the existence of dharmas, you should not even trust the scriptural texts.
That being so, for what reason and by what conditions is it said that "all things are non-existent"?
Therefore, this matter—that all things are non-existent—must be clarified.
If it cannot be clarified through reasons and conditions, then the positions held by others would necessarily be established as true.
Because the opposing argument is established, your doctrine is thereby refuted.
If there are causes and conditions by which something could be established, it cannot be called "non-existent.
147. Chapter on Establishing Non-existence, Number One Hundred and Forty-Seven. The Proponent of Non-existence says:
Although you have used verbal expressions to refute emptiness, all dharmas are in fact non-existent, because the sense faculties and their objects are all unapprehendable. Why is this so?
Within all dharmas there is no part that can be grasped; therefore, all dharmas are ungraspable, and because they are ungraspable, they do not exist.
If you claim that although the whole (avayavin) cannot be apprehended, its parts (avayava) can be apprehended, this is not so; for the mind does not arise with respect to the parts. Why is this?
Because coarse objects such as jars can be apprehended.
Furthermore, the parts do not constitute the whole. Why is this so?
Because there are parts, one speaks of "parts"; because there are no parts, there are also no "parts.
Furthermore, since there are no *dravyas* (substances), there are no *guṇas* (qualities) that possess parts; therefore, there are no parts.
Furthermore, if one perceives the constituent parts, one should constantly give rise to the cognition of parts and not the cognition of a jar.
Why is this? If one is constantly mindful of the cessation of the parts, the cognition of a jar should not arise.
Furthermore, if the cognition of the parts occurred first and the cognition of the jar arose subsequently, then the cognition of the jar would have to arise after a long interval;
yet in reality it does not arise after such a delay, therefore one does not recollect the parts.
Furthermore, when one perceives a jar, no conceptualizing mind arises toward its constituent parts; rather, the mind of "jar" itself arises, and yet there are no such parts at all. Why is this?
All constituent parts can be analyzed and broken down until they reach the level of atoms; and when these atoms are further divided spatially, they ultimately dissolve into nothingness.
Furthermore, all phenomena ultimately give rise to the wisdom of emptiness; therefore, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all constituent parts are non-existent.
Moreover, if one speaks of such parts, one subverts the two truths (*dvaya-satya*).

Why is this so? If one were to say that there is no whole (avayavin) but only its parts (avayava), then there would be no such things as coming, going, seeing, or the various karmas of cutting and so forth; in that case, conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) would not exist.

You take the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) to be emptiness, yet within the ultimate truth there are also no constituent parts (*avayava*). Therefore, one should know that if one speaks only of constituent parts, they do not enter into the two truths; because they do not enter into the two truths, they do not exist.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon can be transcended, it is thereby non-existent; for example, just as one part (avayava) is transcended by the whole (avayavin), so too is the preceding part transcended by other parts. Because it can be transcended, there is no discourse regarding such a part.
Furthermore, form and the other [sense objects] are also non-existent. Why is this?
Because the eye cannot see subtle forms, and the mind cannot apprehend present forms; therefore, form is ungraspable.

Furthermore, visual consciousness cannot differentiate what is form; mental consciousness exists in the past and is not present within form. Therefore, there is no one capable of differentiating form, and because there is no differentiation, form cannot be apprehended.

Furthermore, the initial consciousness cannot differentiate form, and the same is true for the second consciousness and those that follow; therefore, there is no [consciousness] capable of differentiating form.

Question: After the visual consciousness has apprehended form, it is subsequently recollected by the mental consciousness (manovijñāna); therefore, it is not the case that there is no differentiation.

Answer: Once visual consciousness has seen a form, it immediately ceases, and subsequently mental consciousness arises; this mental consciousness does not see the form. Since it does not see it, how could it remember it?
If one could recollect what was not seen, then a blind person should also be able to recollect colors;
yet in reality they do not recollect them. Therefore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot recollect.
Question:
"From visual consciousness, mental consciousness arises; therefore, one is able to recollect.
The answer is: "Not so."

Why is this so? Because all subsequent moments of mind arise based on visual consciousness, they should all be able to remember, and furthermore, one should never forget [the object], since they arise from it;
yet in reality this is not the case, therefore we know that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) likewise cannot remember.
Just as one recollects a false apprehension of form, so too all things such as jars are equally deceptive, being non-existent yet falsely grasped; therefore, no objects exist at all.
Furthermore, if it is said that the eye sees, does it see by reaching the form, or is it able to see without reaching it?
If [the eye] were to reach [the object], it would be unable to see; that the eye has no characteristic of going has already been explained previously.
If it could see without reaching [the object], it should see all forms in every place;
yet in reality it does not see them. Therefore, we know that it is not by not reaching [the object] that it can see.
Question:
When form is within the range of cognition, the eye is able to see it. Answer:
What is meant by "the object of cognition"? Question:
It is called the object of cognition at the time when the eye is capable of seeing.
Answer: If the eye were able to cognize an object even without reaching it, then all forms in every location would be objects of cognition.
Therefore, since neither reaching nor not reaching allows for seeing, we know that form is invisible.
Furthermore, if the eye and visible forms existed first and the visual consciousness arose later, then that visual consciousness would be without a basis and without an object.

If they were simultaneous, it could not be said that consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as its causes and conditions, because there would be no sequential relationship of cause and effect.

Furthermore, the eye is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). If the eye were able to see, then the ear and other faculties should also be able to see, because they are equally composed of the four great elements;
the same applies to visible form (*rūpa*).
Moreover, as for this visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), it must either have a location or lack one; both positions entail logical fallacies.
Why is this? If visual consciousness depends upon the eye, then it must have a location; if a thing has no location, it cannot have a basis for dependence.

If you claim that consciousness arises in a partial portion of the eye, or arises throughout it entirely, or that consciousness arises simultaneously in both eyes, then it would have a location. To have a location is to have parts; if this were so, then a single consciousness would be composed of multiple consciousnesses.
If this were the case, there would be the fault of multiple consciousnesses arising simultaneously.
Furthermore, each individual part of a consciousness could not cognize; it would be the possessor of parts (*avayavin*) that should cognize, yet in reality, no such possessor of parts exists.
There is such a fault.
If there were no locus, then one should not rely upon the eye.
Chapter 148: Refutation of Sound. Proponents of Non-existence say:
Not even a single word exists. Why is this so?
Because the mind perishes moment by moment, and sound likewise perishes moment by moment; it is like saying "puruṣa"—this speech cannot be heard.
Why is this so? Following what one hears "fu," the consciousness does not hear "lou";
hearing "lou," the consciousness does not hear "sha."
There is no single consciousness capable of grasping three words; therefore, there is no consciousness capable of grasping a single phrase. Thus, one knows that sound cannot be heard.
Furthermore, while sound is heard by a distracted mind, it cannot be heard by a concentrated mind. That which is known by a concentrated mind is reality; therefore, sound cannot be heard.
Furthermore, whether sound reaches the ear or does not reach it, it cannot be heard; because it cannot be heard, there is no sound.
Moreover, some say that the ear is of the nature of empty space (*ākāśa*), and it is called "empty space" because it contains no material substance.
Therefore, there is no ear; because there is no ear, there is no sound.
Furthermore, the causes and conditions for sound do not exist; therefore, there is no sound.
The causes and conditions for sound refer to the conjunction of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
This phenomenon of conjunction is unattainable. Why is this so?
If the essences of phenomena were distinct, there could be no conjunction; if they lacked distinct essences, how could they conjoin with themselves?
Even if they were situated in one place, they would still perish moment by moment; therefore, they cannot be combined.
Chapter 149: Refutation of Odor, Flavor, and Tangibility. Odor cannot be apprehended.

Why is this? Because the nose-consciousness cannot distinguish whether this is the fragrance of a campaka flower or other various fragrances, and the mental consciousness cannot smell the fragrance; therefore, the mental consciousness likewise cannot distinguish whether this is the fragrance of a campaka flower.
Question:
Although one cannot distinguish that this is the scent of *campaka*, one can nevertheless apprehend the scent. Answer:
It is not so. Just as when a person does not encounter a *campaka* tree, they may, due to delusion, give rise to the notion that it is a *campaka* tree;
likewise, when one does not perceive the substance of fragrance, one may, due to delusion, give rise to the notion of fragrance.
Furthermore, as previously stated, whether the fragrance reaches [the sense organ] or does not reach it before being perceived, both positions entail faults; therefore, fragrance does not exist.
Taste is likewise. Tangible objects are also non-existent.
Why is this so? Even within the constituent parts of atoms, tactile cognition does not arise, as previously explained; therefore, there is no touch.
Chapter 150: Refutation of Mental Consciousness. Mental consciousness, too, cannot apprehend dharmas.
Why is this? The mental consciousness cannot apprehend present form, odor, taste, or tangible objects.
As has been stated previously, those that are past or future do not exist; therefore, the mental consciousness does not apprehend form and the other [objects].
Question:
If the mental consciousness does not know dharmas such as form, it should know its own self-nature. Answer:
Dharma does not know itself. Why is this?
It cannot know itself in the present, just as a sword cannot cut itself.
Because past and future phenomena do not exist, there is likewise no other mind; therefore, the mental consciousness cannot know itself.
Question:
When a person knows another's mind, then the mental consciousness is able to know that mental factor (citta-dharma).
Answer: Just as the mind does not know itself, yet one also forms this thought, saying:
"I have a mind."
The same applies to the minds of others.

Furthermore, if one could know another's mind even when future dharmas do not exist, what fault would there be in such a case? Moreover, if the mind were able to take dharmas as its object, many errors would follow;

for instance, it would imply that the mind travels to the object, or that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) perceives objects it has not reached, and thus one should not be able to recollect forms and other such things.
Because of this fault, the mental consciousness does not cognize dharmas.
Chapter 151: Refuting Cause and Effect. Those who propound non-existence say:
"If there is a fruit, it must either arise from a quality (*guṇa*) that already existed within the cause, or it must arise from a quality that did not previously exist; both positions entail faults."

Just as there is no sound within the two hands beforehand yet sound can arise from them, just as there is no wine within the ingredients of wine beforehand yet wine can be produced from them, and just as there is no chariot within the parts of a chariot beforehand yet a chariot can be completed from them, it follows that the effect is not produced from qualities (*guṇa*) that already existed within the cause.
If you claim that a quality (guṇa) arises as an effect from a cause in which it previously did not exist, then, just as the subtle atoms of formless wind should be able to produce form,
so too would wind possess form, and diamonds and the like should likewise possess fragrance.

Furthermore, we observe that white threads produce white cloth, while black threads produce black cloth. If the qualities (*guṇa*) were not already present within the cause but were produced in the effect, why would white threads be able to produce only white and never black?
Therefore, it is not the case that a quality (*guṇa*) which previously did not exist within the cause comes to fruition.
This reasoning is exhausted by these two [positions], both of which possess faults; thus, there is no effect (*phala*).
Furthermore, if the effect were already present within the cause, it should not arise again; if it already exists, how could it arise?
If it does not exist, it should not arise either; how can that which is non-existent arise?
[The opponent] asks:
We see with our own eyes the making of a jar; how can there be no result?
Answer: If this jar did not exist beforehand, how could it be made?
Because it would be non-existent.
If it has already been made, how can it be made?
Because it already exists.
He asks:
"The time of acting is called 'acting.
He replied:
"There is no such thing as the time of acting."
Why is this so? Because all that has been performed falls within the category of the "performed," while that which has not yet been performed falls within the category of the "unperformed";

therefore, there is no time of "acting. Furthermore, if a jar were to have an act of production, it would have to be either past, future, or present. It cannot be produced in the past, because what was not produced has already perished. It cannot be produced in the future, because what has not yet come into being does not exist. It cannot be produced in the present, because that which exists is already present.
Because there is an agent, there is the accomplishment of an action; yet within this, an agent cannot be found as a reality. Why is this so?
Because the parts of the body, such as the head and so forth, have no role in the act of acting, they are not the agent; and since there is no agent, the action itself also does not exist.
Furthermore, regarding the cause in relation to the effect—whether it be prior, posterior, or simultaneous—it is in all cases untenable.
Why is this so? If the cause were prior and the effect posterior, the cause would have already ceased; by what, then, could the effect be produced?
If there were no father, how could a son be born?
If the cause comes after the effect, the cause itself has not yet arisen; how then could it produce the effect?
It is like a father who has not yet been born—how could he be able to beget a son?
If cause and effect were simultaneous, this principle would not hold; it would be like two horns emerging together, such that one cannot say the left is caused by the right.
Since these three logical possibilities are ultimately untenable, there is no effect.
Furthermore, regarding this cause and effect, whether they are identical or different, both positions entail faults. Why is this so?
If they were different, then the cloth would exist independently of the threads.
If they were one, then there would be no distinction between a single thread and a bundle of them.
Furthermore, in the world, it is never observed that there is a phenomenon where cause and effect are not distinct.
Moreover, if there were such an effect, it would have to be produced by itself, produced by another, produced by both, or produced without a cause.
None of these are tenable. Why is this so?
There is no dharma that can produce its own self-nature.
If it already possesses a self-nature, what need is there for it to produce itself? If it lacks a self-nature, how could it produce itself?
Furthermore, since no dharma is seen that can produce its own self-nature, it is not self-made.
Nor is it made by another. Why is this so?
The eye and visible forms have no agency in the arising of consciousness; therefore, they are not created by another.
Furthermore, because they lack the characteristic of agency, all phenomena are without a creator.
It is as when a seed does not form this thought:
I should produce the sprout.
Nor do the eye and forms form this thought:
"We should together produce consciousness."
Therefore, all phenomena lack the notion of an agent.
Nor is it the case that they are produced by a collective agent, for that would entail the fallacies of both self-causation and other-causation.
Furthermore, it is not the case that they are produced without a cause; if there were no cause, there could be no designation of an effect.
If all four types are non-existent, how can there be a fruit?
If it exists, it should be explained.
Furthermore, this fruit must be either produced by a prior conscious mind or produced by a prior unconscious mind.
If it were produced by a prior conscious mind, who would possess the conscious mind to produce the eyes and other bodily parts of the infant within the womb?
Even Īśvara and others could not produce them.
As has already been stated, karma itself is also devoid of consciousness in its production.
Since this karma exists in the past, how could there be a mind that performs it?
Therefore, karma itself is also without mind.
If there was no prior mental action, how could one who causes suffering to others receive suffering, or one who causes happiness to others receive happiness?
Even while performing manifest actions, one discriminates with the mind, thinking, "It should be done in this way; it should not be done in that way.
If there were no mental activity, how could such distinctions exist?
Therefore, the prior existence of mind or the absence of mind are both untenable.
Since all such faculties and objects are unapprehendable, there is no dharma.
Chapter 152: On Conventional Truth (Saṃvṛti-satya). Response:
Although you employ various causes and conditions to argue that all dharmas are empty, this interpretation is not correct.
Why is this? I have previously stated that if all things were non-existent, then this treatise would also not exist, nor would it be among all dharmas.
You have failed to respond to such refutations of emptiness, yet you still maintain that emptiness exists; therefore, it is not the case that all dharmas are non-existent.
Furthermore, as for what you have said regarding the absence of faculties (*indriya*) and the absence of objects (*ālambana*), this matter is not something we elucidate. Why is that?

Because within the Buddha’s sūtras, these matters are themselves excluded; namely, five things are inconceivable: worldly matters, matters concerning sentient beings, matters concerning the causes and conditions of karma, matters concerning those engaged in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and matters concerning the Buddhas.
This matter cannot be deliberated upon or decided by anyone who is not an omniscient one; only the Buddhas possess the wisdom that can discern all phenomena.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess only the wisdom that penetrates Nirvāṇa, and within the wisdom that discerns all phenomena, they obtain but a small portion.
The Buddhas are able to penetrate all phenomena in every respect—their origins and ends, their essential natures, their general characteristics, and their specific characteristics.

Just as a person’s house or other possessions are easy to destroy but difficult to construct, so too is the wisdom of emptiness easy to attain, whereas the wisdom that correctly discerns all phenomena is difficult to give rise to.
Question:
One should speak of the characteristics of all dharmas as they were attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment, just as the Buddha has taught them.
Answer: [As follows:]
Although the Buddha has taught all phenomena (*dharma*), he has not taught them in every particular aspect, because such detail does not conduce to liberation.

For example, when the Buddha says that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, he does not specify the individual causes and conditions for each one; he teaches only those essential factors capable of extinguishing suffering.

The various colors such as those of painted images, the various sounds such as those of music, and the infinite distinctions of odors, tastes, and tangibles cannot be fully described; yet even if they were described, there would be no great benefit. Therefore, the Buddha did not speak of such matters, but one must not say that they do not exist.
Furthermore, it is like a person who, not knowing the methods for distinguishing and painting colors and patterns, declares them to be non-existent.
You are just like this: you declare something to be non-existent simply because you are unable to establish it.
This matter exists for the wise, yet is considered non-existent by those who do not know it. It is like one born blind saying that black and white do not exist because he does not see them;
one cannot claim that colors do not exist simply because they are not seen. Likewise, if one cannot establish things through their own conditions, one may as well say that all phenomena do not exist.

Furthermore, we place our trust in the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who possess all-knowledge; for the Buddha has taught that there are five aggregates (*skandha*). Therefore, we know that all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) exist, just as jars and other objects exist by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
*Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven;

Composed by Harivarman.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 153: On the Cessation of the Mind of Dharma. Question:
You previously stated that the cessation of the three minds is called the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
Having already understood the causes and conditions for the cessation of the mind that conceives of conventional designations, what now is the "dharma-mind," and how should it be ceased?
The answer is:
the mind that perceives the five aggregates as real is called the dharma-mind.
By skillfully cultivating the wisdom of emptiness, one perceives the five aggregates as empty, and the conceptual mind regarding phenomena then ceases.
A question is asked:

When a practitioner contemplates the emptiness of the five aggregates, they mean that within the five aggregates there are no phenomena that are permanent, fixed, indestructible, unchanging, or characterized by a self or what belongs to a self.
Because these dharmas do not exist, they are said to be empty; it is not that one does not perceive the five aggregates.
The answer is:
the practitioner likewise does not perceive the five aggregates.

Why is this? Because the practitioner severs the mind that takes conditioned phenomena as its object and attains the mind that takes the unconditioned as its object; therefore, the practitioner does not perceive the five aggregates, but perceives only the cessation of the aggregates.
Furthermore, if one perceives the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they cannot be called empty; because the aggregates are not empty, such wisdom of emptiness is not complete.
Question: When a practitioner perceives form (*rūpa*), it is empty because it is without self (*anātman*), as stated in the Sūtras:
The practitioner sees that this form is empty, and so on, up to seeing that this consciousness is empty.
One should know that it is not that the aggregates, such as form and the rest, do not exist.
The answer says:
There is such a statement, yet it is not yet pure.
As stated in the *Dharmamudrā-sūtra*:

"When a practitioner perceives the marks of impermanence, decay, ruin, and falsity in form and so forth, and feels weary detachment toward them, this is also called emptiness, but it is not yet pure."
This person later perceives the cessation of the five aggregates; because this contemplation is pure, one knows that they perceive the cessation of all aggregates.
Question:
Why is it that knowledge conditioned by existence cannot attain purity?
Answer:

At times, the practitioner gives rise to the marks of the five aggregates; therefore, the mind that relies on conventional designations arises again, and for this reason, the mind conditioned by the conditioned cannot attain purity.

If one realizes the cessation of the aggregates, then the five aggregates no longer manifest; because the causes and conditions for conventional designations have ceased, the conceptualization of conventional designations no longer follows after them.
It is like a tree that has been cut down, felled, burned, and reduced entirely to ashes and charcoal; once the perception of the tree has ceased, it no longer persists. This matter is likewise.
Furthermore, the Buddha said to Rādha:
"You must shatter, break apart, and destroy the notion of a sentient being so that it no longer manifests."
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"Rādha, you must shatter, break apart, and disintegrate form, up to and including consciousness, so that they no longer appear.

Thus we know that if one dismantles the sentient being, it is called the emptiness of the provisional designation (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*); if one dismantles form, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of contemplation: the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).
Regarding the contemplation of emptiness: one does not perceive a nominally designated sentient being.
Just as a person sees that a jar is empty because it lacks water, so too one sees that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are empty because they lack a person (*pudgala*).
If one does not perceive phenomena, this is called "non-self.
Furthermore, it is said in a sutra:
"One who attains the wisdom of non-self is rightly liberated."

Therefore, one knows that the nature of form ceases, and the natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cease; this is called "non-self," and non-self is precisely the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Question:
If "non-self" is defined by the absence of intrinsic nature, do the five aggregates not truly exist?
