the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses are only knowledge and not views.
The answer is:
Why are the various patiences (kṣānti) not considered knowledges (jñāna)? Question:
Because one desires to know what is as yet unknown, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya).

If the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) were knowledge (*jñāna*), then once that patience had known [the truth], the subsequent knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) should be called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*) rather than the faculty of "not yet having known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). Therefore, patience is not knowledge.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:

"If a practitioner is able to contemplate these various phenomena even slightly with wisdom, that which is called 'patience' (kṣānti) has not yet reached completion; that which has reached completion is called 'knowledge' (jñāna).

If patience is defined as contemplation that has not yet reached completion, and since initial untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā) that first perceives is called patience, one should not consider this initial perception to be knowledge."
Furthermore, at the time of patience (*kṣānti*), one does not have full comprehension, whereas at the time of knowledge (*jñāna*), there is decisive comprehension.
Moreover, when patience arises, doubt still persists; therefore, patience is not knowledge.
The answer is as follows:
Patience is itself wisdom.
Why is this so? Because desire, delight, and patience are all one and the same meaning.
The practitioner first understands suffering and only thereafter endures it with equanimity;
if they did not first understand it, what would there be to endure with equanimity?

Furthermore, within this brief discourse, only contemplative endurance (*kṣānti*) is mentioned and not wisdom (*jñāna*); if that were so, then those who receive the fruit of practice would be devoid of wisdom.
If you intend that the practitioner possesses wisdom which is termed "patience" (kṣānti), then one must also accept that patience is itself wisdom.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"When the practitioner knows the time and sees the time, he immediately attains the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya)."
Furthermore, it is said that "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "vision" (*darśana*) have the same meaning.
Moreover, the Buddha spoke of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, cessation, and the path, but did not speak of "patience" (*kṣānti*).
Therefore, one should know that wisdom (*jñāna*) is itself patience (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, within the Buddha’s exposition on the meaning of wisdom, it is said:
"Because one knows things as they truly are, it is called wisdom."
Since patience (*kṣānti*) is also known as it truly is, there should be no difference [between them].

If you claim that it is called "patience" because it is not yet knowledge (*jñāna*), this is not the case; we do not say that patience comes first and knowledge follows later, but rather that within a single moment of mind, it is designated as both patience and knowledge.
This argument is not established; how can you establish [your point] with something that is unestablished?

You say that the term "patience" (*kṣānti*) has not yet been completed, but I have already answered this: namely, that one first knows and subsequently practices patience; thus, one should know that patience itself constitutes completion.
If one does not know [the object] thoroughly, how can one practice patience?
You say that patience is practiced before full understanding; yet in your own doctrine, it is through patience that fetters are severed. If there is no such understanding, how can fetters be severed?

You say that when patience (*kṣānti*) arises, doubt (*vicikitsā*) still persists; if that were so, then within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), doubt would accompany all [moments], and thus the wisdom (*jñāna*) arising therein would all necessarily fail to be wisdom.

Furthermore, there is no such distinction as "this is patience" and "this is wisdom. Just as in the mundane world, observing in accordance with the Four Noble Truths is called both patience and wisdom, so too should it be for untainted patience and wisdom.
Question: It is asked, "The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are merely knowledge (*jñāna*), not vision (*darśana*). Answer:
What is the reason for this?
It is asked:
Since the Sūtras distinguish between right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) and right knowledge (samyagjñāna), knowledge is not view.
Answer: If that were so, then right view would not be called right knowledge.
If you claim that right view is right knowledge, then right knowledge should likewise be right view.

Furthermore, regarding the fivefold Dharma-body, liberation-knowledge-and-vision (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) is separately taught from within the category of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*); it should therefore not be wisdom. If that were so, then the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) would likewise not be wisdom.

Now, right view is designated as "right knowledge" because it possesses distinct characteristics; that is to say, it arises within the mind of an Arhat who has exhausted all afflictions, and for this reason it is called right knowledge.
Question:
If right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) were identical to right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), then an Arhat would not be said to have achieved the ten factors. Answer:
The substance is one while the names differ, as in the case of *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena) and *duḥkhajñāna* (knowledge of suffering).
Furthermore, it is said:
"An Arhat is called one who has accomplished the field of merit endowed with the eight qualities."
Therefore, right knowledge is itself right view.

Furthermore, among the six points of concordant respect (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*), the sixth is called "concordance in view. If it were as you say, then the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising would not be called concordance.

Furthermore, it is called right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) because it is correct observation; since the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) are also correct observations, they too are called right view. Question:
Is the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses merely knowledge (jñāna) and not view?
Answer: For what reason is it not "view"? Question:
The five consciousnesses are all devoid of discrimination; because they first encounter their objects, they are termed "seeing," while mental application and investigation are termed "viewing.
Furthermore, since the five consciousnesses only take the present as their object, they do not constitute "viewing."
Answer: Because there is no vitarka or vicāra therein, it cannot perform discrimination.
If you say that it is not "seeing" because it initially rests upon an object, this is not the case.

Why is this so? Because in your view, visual consciousness has a continuous causal condition, just like mental consciousness; therefore, one should not say that it first arises in dependence upon an object.
If that were the case, then mental consciousness would likewise not possess the capacity for seeing.

Furthermore, your claim that it is not "vision" because it takes the present as its object is also incorrect; since the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) also takes the present as its object, it too would have to be non-vision.

Within the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), there is no true knowledge, as they lack mental formations (*saṃskāra*) and always follow conventional designations (*prajñapti*); thus, vision, wisdom (*prajñā*), and all such qualities are entirely absent—how much more so is mere vision?
Question: Some say that the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya) is called "seeing. How is this so?

Answer: The visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is not seeing; it is the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) that is able to take an object. However, in accordance with conventional discourse, it is said that "the eye sees. Question:
Some say there are eight types of views (*dṛṣṭi*): namely, the five false views, mundane right view, the view of one in training (*śaikṣa*), and the view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Apart from these eight views, other forms of wisdom (*prajñā*) are not designated as "views."
What does this mean?
The answer is:
seeing, knowing, attaining understanding, and direct realization are all one and the same meaning.
If one says, "This is seeing" or "This is not seeing," all such statements are spoken from one's own recollections, conceptions, and discriminations.
A question is asked:
The sutras state that the knower and the seer attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
What is the distinction between them?
The answer is:
if wisdom first breaks through conventional designations, it is called "knowledge" (jñāna); once one has entered the stage of the Dharma-position (dharmāvasthā), it is called "vision" (darśana).
Initial observation is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*); thorough comprehension is called "vision" (*darśana*).
Thus, there are distinctions among these dharmas regarding their depth and shallowness.

Chapter 194: The Chapter on the Threefold Wisdom. The threefold wisdom consists of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
That which arises from the twelve divisions of the scriptures, such as the Sūtras, is called "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Because this can give rise to the untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-ārya-prajñā*), it is termed "wisdom."
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The bhikṣu Rāhula is now able to achieve the wisdom of liberation.
Although he has heard worldly scriptures such as the Vedas, because these cannot give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), they are not called the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*).
If one is able to contemplate the meaning within the various sūtras, this is called "wisdom born of reflection" (cintāmayī-prajñā). As it is said:
"The practitioner hears the Dharma and contemplates its underlying significance.
It is further stated:
After the practitioner has heard the Dharma and contemplated its meaning, they should practice in accordance with it.
If they are able to know and see this directly before them, this is called the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). As it is said:
"The practitioner, within a concentrated mind, perceives the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates."
As it is said in various sūtras:
"O bhikṣus, by practicing meditative concentration, you shall attain direct knowledge and vision according to reality.
Furthermore, the *Saptasamyagjñāna-sūtra* states:

If a bhikṣu knows the names of the dharmas, this is called wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); if he knows their meanings, this is called wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);

and if he knows the proper timing and so forth, this is called wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, as in the case of Rāhula: his recitation of the section on the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) and so forth is called wisdom derived from hearing; his solitary contemplation of their meaning is called wisdom derived from reflection; and his subsequent attainment of the Path is called wisdom derived from cultivation.
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras that there are three kinds of weapons: the weapon of hearing, the weapon of detachment, and the weapon of wisdom.

The weapon of hearing refers to the wisdom derived from hearing; the weapon of detachment refers to the wisdom derived from reflection; and the weapon of wisdom refers to the wisdom derived from cultivation.

Furthermore, the Sūtras speak of five benefits of hearing the Dharma: hearing what has not been heard before; clarifying what has already been heard; severing doubt; attaining right view; and penetrating the profound meaning and intent through wisdom.

To hear what has not been heard before, and to clarify what has already been heard, is called the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). To sever doubt and attain right view is called the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). To penetrate through with wisdom is called the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Furthermore, it is said within the benefits of hearing the Dharma: when a practitioner listens to the Dharma with the ears and recites and studies it with the mouth, this is called the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā); when one reflects upon it with the mind, this is called the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā); and when one penetrates it through direct vision, this is called the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).

Furthermore, among the four factors of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-aṅga*): hearing the true Dharma is called the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); correct mindfulness is called the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and practicing in accordance with the Dharma is called the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

Moreover, among the five gates of liberation: hearing the Dharma from one’s honored teacher is called the wisdom of hearing; penetrating the meaning of the words is called the wisdom of reflection; and the arising of joy and so forth is called the wisdom of cultivation.
Furthermore, it is said in a sutra:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha is excellent in its three periods [of time], and so forth.

Good son, whether old or young, upon hearing the Dharma one gives rise to this thought: "The household life is tumultuous, while the life of renunciation is tranquil. If I do not renounce the world, I will be unable to purely cultivate wholesome dharmas. Thereupon, one abandons all relatives and wealth, renounces the world, upholds the precepts, guards the sense faculties, conducts oneself with careful deliberation in deportment, dwells alone in contemplation, distances oneself from the five hindrances, and attains the first dhyāna and so forth, until the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

In this context, when those of all ages hear the Dharma, it is called the wisdom of hearing; reflecting that household life is tumultuous while the life of renunciation is tranquil is called the wisdom of reflection; and distancing oneself from the five hindrances up until the exhaustion of the outflows is called the wisdom of cultivation.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras:
"Right view arises from two causes and conditions: hearing the Dharma from others and correct recollection within oneself.

Hearing the Dharma from others is called the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); correct recollection within oneself is called the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); that which can give rise to right view is called the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Furthermore, a verse states:
"One should associate with virtuous persons, listen to and receive the true Dharma, delight in solitude, and subdue the mind.

Among these, associating with virtuous persons and listening to and receiving the true Dharma are called the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); delighting in solitude is called the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and subduing the mind is called the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Furthermore, the Buddha instructed the bhikṣus:
"When you speak, you should speak of the Four Noble Truths; when you reflect, you should reflect upon the Four Noble Truths.

Within this, speaking of the names of the Four Noble Truths is called the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā); reflecting upon the Four Noble Truths is called the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā); and realizing the Four Noble Truths is called the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā)."
In various sūtras such as these, the Buddha has spoken of the three types of wisdom. Question:
Of these three types of wisdom, how many belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how many to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and how many to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Answer: All those of the desire realm and the form realm.
For example, when the householder Hastaka was born in the Atapa Heaven, he preached the Dharma there.
If a person teaches the Dharma, they must necessarily contemplate its meaning; therefore, we know that the realm of form (rūpadhātu) also possesses wisdom derived from reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā).
Within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is only wisdom derived from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā). Question:
Some say that in the desire realm there is no wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), and in the form realm there is no wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). How is this so?
The answer is:
For what reason is there no wisdom cultivated through meditation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) in the desire realm? Question:
Because the path of the desire realm cannot sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), obstruct the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), and prevent the envelopments of the desire realm from manifesting.
Answer:

Within the Buddha-dharma, there is no such statement; for the path of the desire realm cannot sever the various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) or the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), nor can it prevent the entanglements of the desire realm from manifesting.
Furthermore, it is said that the path of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is able to destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why? Because within the desire realm there exist practices such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The thorough cultivation of the contemplation of impurity can destroy lust; the same applies to loving-kindness and the others.
Question:
Question: These practices such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) cannot permanently sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). Answer:
Contemplations such as the contemplation of impurity in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) likewise cannot ultimately sever all afflictions.
Question: It is by means of practices such as the coarse, the heavy, and the disagreeable that afflictions are severed, not by means of [practices] such as the impure. Answer:
There is no sūtra that states that the coarse [meditation] and so forth can sever the afflictions while the impure [contemplation] and so forth cannot;
rather, the sūtras state that one severs the afflictions by means of the impure [contemplation] and so forth.
Furthermore, what power do the "coarse" and other such modes of contemplation possess that enables them to sever the afflictions, while the "impure" and others cannot?
Moreover, if the modes of contemplation such as the "coarse" exist within the desire realm, then one should be able to sever all afflictions by means of these very modes.
If they do not exist, you should state the reason: why is it that while impurity and so forth exist, coarseness and so forth do not?
If they do exist, yet one does not abandon the afflictions, then even though they exist in the form realm, they likewise should not be able to bring about such abandonment.
This too should be explained by means of causes and conditions: why is it that [beings] in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) cannot [attain this], while those in the form realm (rūpadhātu) can? Question:

Although the desire realm possesses coarseness and so forth, one cannot sever the various afflictions (kleśa) therein because it is a realm of distraction; for one whose mind is distracted is incapable of severing anything.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"A concentrated mind is the Path; a distracted mind is not the Path.
The answer is:
One should explain the causal conditions: for what reason is the desire realm called the "realm of distraction"?

Since it contains practices such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), if it were a realm of distraction, how could one contemplate the various distinct characteristics of skeletons and so forth?
Furthermore, what distinct characteristics does the concentrated mind encompassed by the form realm (rūpadhātu) possess that the desire realm lacks?
Question:
Because the path of the form realm can achieve detachment from desire, one dies here and is reborn within the form realm, like a wedge driving out another wedge.
Answer: What is called "detachment from desire"? Question:

The severance of afflictions is called "detachment from desire" (*vairāgya*); this is because it is through the path of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that one can sever afflictions, not through the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The answer is:

although various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) sever their fetters (*saṃyojana*), they arise again and are reborn in the desire realm; therefore, such ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are not said to have severed their fetters.
If that which has already been severed were to arise again, then the untainted severance of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) would also have to arise again; this is impossible.
Furthermore, it is stated in the Sūtra:
"Having severed the three fetters, one is able to sever the three poisons."
Ordinary persons cannot sever the three fetters; therefore, they are unable to attain freedom from desire.
Furthermore, because ordinary persons constantly harbor the notion of a self and so forth, they are incapable of severing the view of a self-identity and other such afflictions.
If an ordinary person were able to abandon desire, no afflictions whatsoever should exist.
Why is this? Because all afflictions are produced through a multitude of conditions.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The self is established from various conditions.

If this ordinary person does not give rise to the view of a body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) regarding the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and has furthermore not yet attained the aggregates of the higher realms, then there should be no view of a body; [yet, such a view does exist].
If this were the case, such afflictions (*kleśa*) would have been eternally exhausted, and this ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would be an Arhat.
Yet, in reality, one does not attain the total exhaustion of afflictions; as it is said in the Sūtra:
"When the sound of a great thunderclap is heard, two persons do not fear: the Cakravartin King and the Arhat."
Now, this ordinary person should likewise not be afraid.

Furthermore, an Arhat does not rejoice in birth nor loathe death; just as when the Arhat Upasena was bitten by a venomous snake and was about to die, his faculties remained unchanged and his complexion did not alter—this person should also be like that.
Furthermore, the eight worldly dharmas cannot obscure the mind of an Arhat; this person should likewise be so because they have abandoned desire.
Yet, in reality, although ordinary persons claim to have abandoned desire, none of them possess these characteristics; thus we know that they have not severed their afflictions.
Question:
Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) and, upon the end of life in this realm, are reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
If they do not sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), how can they be born there?
The Sūtras also state that there are non-Buddhist practitioners who have attained freedom from desire;
furthermore, they state that the Arhats Kālāma and Udraka Rāmaputra, having abandoned desire for the realm of form, were reborn in the formless realm.

Furthermore, it is taught that one becomes free from desire through the realm of form (*rūpa*), free from desire through the formless realm (*ārūpya*), and that one eliminates the arising of thoughts through cessation (*nirodha*).
Therefore, your claim that although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) sever afflictions (*kleśa*), these are not called "severed" because they arise again, is incorrect.

You also state that whatever is severed by ordinary persons is in reality merely a negation; it is only nominally called "severance" or "detachment. In truth, it is not severed, yet it is called "severed"; in truth, there is no detachment from desire, yet it is called "detachment from desire."
As it is said in a verse:
"If one clings to 'I' and 'mine,' death will surely sever them.
When children play with sand, they cherish and protect it according to their attachment; yet when their hearts grow weary and detached, they immediately destroy it and abandon it."
This is also called "freedom from desire.
However, the cessation [of defilements] achieved by non-Buddhists differs from cessation through death; cessation through death does not lead to rebirth in the realms of form or formlessness.
Just as a child who abandons soil receives no great reward even if it is honored, one who honors a non-Buddhist who has attained freedom from desire obtains a great reward.
Although the terminology is the same, its meaning differs; therefore, we know that ordinary beings truly possess the severance and detachment [of afflictions].
The answer is:
there is a distinction within the negation.
If one can deeply obstruct the afflictions, then one will be born in the realms of form or formlessness.
Furthermore, as for the obstruction of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), this has already been explained previously.
If one cannot obstruct the view of a self-identity within the desire realm, how could one be born in the realms of form or formlessness?

It is only because greed and hatred are suppressed that one is born in the form realm, not because views such as the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) are suppressed; therefore, we know that ordinary persons do not actually sever their fetters.
Furthermore, since wholesome dharmas of the desire realm can also suppress afflictions, we know that the desire realm also possesses cultivated wisdom (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).
Furthermore, it is stated in the Sūtras that one may attain the Path even by excluding the seven stages of meditative reliance (*niśraya*). Therefore,
we know that true wisdom can arise based on the dhyāna of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Question:
This person attains the path of Arhatship by relying on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna, not upon the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*). Answer:
Not so. To say that the seven supports are excluded implies that the first dhyāna and its preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) are already excluded.
Furthermore, there is no cause or condition herein for anything to rely upon the preparatory stage, as it is not a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
If this practitioner is able to enter the "near-ground" (sāmantaka), why is it that they cannot enter the first dhyāna?
There is likewise no causal reason for this.
Furthermore, the *Susīma Sūtra* states:
First comes the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*), and afterwards the knowledge of *nirvāṇa*.

This principle does not necessarily require that one first attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and only thereafter reach the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*); rather, it is simply necessary that the knowledge of the stability of phenomena precedes the exhaustion of outflows. Therefore, we know that [the attainment of] various meditative concentrations is excluded [as a prerequisite].
Because it excludes dhyāna-concentration, the *Suśīma Sūtra* was taught.
If one were to receive the "near-ground" (*sāmantaka*), it would be identical to the faults of the various dhyānas.
Furthermore, there is no mention of the term "near-ground" in any sūtra; this is merely your own conceptual construction and discrimination.
Question: I have previously explained the analogy of the wedge; therefore, we know that one can sever the fetters of a different stage by means of a path belonging to another stage.
Just as a fine wedge can extract a coarse wedge, so too can the path of the form realm sever the fetters of the desire realm.

If a practitioner first abandons sensual desire and unwholesome states, and is subsequently able to enter the first dhyāna, one knows that there must necessarily be a "near-ground" (sāmantaka) by means of which desire is abandoned.
Furthermore, it is said that one emerges from desire by means of form (*rūpa*). If there were no "near-ground" (*upabhūmi*), how could one emerge by means of form?
Moreover, a sutra states:

"If a practitioner attains pure joy (*śuddha-prīti*), he is then able to abandon impure joy (*aśuddha-prīti*); just as Nanda was able to abandon his original desire through his attachment to a celestial maiden."
Furthermore, if one does not attain the flavor of the tranquility of the first dhyāna, one cannot give rise to a sense of coarseness and defectiveness toward the five desires.
Thus, we know that by first attaining the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna, one is able to relinquish the desire realm.
Answer: One attains the pure wholesome states of the desire realm that are capable of severing unwholesome states, as described in the teaching on the five natures of emergence.
If a noble disciple should contemplate the five desires, they do not give rise to joy or pleasure, and their mind does not become at ease, just like burning sinew or feathers.
If one contemplates the dharma of emergence, the mind becomes unobstructed and expansive.
Furthermore, it is said:

when a practitioner gives rise to unwholesome thoughts and observations, they should extinguish them with wholesome thoughts and observations; therefore, the analogy of the wedge you mentioned can also apply to the desire realm.

As for your statement that the detachment from form (*rūpa*) is the final stage: a practitioner severs all afflictions through the path of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), severing them gradually in succession until they are able to attain the wholesome dharmas of the form realm. At that time, what is called the "complete severance" of the desire realm occurs, and the dharmas of the form realm are attained.
You are an Arhat who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and has also attained all other concentrations; however, you have spoken only of their flavor (āsvāda).
Your statement that you have attained the flavor of pure, sublime joy and tranquility has already been answered in its entirety.
Furthermore, if there is no meditative concentration (samādhi) in the desire realm, how can one realize the wholesome states of the form realm with a distracted mind?
Question:
An Arhat liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) also lacks meditative concentration and possesses only wisdom.
Answer: In this context, only meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) is excluded; however, there must necessarily be a brief period of mental focus, even for a single thought-moment (ekacitta).
As the Buddha said in a sutra:
When a bhikṣu takes up a robe, the three poisons are present; once he has put it on, they are extinguished.
There is no sūtra that says true wisdom can arise within a distracted mind; all say that by collecting the mind, one gives rise to wisdom as it truly is.
Chapter 195: The Four Unhindered Knowledges (Catuḥpratisaṃvid-varga) Question:
There is a worldly wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that is proximate to the stage of the Dharma-position (*dharmāvasthā*). What is it?
Answer:

It is the wisdom within the factors such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) that is capable of breaking through conventional designations. Because this wisdom perceives the truths according to worldly convention, it is called "worldly wisdom" (*laukika-jñāna*); because it is proximate to the Noble Path, it is called "proximate to the stage of the Dharma" (*dharmāvasthā-pratyāsanna*).
Question: Is conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) cultivated in the future within the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga)?
Answer: Yes.
There is no cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) in the future; this will be explained later. Why is this?

Because within the destruction of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), there is no mind of provisional designation (*prajñapti-citta*); therefore, conventional knowledge is not cultivated within the path of seeing the truths (*darśana-mārga*).
Question:
The sūtras speak of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*);
what are they? Answer:
Unimpeded knowledge regarding names is called the unimpeded knowledge of dharmas (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).

Unimpeded knowledge regarding speech and sounds is called the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), which refers to the distinctions among the speech and sounds of various regions and different customs.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

A practitioner should not be greedily attached to the dialects of a particular land. If the spoken sounds are not convenient, the meaning is difficult to understand; yet, if there were no names, the meaning could not be clarified.
This very eloquence, which is neither obstructed nor exhausted, is called the unimpeded knowledge of elocution (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"There are four ways of preaching the Dharma: some preach with meaningful intent that cannot be exhausted; some are able to preach exhaustively but lack meaningful intent; some possess both [qualities]; and some possess neither."
These three kinds of knowledge are termed the skillful means of language and expression.
Knowledge of the meaning within names and phrases is termed the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
As it is said, there are four kinds of preaching the Dharma:

There are those who possess the skillful means of meaning but lack the skillful means of speech; those who possess the skillful means of speech but lack the skillful means of meaning; those who possess both; and those who possess neither.

If a person can attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), they are said to be fully endowed with skillful means. Such a person is difficult to challenge and difficult to approach; they are supreme among those who preach the Dharma, possessing inexhaustible eloquence, as well as infinite wisdom regarding the underlying significance and unimpeded command of language.
Question:
How is this unimpeded knowledge (anāvaraṇajñāna) to be attained? Answer:
It is obtained through the causal conditions of karma from previous lives.

If one has been able to skillfully cultivate the wisdom of causal conditions and the skillful means regarding the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth in life after life, then by the power of such cultivation, one can come to know [these matters] even in the present life without studying written texts or reciting the scriptures—just as in the case of the supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣus).
Question: Who is able to attain it? Answer:
Only sages attain it.
Furthermore, some say that only arhats attain it, and not those who are still in training (śaikṣas).
This is not necessarily so; since those in training can also attain the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), why should they be unable to attain this wisdom?
Question:
In which realm do these four unhindered knowledges (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) reside? Answer:
In the realms of desire and form, all [four analytical knowledges] are present; in the formless realm, there is only the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
Regarding these two types of unimpeded knowledge, they are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Those in training (*śaikṣa*) possess both types, while those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possess only the uncontaminated.
If one attains them, one attains them all at once.
Women also attain them, such as the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā and others. Chapter 196:

The Chapter on the Five Knowledges. There are five knowledges: knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), knowledge of nirvāṇa, knowledge of non-contention (araṇā-jñāna), knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhi-jñāna), and knowledge of the limit (prāntakoṭika-jñāna).

To know that the arising of all phenomena is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharmasthitijñāna*); for instance, from birth as a condition for old age and death, down to ignorance as a condition for volitional formations—because this nature remains eternally constant whether a Buddha appears or not—it is therefore called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena."

This knowledge of the cessation of phenomena is called the knowledge of *nirvāṇa*; it is like the cessation of old age and death due to the cessation of birth, and so on, up to the cessation of all formations (*saṃskāra*) due to the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Question: If that is so, then the knowledge of *nirvāṇa* is also called the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).
Why is this? Because whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, this nature remains eternally constant.
He replied:
The total cessation of all phenomena is called nirvāṇa; within this total cessation, what phenomenon could remain? Question:
Is nirvāṇa not a real existence?
Answer: Because the aggregates (skandhas) have ceased without remainder, it is called Nirvāṇa; what could there be within this? Question:
Nirvana truly exists.
How do we know this?
Because the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) is named Nirvana.
Since the various truths such as suffering truly exist, nirvāṇa must also truly exist.
Furthermore, the wisdom regarding nirvāṇa is called "wisdom of cessation"; if there were no phenomenon [of nirvāṇa], how could such wisdom arise?
Furthermore, in a sutra, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"There are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that arise through volitional activity (*abhisaṃskāra*), and there are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) that do not arise through volitional activity.
Moreover, it is said in another sutra:
There are only two kinds of phenomena: conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.
Conditioned phenomena possess arising, ceasing, abiding, and change; unconditioned phenomena lack arising, ceasing, abiding, and change.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:
"Of all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, the extinction of nirvāṇa alone is supreme.
It is also said:
Form is impermanent; because form is extinguished, nirvāṇa is permanent. This applies likewise to everything up to consciousness.
Furthermore, it is said in a sutra:
"The cessation [of suffering] should be realized."
If there were no phenomena (*dharma*), what would there be to realize?
Furthermore, in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"The wise one knows, as it truly is, the conditioned nature (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*) and the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*)."
The unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) is precisely nirvāṇa; since it is known through true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*), how can you say it does not exist?

Furthermore, among the various sūtras, there is no definitive teaching that nirvāṇa is a non-existent dharma; therefore, know that you yourself merely conceive of and discriminate [it] as being "no nirvāṇa."
The answer is: If there were a distinct dharma apart from the aggregates (skandhas) named nirvāṇa, then it would not be appropriate to define nirvāṇa as the total extinction of the aggregates.
Furthermore, if nirvāṇa exists, its essential nature (svabhāva) should be explained.

What is this? Furthermore, the meditative concentration (samādhi) conditioned by nirvāṇa is called "signless" (animitta). If the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) still persist, how could it be called signless?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The practitioner perceives the cessation of the characteristics of form, up to and including the cessation of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma*).

Furthermore, it is stated in various places throughout the sūtras that all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, all phenomena are selfless, and nirvāṇa is quiescent. In this context, "self" refers to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.

If not seeing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is called "seeing non-self," then if nirvāṇa were a phenomenon, it would have no intrinsic nature and could not be seen, because this phenomenon is indestructible.

Just as when a jar exists, there is no "destruction of the jar," yet when the jar is destroyed, one can say "the jar is destroyed"—and the same applies to the felling of a tree and so forth—likewise, as long as the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) still persist, at that time it is not called *nirvāṇa*;
it is only because the conditioned phenomena have ceased that the designation "*nirvāṇa*" exists.
Furthermore, the cessation of suffering is not designated as some other distinct phenomenon. As it is said in the Sūtra:

"O Bhikṣus, when this suffering ceases and no further suffering arises, such that there is no further continuity—this state is the foremost tranquility and security, namely, the relinquishment of all things, the eternal exhaustion and departure of craving of body and mind, cessation, Nirvāṇa."
In this context, when it is said that "this suffering ceases and other suffering does not arise," what further dharma could there be that is called *nirvāṇa*?

Furthermore, there is no separate dharma of extinction; rather, it is simply the cessation of craving that has already arisen and the non-arising of that which has not yet arisen—this state is called "extinction. What further dharma could there be that is designated as "extinction"?
In truth, it cannot be so described.

Furthermore, there is another designation for this dharma: the non-existence of the five aggregates is called nirvāṇa. To say that within this there is "existence" when there is actually nothing would be incorrect.
Because it is characterized by total extinction, it is called *nirvāṇa*, just as when a garment is exhausted there is no separate dharma [apart from that exhaustion].
If this were not so, there would likewise have to exist a separate dharma such as "the exhaustion of a garment."

Your statement that there is a cognition of cessation does not present any obstacle; it is like the arising of a cognition regarding the cutting of a tree, where there is no separate "dharma of cutting" apart from the act itself.

Furthermore, this cognition arises on account of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); that is to say, nirvāṇa is designated according to the non-existence of those conditioned phenomena, just as one knows a thing to be empty by virtue of the absence of that thing.
Question: Is there no nirvāṇa now? Answer:
It is not that nirvāṇa does not exist, but rather that there is no substantial dharma [within it].
If nirvāṇa did not exist, one would remain forever in saṃsāra with no time of liberation.
It is like the breaking of a jar or the cutting down of a tree; there is simply no separate, substantially existent dharma [apart from these].
Regarding the statement that the remaining truths and so forth have all been answered comprehensively: why is this?

Because there is the cessation of suffering, it is said that there exists the unconditioned dharma which is non-arising, non-origination, and non-action; thus, none of these [teachings] are undermined.
Regarding "the wisdom of non-contention" (*araṇā-jñāna*): whatever wisdom one employs that does not lead to contention with others is called "non-contention.
Some say this refers to the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*), for by means of a loving mind, one does not afflict sentient beings.
Furthermore, some say it is the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-caryā*), for by means of this practice of emptiness one does not contend with things.
Others say it is the mind that delights in *nirvāṇa*, for because one delights in *nirvāṇa*, there is nothing with which to contend.
Some say it exists in the fourth dhyāna;
this is not necessarily so. These arhats cultivate their minds with this wisdom such that they have no contention whatsoever.
Regarding "wisdom of aspiration" (praṇidhijñāna): within all phenomena, unobstructed wisdom is called the wisdom of aspiration.
Question:
If that is so, then only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, alone possesses this wisdom. Answer:
Thus, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is fully endowed with this wisdom; others attain it without obstruction according to their respective capacities.

As for "limit-reaching wisdom" (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*), it is the supreme wisdom attained by a practitioner through the cultivation and increase of all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). If one attains mastery over such matters as the extension or reduction of one's lifespan, it is called limit-reaching wisdom.

Chapter 197: The Chapter on the Knowledge of the Six Supernatural Powers (Ṣaḍabhijñājñāna). There are six types of knowledge regarding the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). The six supernatural powers are:

the power of bodily transformation (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

The supernormal power of the body (*kāyābhijñā*) refers to the practitioner’s ability to emit water and fire from the body, to fly, to appear and disappear, to touch the sun and moon, to reach the Brahma-world with mastery, and to perform various transformations; such activities are termed the supernormal power of the body.
Question: How shall this matter be accomplished? Answer:
The practitioner attains it by deeply cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
As it is said in the sūtras:
"The power of one in meditative concentration is inconceivable."
Some say that the mind of transformation (nirmāṇa-citta) is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
This is not so; if a practitioner manifests various transformations for the sake of benefiting others, why would it be called indeterminate?
Some say that one produces transformations of the desire realm with a mind of the desire realm, and produces transformations of the form realm with a mind of the form realm.
This is also not the case; the eyes and other faculties should likewise be so: can one see forms of the desire realm with a consciousness of the desire realm?
If this were so, what fault would there be in a mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) manifesting transformations in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Furthermore, some say that the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the first dhyāna can reach the Brahma-world, and those of the fourth dhyāna can reach the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

This is also not the case; it depends on the reach of one's faculties and powers. If one possesses sharp faculties, one can reach the fourth dhyāna through the supernormal power of the first dhyāna; if one possesses dull faculties, one cannot even utilize the supernormal power of the first dhyāna through the supernormal power of the second dhyāna. It is like the Great Brahmā King reaching the intermediate dhyāna, wherein no supernormal power exists.
By the power of the first dhyāna, one can reach the various other Brahmā heavens; yet, by means of that same first dhyāna, one cannot know the dwelling place of the Brahmā King.
Furthermore, the Buddha recollects the formless realms through his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), as it is said in the sūtras:
"Whether among the realms of form or the formless, the places where he was previously born, the Buddha knows them all."
Therefore, it is not fixed.
Furthermore, some say that the divine eye (divyacakṣus) is of the nature of wisdom (prajñā).
This is not so; the divine eye is accomplished through light, whereas wisdom is not like this.
Question:
The sūtras state that by cultivating the mark of light, one can achieve knowledge and vision (jñānadarśana), and that this knowledge and vision is precisely the divine eye (divyacakṣus).
Answer:
Otherwise, it is also called the "divine ear" (divya-śrotra); since it is not named "ear" by virtue of its nature as wisdom (*prajñā*), it is therefore not wisdom.
Furthermore, the divine eye takes present forms as its object, whereas the mental consciousness does not.

Regarding the explanation of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it is said therein that one knows the karmic retributions of sentient beings; however, the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) lacks this power. Rather, it is known within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it arises at the time when the visual consciousness is functioning.
To know that form arises from meditative concentration is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Question: What are the dimensions and location of the physical form of the divine eye?
He replied:
"It is the size of a young child.
He asked again:
What about the blind?
The answer is:
they are likewise limited by the locus of the eye.
He asked again:
"Is the divine eye one or two?
He replied:
"These two.
He asked again:
"Does it follow the direction one is facing?"
He replied:
"I see all directions clearly.
He asked again:
"Are there any created persons?
He replied, "No."
The creator exists;
the same applies to the discourse on the divine ear.
If a practitioner knows the minds of others, it is called the knowledge of others' minds.
Question:
For what reason is the knowledge of others' mental factors (*caitasika*) not mentioned? Answer:
For this reason, there are no separate mental factors (*caitta*); knowing the feelings, perceptions, and so forth of others is likewise called the "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*).

Furthermore, some say that this knowledge has the same nature as its object, just as one uses outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) knowledge to know the tainted, or untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge to know the untainted.
This is not the case; this person does not state a definitive causal condition, yet by means of these conditions, one knows the homogeneous condition (*sabhāga-pratyaya*).
Some say that it takes only the present as its condition.

This is also not the case; for there may be cognition of the future, such as when a person enters a state of non-perceptual concentration and knows that upon arising from this concentration, they will perceive such-and-such matters.
Some say that this wisdom does not know or see the Path of Seeing the Truths (*darśanamārga*).
This is not so; for if it were to know them, what fault would there be?
Some say that when a Pratyekabuddha wishes to know the third moment of mind within the Path of Seeing the Truths, he immediately sees the seventh moment of mind.
If a śrāvaka wishes to know the third mind, he sees the sixteenth mind.
Is this not called "knowing and seeing the path of the truths" (satyadarśanamārga)?
Furthermore, some say that this wisdom does not know the higher stages, nor those of a superior person or superior faculties.
This is also not fixed; even the devas know the Buddha’s mind.
For instance, there was once a time when the Buddha strictly excluded the assembly of monks, yet he later reflected that he wished to take them back in, and Brahmā King fully knew this.
Furthermore, at one time, he thought to himself that he would become a king and transform the world according to the Dharma; the Mara King immediately knew this and came to entreat him.
Moreover, the various devas also knew that he was an Arhat, and even that he was one practicing for the stage of Srotāpanna.

Furthermore, the bhikṣus also know the Buddha’s mind; for instance, when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Āniruddha successively knew the various dhyāna-samādhis into which the Buddha had entered.
Moreover, some people say that this knowledge does not know the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu).
This is also not the case; for the Buddha, by means of his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), is able to know the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It is the same with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); what fault is there in knowing [the formless]? Question:
How does one know the minds of others?
Answer: One knows them within the context of their objects.
If the mind operates upon form, it is called "a mind conditioned by form," and so forth. Question:
If that is the case, then the knowledge of others' minds would be conditioned by all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
Answer: It is so.
If one does not know conditions (*pratyaya*), how can one know the mind?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"I know your mind to be such and such" refers precisely to the cognition of others' minds based on form and so forth.

There are three types of such knowledge of others' minds: first, that acquired through signs; second, that obtained as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*); and third, that obtained through cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
"Known through mutual understanding" refers to knowing by means of spells such as the Aṅga-mantras.
"Obtained through retribution" refers to those such as ghosts and spirits.

"Obtained through cultivation" refers to the knowledge of others' minds attained through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*); this is explained among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*).
Regarding "attained through cultivation": if one recollects the various aggregates (*skandha*) within past lives, it is called the knowledge of past existences (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*). Question:
Which aggregates does one recollect?
Answer:

One recollects one's own aggregates (*skandha*), the aggregates of others, and the aggregates of non-sentient beings; however, while one cannot recollect the superior aggregates of a superior person, one can recollect their superior dharmas such as ethical discipline (*śīla*).
How is this known?
It is as Śāriputra replied to the World-Honored One:
"Although I do not know the minds of the Buddhas of the past and future, I am able to know their Dharma."
Furthermore, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, knowing the Buddha’s mind, came and addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is so,
World-Honored One!"
The majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) of all past Buddhas was likewise so.
Question: In the explanation of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), why are the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) mentioned?
Answer: Because recollection is clear and distinct, one speaks of "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) and "names" (nāman), such as "so-and-so" and the like.
Furthermore, because it cognizes an object, it is called a "characteristic"; "nature" (prakṛti) refers to lineage, as in saying, "This is your family; this is your nature."
Because the characteristics and nature are explained in conjunction, one’s knowledge and vision become clear and lucid.
Question: For what reason is it called "clear and lucid recollection"?
The answer is:
It is extraordinary that one can know past phenomena, which have utterly ceased and are without marks.

Some people perceive through conceptual deliberation and cannot understand clearly; they claim that the disciples of the Buddha are likewise so. For this reason, nature and characteristics are explained in conjunction.

Some individuals, through the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) or through the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmaya-prajñā*) pertaining to the path, know the past, such as how volitional formations condition consciousness (*saṃskārapratyaya-vijñāna*).
Between these two types, the wisdom of reflection is superior.

Why is this? Although such a person knows eighty thousand great kalpas, because they lack this wisdom of reflection, they give rise to false views, claiming that from this point onward is what is called birth and death, and that beyond this there is nothing more;
yet one who possesses the wisdom of reflection regarding the Path will never harbor such a thought.
Some say that this wisdom sequentially recollects the past. This is not so;
if one were to recollect sequentially moment by moment, even the events within a single kalpa would be difficult to know exhaustively, let alone those of immeasurable kalpas.
Question:
Why does the Sūtra state, "For ninety-one kalpas, I have never seen a gift that was diminished and yet lacked its reward"?
Answer:
In this context, the Buddha takes the seven Buddhas as witnesses; there are also long-lived Śuddhāvāsa deities who share the same vision as the Buddha.
Furthermore, because the Buddha has attained true wisdom, his merit is pure; since those who make offerings to him obtain blessings in both worlds, he speaks thus up to this point.
Some say that this wisdom does not know the higher stages.
This is not so, as has already been answered in the section on the supernormal powers of the upper body and so forth. Question:
If it were of the nature of recollection (*smṛti*), why would it be called wisdom (*jñāna*)?
The answer is:

while recollection arises following signs (*nimitta*), one is able to recollect that which is signless (*animitta*) in the past; therefore, one should know that this superior wisdom is designated as "recollection."

There are three types of recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa-anusmṛti*): first, that which employs the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*); second, that obtained as a result of karmic retribution (*vipākaja*); and third, that which one spontaneously recollects upon birth, which is called "attained through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-maya*).
Regarding those who obtain [recollection] as a karmic result: this refers to beings such as ghosts and spirits who, upon birth, spontaneously remember their previous existence in the human realm.
Question: By what karma is it that they spontaneously remember [their past lives] upon birth?
Answer: This karma can be attained by not harming sentient beings. Why is this?
Because one is oppressed by intense suffering at the time of death and at the time of birth, one loses mindfulness.
In this context, it is difficult not to lose it; therefore, wholesome karma is required.
Furthermore, some say that this recollection of the past extends back as far as seven lifetimes.
This matter is not fixed; there are those who, throughout successive lifetimes, have deeply cultivated the dharma of non-affliction, and are therefore able to recollect events from long ago.
That which realizes the supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is the Vajra-samādhi.

The Vajra-samādhi is the unimpeded path for the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows; it is called the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-jñāna*).
Because all outflows are extinguished by means of the Vajra-samādhi, it is termed the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānābhijñā*).
Question: The other supernormal powers (abhijñā) should also be explained as being realized by which dharmas? Answer:
It has already been stated that by deeply cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one realizes the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Furthermore, whatever is employed, both the realization itself and the object realized are termed "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*).
Some say that all noble paths (*āryamārga*) are expedient means for the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), as it is said in the Sūtra:

Whether a Buddha appears in the world, or whether a person hears the Dharma and leaves the household life to uphold the precepts, abandon the five hindrances, cultivate meditative concentration, and realize the Truths—all such practices are called the means for the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-upāya*).
Furthermore, some say that wholesome dharmas such as giving are also causes and conditions for the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). As it is said in a sutra:

"When a practitioner practices giving to assist in the perfection of the wisdom of emptiness and non-self that exhausts the outflows, this is called the supernormal knowledge of the true realization of the exhaustion of outflows."
This dharma has another name: the Vajra-samādhi. It is called "Vajra" because it can shatter all marks (lakṣaṇa).
Those who follow non-Buddhist paths merely possess the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā), for they have not attained this true wisdom (tattvajñāna).
Question:
Since the wisdom of non-self (*anātma-jñāna*) should destroy the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), how can it sever greed, hatred, and so forth?
Answer:
The wisdom of non-self can extinguish all marks; because there are no marks, all afflictions are extinguished.
Question:
Since the first wisdom of non-self can destroy all marks, what further use is there for the second wisdom and the others?
Answer: Although the various marks (lakṣaṇa) cease, they arise again; therefore, a second [moment] and so forth are required.
Question:
If, after ceasing, it were to arise again, its characteristics would be infinite; in that case, there would be no path of Arhatship.
The answer is:
it has a limit. As we see now, when milk ceases and arises again, at times the milk ceases and curd arises; this constitutes a limit, and the same applies to its characteristics.
Furthermore, it is like heating iron: when its black appearance ceases and a red appearance arises once again, that moment is called the limit (*anta*).
The various analogies, such as the *kalala* and so forth, are also like this.
Whenever all marks (*nimitta*) cease and no further marks arise, at that time one is said to have attained the path of an Arhat.
Question:
Are there no marks whatsoever for an Arhat?
Answer: If one is in a state of undetermined mind (*aniyata-citta*), at that time there are likewise the various marks such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, yet they do not give rise to faults.
If a person sees a form with the eye and, through a distorted mind and distorted discrimination, at that time the marks can give rise to faults.
Question:
What is the wisdom of emptiness and non-self? Answer:

If a practitioner does not perceive a conventionally designated sentient being within the five aggregates, and because of the emptiness of phenomena perceives the cessation of the substance of form up to the cessation of consciousness, this is called the wisdom of emptiness and non-self.
Question:

Suppose all phenomena were eternally present; even so, afflictions such as craving could still be eliminated entirely. As it is said that although all things are eternally present, one who exerts diligence can eliminate greed and craving—why, then, is there a need for the characteristic of cessation?
The answer is:
It is said in the Sūtras that one who perceives the characteristic of arising in all things knows the characteristic of cessation, and thereby attains the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

If "ultimate abandonment" is defined as abandonment through cessation, then for those practitioners who have detached from the desires of form and have suppressed and extinguished greed and anger, the Buddha spoke this verse for their sake:

Furthermore, it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty by nature and like an illusion; ordinary beings, lacking wisdom, claim they are truly existent, while those in training understand them to be deceptive and illusory, and even Arhats do not perceive them as illusions.

Therefore, it is known that whichever wisdom one employs to realize the cessation of all phenomena is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānābhijñā*).
Chapter 198: On Patience and Wisdom (*Kṣāntijñānavarga*) Question:

The Sūtras state that if a practitioner possesses the seven skillful means (*saptopāya*) and the threefold meaning of contemplation (*trividhāvalokanārtha*), they will swiftly attain the exhaustion of outflows within this Dharma.
What kind of wisdom is this?
The answer is:
the seven stages of preparation (saptavidha-prayoga) are called the wisdom derived from hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā) and the wisdom derived from reflection (cintā-mayī-prajñā).

Why is this? One whose mind is not yet concentrated performs such contemplation as follows: "This is form, the origin of form, the cessation of form, and the path leading to the cessation of form; the gratification of form, its danger, and the escape from it."
Question: If these are the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī* prajñā), why is it said that one quickly attains the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)? Answer:

Although these consist of the wisdom derived from hearing and the wisdom derived from reflection, such discernment of the five aggregates can destroy the notion of a self; therefore, it is said that one quickly attains the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
The three types of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanājñāna*) refer to contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
If one contemplates conditioned phenomena by way of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), there is no benefit.
A question is asked:

"If that is so, since impermanence and suffering were already explained during the section on 'entry' (*praveśa*), and selflessness was already explained during the section on 'emergence' (*niṣkramaṇa*), why are these three types of contemplation stated again?"
Answer: One practices and studies three types of wisdom: first, the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, and subsequently, the wisdom of cultivation.
Within the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, seven types are explained; within the wisdom of cultivation, three types are explained.

Why is this so? If one speaks of the characteristic of destruction within impermanence and suffering as "destructive impermanence," it does not refer to the impermanence of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Although it is said that desire and defilement are to be removed, it does not explain how they are removed; only later is the meaning of the three kinds of contemplation explained.
Question: What are the eight patiences? Answer:
If wisdom can break through conventional designations, this is called "patience" (kṣānti).
This patience exists within the stages of Heat (uṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma).
Question:
The practitioner also possesses patience toward the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and the precepts; why, then, are only eight mentioned?
The answer is:
they are mentioned because they are preeminent, and "preeminence" means being close to the Path.
This wisdom constitutes knowledge; therefore, it is termed "patience" (*kṣānti*).
For example, that which is the knowledge of the dharma of suffering is called the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), and so forth. Why is this so?

First one employs the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) in accordance with the Path, and subsequently attains direct knowledge (pratyakṣa-jñāna). It is like an elephant tracker who first observes the elephant's tracks and, through inferential knowledge (anumāna), knows that the elephant is therein, and later perceives it directly.
The practitioner is likewise: first, they infer, know through comparison, and contemplate nirvāṇa; subsequently, they perceive it directly through wisdom.
Therefore, it is said in the sūtra: "One who knows and one who sees is able to attain the exhaustion of outflows."
Chapter 199: The Chapter on the Nine Knowledges (Jñāna-varga). Question:

Some masters of the Abhidharma say that when an Arhat realizes the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), he attains nine conventional knowledges (saṃvṛtijñāna), namely: the wholesome and indeterminate [states] bound to the desire realm, up to the wholesome and indeterminate [states] of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is:
Not all arhats attain all the dhyānas and samādhis; how, then, could they attain the nine knowledges?
Question:
All Arhats attain meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), yet not all are able to manifest entry into it.
Answer:
If one cannot manifest entry [into it], how can it be called "attainment"?
It is just as when a person claims to know writing yet does not recognize a single character; this matter is likewise so.
Question:
If a person has become detached from desire but is not yet able to enter the first dhyāna in the present life, will such a person not be reborn there at the end of their life?
The answer is:
The sūtras state that one enters it here first, and shall subsequently be reborn there.
Now, how is it that one can be born there without entering [the meditative states] here?
A question is asked:
When one becomes free from desire, all past and future dhyānas are attained as they were originally acquired; by means of this retribution, one is born [there].
Answer: Future karma is without action and without arising; it should not receive retribution.
As for the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna) of the past, they have already arisen within the mind; if they were to grant a fruit-retribution, there would be no harm.
Furthermore, one should not obtain future karmas; if they could be obtained, then all that is future would necessarily be obtainable. By what obstruction, then, is there obtaining and non-obtaining?
Question:

If future dharmas cannot be apprehended, then a practitioner in training (śaikṣa) should not be accomplished in the eight factors, and one beyond training (aśaikṣa) should not be accomplished in the ten factors.

Why is this so? If one enters the stage of the determination for the true dharma (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the second dhyāna or others, that person will attain right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) in the future.
Furthermore, if a practitioner brings the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) to manifestation, at that time they will attain mundane right view (*laukika-samyag-dṛṣṭi*) in the future.

Furthermore, when a person attains the fruit of Arhatship by relying on the formless absorptions (ārūpya-samādhi), that person will in the future attain right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Moreover, if a person attains the Noble Path by relying on the third dhyāna or others, they will in the future attain joy (prīti).
If such dharmas as these were non-existent, they would all be absent; therefore, we know that future dharmas exist.
Furthermore, if there were no cultivation of future [dharmas], how could one ever attain the various fruits, the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and so forth?
If the practitioner is within the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the path, they fully attain all the knowledges and concentrations subsumed under the first fruit.
Were it otherwise, the fruits and so forth would have to be attained repeatedly.
Why is this so? Because all fruits ought to be attained at the very moment they manifest.
Since this is impossible, we know that there must be cultivation within the future.
Answer: Your statement that there are no constituent parts poses no contradiction. Why is this so?
I have stated that the various factors such as the precepts are attained sequentially and not all at once; therefore, there is no difficulty.

As for your statement that "the attainment [of a dharma] attains its own category," when a practitioner attains the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), all other seeds of the knowledge of suffering are likewise said to be attained. This is just as one is said to "attain human characteristics" upon attaining the seeds of a human being; yet this does not mean that one gradually attains human characteristics moment by moment. The same principle applies here.
Question:

The practitioner has already abandoned all the various knowledges, such as that of suffering, which were acquired sequentially; now, they simultaneously attain the various knowledges subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
Answer: The various untainted knowledges (anāsrava-jñāna) are not lost once they have been attained.
Question:
If that which was previously attained is not lost, then there would be no distinction between the attainment and the practice. Why is this so?
Because the one who attains the fruit would be identical to the practitioner; such would be the fault.
Answer: If there were no distinction, what fault would there be?
Just as one who has accomplished the fruit is also called a practitioner, so it is in this case as well.
Furthermore, because this person additionally attains a superior dharma, there is a distinction; therefore, there is no fault.
It is like one who has received the five precepts and subsequently attains the monastic discipline (*pravrajyā-śīla*), yet does not lose the original precepts.

Furthermore, regarding those who have attained the fruit, there is no distinction based on the path of seeing; it is like a person who, although already knowing an initial matter, is further distinguished by a superior matter.
This matter is likewise; therefore, one should know that there is no acquisition of future dharmas.
Furthermore, when a practitioner abides in the wisdom of emptiness and non-self, how at that time could they acquire worldly dharmas?
Therefore, we know that at the time one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one does not attain worldly knowledge (*lokajñāna*). Question:
These various types of worldly knowledge are acquired together with the knowledge of exhaustion and serve as the mind for an Arhat’s entering and emerging from meditative absorption.

Answer: The mental continuum of an Arhat arises such that every moment is pure; if he were to further attain the nine knowledges, then his eyes and other faculties should likewise all be further attained.
If this were not the case, it would be improper for him to attain only the nine knowledges.
Furthermore, it is said that those who cultivate [the path] in the future all lack causes and conditions. Why is this?

These [teachings] state that within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), one cultivates only the semblance-knowledge (sādṛśajñāna); whereas within the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), one cultivates both the semblance and the non-semblance.
Within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), one does not cultivate the higher stages; within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one does.
Within the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), one does not cultivate mundane wholesome states; within the other knowledges, one does.
Within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

When one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms into one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), one does not cultivate the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) within any of the paths of non-obstruction or the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

When the liberation of occasional attainment (*sāmayikī vimukti*) transforms into the indestructible liberation (*akopyā vimukti*), one does not cultivate the mundane path during the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) and eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); it is cultivated during the ninth path of liberation. Furthermore, within the subtle mind, one does not cultivate any untainted (*anāsrava*) states.
All such things as these lack causes and conditions.

Therefore, whether you now speak of the true cause, or that which should be accepted with faith, or that which is cultivated through study, when one is in the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, all the aforementioned wholesome roots are cultivated, because they are all fully augmented.

Just as when one recites and studies scriptures, they all become clear and sharp, so too, during the stages of *uṣmagata* and the others, up until the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), everything is cultivated.
If this were not the case, you should state the correct reason.

Chapter 200: The Chapter on the Ten Knowledges. The ten knowledges are: knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of the four truths (*caturāryasatyajñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
To know the phenomena of the present is called dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
As it is said in the Sūtra, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Regarding these phenomena, you see and know them thus, and you penetrate them thus; you should know that the past and the future are likewise."
One should say "knowledge of the present dharma" (*pratyutpanna-dharma-jñāna*); however, because "present" is not explicitly stated here, it is simply called "dharma-knowledge" (*dharma-jñāna*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The fool prizes the present dharma; the wise man prizes the future."
Furthermore, it is said:
"All present desires and all future desires are the net of Māra, the bond of Māra, and the fetter of Māra.
In such passages, the term "present" is used; because the term "present" is abbreviated, only "dharma-knowledge" (dharma-jñāna) is mentioned.

Knowledge of the remaining phenomena is called inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). "Remaining" refers to past and future phenomena; because they are known subsequent to the present phenomena, it is called inferential knowledge. Why is this so?
Having first known through direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*), one subsequently knows through inference (*anumānajñāna*).
Knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is termed direct knowledge; the inferential knowledge that follows and deliberates upon this *dharmajñāna* is termed subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Question:
This wisdom is untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna). How can untainted wisdom be called inferential wisdom (anvaya-jñāna)? Answer:
There is also inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) in the world. Why is this so?

Because dharma-knowledge, inferential knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin, knowledge of cessation, and knowledge of the path all possess both outflow-tainted (sāsrava) and outflow-free (anāsrava) aspects.

These various knowledges are with-outflow (*sāsrava*) while within the stages of *uṣmagata* and so forth; once they have entered the stage of the dharma-position (*dharmāvasthā*), that which is attained is called without-outflow (*anāsrava*).
Question:

Some say that knowing the formations (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm, the origin of formations, the cessation of formations, and the path leading to the cessation of formations is termed "dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*).
To know the four types of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the realm of form and the formless realm is called inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). How is this so?
The answer is:
The Sūtra states that the Buddha told Ānanda:
"One should know the past and future worlds in this same way.
There is no sūtra that says the knowledge regarding the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the form and formless realms is called "inferential knowledge" (*anumāna-jñāna*).
Furthermore, it is said in a sutra:
